sources.source_text: The verb être (to be) The verbs être (to be) and avoir (to have) are essential verbs you need to memorize. They are both irregular. Let’s start with être: je suis / I am / nous sommes / we are / tu es / you are (familiar) / vous êtes / you are / il/elle est / he/she is / ils/elles sont / they are

The verb avoir (to have) The verb avoir (to have) also has an irregular conjugation. j’ai / I have / nous avons / we have / tu as / you have / vous avez / you have / il/elle a / he/she has / ils/elles ont / they have
The -oir verbs The -oir verbs do not all follow the same conjugation pattern. We’ll start with the very useful verb savoir (to know).

Savoir means to know a fact, to know how to do something from memory or study. je sais / I know / nous savons / we know / tu sais / you know / vous savez / you know / il/elle sait / he/she knows / ils/elles savent / they know

Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, to be familiar with. In a figurative way, it means to enjoy, to experience. It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause. je connais / I know / nous connaissons / we know / tu connais / you know / vous connaissez / you know / il/elle connaît / he/she knows / ils/elles connaissent / they know
Pouvoir (can, may) expresses ability and capability. je peux / I can / nous pouvons / we can / tu peux / you can / vous pouvez / you can / il/elle peut / he/she can / ils/elles peuvent / they can

A number of other verbs ending in -oir are irregular. Let’s look at a few examples in their first-person singular and plural forms: apercevoir to see, to perceive / j’aperçois / I see, I perceive / nous apercevons / we see, we perceive / décevoir to disappoint / je déçois / I disappoint / nous décevons / we disappoint / devoir must, to have to / je dois / I must, I have to / nous devons / we must, we have to / émouvoir to move, to stir / j’émeus / I move, I stir / nous émouvons / we move, we stir / prévoir to foresee, to predict / je prévois / I foresee / nous prévoyons / we foresee / promouvoir to promote / je promeus / I promote / nous promouvons / we promote / recevoir to receive / je reçois / I receive / nous recevons / we receive / valoir to be worth / cela vaut / it is worth / nous valons / we are worth / voir to see / je vois / I see / nous voyons / we see
Falloir and pleuvoir are used only in the third-person singular. falloir / to be necessary / il faut / it is necessary / pleuvoir / to rain / il pleut / it is raining

chapters.notes: Chapter reviews être, avoir, major -oir verbs, the distinction between savoir and connaître, and the impersonal verbs falloir and pleuvoir.

Wherever you want to go, you’ll need the verb aller (to go). It is an -er irregular verb, also used in many idiomatic expressions.
Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.
Aller is also used to form the immediate future. So, to talk about what you are going to do, use aller in the present indicative followed immediately by a verb in the infinitive.
The verb venir (to come) and its derivatives, devenir (to become), prévenir (to warn, to inform), survenir (to occur), are all commonly used verbs.
The verb venir (to come) in the present tense + de, combined with a verb in the infinitive, expresses an action that has just taken place.
Another verb conjugated like venir is tenir (to hold)

sources.source_text:
Reflexive verbs
The action of a reflexive verb is, for the most part, reflected back on the subject, the action being done to oneself.
The second type of pronominal verb is called reciprocal. It describes an action two or more people perform with or for each other.
A third type of pronominal verb is called passive. With the passive pronominal verbs, the subject is not a person or an animal.
The last type of pronominal verb is called subjective. These verbs are neither reflexive nor reciprocal.

sources.source_text: The passé composé is one of the tenses colloquially used in French to talk about past events. It is built of two parts: the auxiliary or helping verb, avoir or être, + a past participle.
Most verbs in the passé composé are conjugated with avoir.
Many verbs conjugated with avoir in the passé composé have irregular past participles that you simply have to learn by heart.
Some verbs use être instead of avoir in the passé composé. It is very important to memorize the (finite) list of verbs conjugated with être.

sources.source_text: The uses of the imparfait (imperfect) are some of the most difficult aspects of French grammar to master. While the passé composé is used to talk about an action that took place on a specific occasion in the past, the imparfait plays a different role. It is used to describe a state of mind and being in the past as well as continuous, repeated, or habitual past actions.

To form the imperfect, take the nous form of the present tense and remove the -ons ending, which gives you the stem. Then add the imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) to this stem.
j’étais, tu étais, il/elle était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils/elles étaient

VOCABULAIRE les vacances (f.pl.) vacation faire un voyage to go on a trip un voyage d’agrément a pleasure trip un voyage d’affaires a business trip un pèlerinage a pilgrimage à la mer by the sea à la plage at the beach à la campagne in the country à la montagne in the mountains le paysage landscape, countryside dans le parc in the park randonner to go hiking escalader to climb une étape a stopover (car travel) explorer to explore une expédition an expedition une visite guidée a guided tour visiter to visit (a place) rendre visite à to visit (someone) accueillir to welcome un festival a festival un divertissement an entertainment, an amusement les loisirs (m.pl.) leisure time

sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: background and description

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: background and description
sources.source_text: Let’s look at the different uses of the imparfait. It is used for background and description. It describes a situation that existed in the past, a state of mind or being. Les rues étaient embouteillées. The streets were jammed. La circulation était fluide. The traffic was flowing. Il faisait trop chaud. It was too hot. Il avait faim. He was hungry. Elle ne savait pas quoi faire. She did not know what to do.

sections.title: The imparfait versus the passé composé

sources.section_title: The imparfait versus the passé composé
sources.source_text: As they express a mental or physical state of being, some verbs tend to be used more often in the imparfait than in the passé composé. Among these verbs are: être (to be), avoir (to have), penser (to think), croire (to believe), savoir (to know), espérer (to hope), sembler (to seem), paraître (to appear). However, when these verbs are used in the passé composé, they may take on a different meaning. Il semblait déprimé. He looked depressed. Tout à coup il a semblé comprendre la situation. Suddenly he seemed to understand the situation. Je savais qu’il avait raison. I knew he was right. Immédiatement, j’ai su qu’il était innocent. Immediately, I realized he was innocent.

sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action
sources.source_text: Another use of the imparfait is to express habitual, repetitive action. It describes past events that were repeated. Used to and would (meaning habitually) are translated into French by the imparfait. Autrefois, elle faisait partie de la chorale. In the past, she used to belong to the choir. Ils allaient en Inde chaque année. They used to go (would go) to India every year. Il jouait au tennis le mardi. He used to (would) play tennis on Tuesdays.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action
sources.source_text: souvent often fréquemment frequently toujours always le mardi on Tuesdays le vendredi on Fridays chaque jour every day tous les jours every day chaque semaine every week chaque mois every month chaque année every year d’ordinaire ordinarily d’habitude usually habituellement usually régulièrement regularly comme à l’accoutumée as usual autrefois formerly jadis in times past

sections.title: Uses of the imparfait: interrupted continuous action

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: interrupted continuous action
sources.source_text: The imparfait is also used to describe a continuous action that was going on in the past when another action (expressed in the passé composé) interrupted it. Elle regardait la télévision quand soudain elle a entendu un grand bruit. She was watching television when suddenly she heard a loud noise. Il faisait ses devoirs quand son frère est arrivé. He was doing his homework when his brother arrived. To express the idea that an action had been going on for a period of time before being interrupted, use the imparfait with depuis. Ils étaient à la montagne depuis une semaine quand ils ont décidé d’aller au bord de la mer. They had been in the mountains for a week when they decided to go to the seashore. Il randonnait depuis trois jours quand il a trouvé cette belle auberge. He had been hiking for three days when he found this beautiful inn.

With a si + on construction, the imparfait is used to make a suggestion or to invite someone to do something. The informal on refers to two or more people and is conjugated in the third-person singular. Si on allait en France cet été? What about going to France this summer? Si on achetait des billets? What about buying tickets? Si on allait nager dans le lac? What about going swimming in the lake? Si on allait rendre visite à Léo? What about paying a visit to Léo?

You will encounter the imparfait in other idiomatic constructions, for instance, preceded by si seulement, to express a wish or a regret. Si seulement on pouvait prendre des vacances! If only we could take a vacation! Si seulement elle était à l’heure! If only she were on time! Si seulement ils habitaient plus près! If only they lived closer! Si seulement vous saviez! If only you knew!

sections.title: Immediate past in the imparfait (venir de + infinitive)

sources.section_title: Immediate past in the imparfait (venir de + infinitive)
sources.source_text: In Chapter 4, you studied the immediate past with the verb venir + de + infinitive. The immediate past can also be used in the imparfait to describe an action that had just happened. Elle vient de téléphoner. She has just called. Elle venait de téléphoner quand il est entré. She had just called when he walked in. Il vient d’accepter ce poste. He just accepted this position. Il venait d’accepter ce poste quand on lui en a proposé un autre. He had just accepted this position when he was offered another one.

sources.source_text: The plus-que-parfait (pluperfect) indicates a past action that happened before another past action started (in English, had done). It can be seen as “past” past tense.
To form the plus-que-parfait, use the forms of avoir or être in the imparfait + the past participle of the main verb.

sections.title: Review of imparfait of avoir and être

sources.section_title: Review of imparfait of avoir and être
sources.source_text: être to be: j’étais, tu étais, il/elle était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils/elles étaient. avoir to have: j’avais, tu avais, il/elle avait, nous avions, vous aviez, ils/elles avaient.
In the plus-que-parfait, all pronominal verbs are conjugated with être and agree in gender and number with the subject.
the plus-que-parfait indicates a past action that happened before another past action started.
Sometimes in English the French plus-que-parfait is translated as a simple tense.
In Chapter 1, you studied depuis with the present tense. In Chapter 8, you studied depuis with the imparfait.
The plus-que-parfait, when used with si seulement, expresses a wish or regret about past events.

sources.source_text: When could refers to a single, unique action in the past, the passé composé of pouvoir is used.
Il n’a pas pu lui parler. He could not talk to him.
When should means ought to, the conditionnel (présent or passé) is used.
When would refers to a repeated action in the past, the imparfait is used.

sources.source_text: The subjunctive is a mood, not a tense. ... For most verbs, the present of the subjunctive is formed by adding the subjunctive endings (-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent) to the stem.
Some verbs have irregular forms in the present subjunctive. Être (to be) and avoir (to have) have both irregular stems and endings.

sections.title: Subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing the notion of wish and desire. It is used when the subject of the main clause is different from the subject of the dependent clause.
The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion.
The subjunctive is also used after expressions of doubt.
The subjunctive is also used after certain impersonal expressions...
When you use conjunctions, you will also have to decide whether to use the indicative or the subjunctive in the following clause.
Pourvu que has the sense of provided that. ... When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning.

sections.title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea...
The past subjunctive is used in the same way as the present subjunctive. In such sentences, the action of the dependent clause is anterior to the action of the main clause.

sources.source_text: The infinitif is also used for general instructions, prescriptions, public notices, and proverbs
Since a verb in the infinitive mood is not conjugated, the negation (ne… pas) does not surround the verb but rather precedes it, and is not separated.
The infinitive is used after verbs of perception (where the present participle is used in English).
The infinitive is used in the interrogative infinitive.
You learned faire in Chapter 4. This causative form with faire is used to express the idea of having something done by someone or of causing something to happen.

sources.source_text: The passé simple (simple past, historical past) is a verb tense used mainly in written French, for literary and historical material. It may also be heard during a formal speech. It is the equivalent of the passé composé, used to recount a specific action in the past.

sections.title: Formation of the passé simple: regular -er verbs

sources.section_title: Formation of the passé simple: regular -er verbs
sources.source_text: The passé simple of regular -er verbs is formed by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent to the infinitive stem.

sources.source_text: Verbs like commencer and manger have a spelling change. When the passé simple ending starts with -a, use the cedilla (ç) for verbs ending in -cer and add an extra -e- for verbs ending in -ger.

sources.section_title: Formation of the passé simple: regular -ir and -re verbs
sources.source_text: The passé simple of regular -ir and -re verbs like partir (to leave) and répondre (to answer) is formed by adding the endings -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent to the infinitive stem.

sources.source_text: A sentence can either be in the active or the passive voice.
The passive voice is formed with être in the tense required + the past participle of the main verb.

sections.title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice

sources.section_title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice
sources.source_text: In most cases, the agent is introduced by par. However, the preposition de is commonly used after verbs expressing emotion or opinion.
The voix passive is used to emphasize the subject. The voix passive is also used to avoid specifying the agent of the action.

sections.title: Avoiding the passive voice in French

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: The voix passive can be replaced by the active voice in French with the following reflexive verbs: se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire.
Mettre les phrases suivantes à la voix passive. Attention aux temps de verbe!
Mettre les phrases suivantes à la voix active. Attention aux temps de verbe!
Traduire les phrases suivantes en utilisant la voix passive.

sources.source_text: In direct speech (le discours direct), one says something or asks a question directly. ... In indirect speech (le discours indirect), the words of one or more people are reported or a question is asked indirectly.

sections.title: Main clause verbs in indirect speech

sources.section_title: Main clause verbs in indirect speech
sources.source_text: Verbs in the main clause of indirect speech are followed by que (où, si, etc.); the verb in the dependent clause is usually in the indicative. Here are some typical main clause verbs: affirmer, annoncer, assurer, avouer, confier, constater, crier, déclarer, dire, expliquer, observer, prétendre, promettre, remarquer, répondre, révéler, s'apercevoir, savoir, se rendre compte.

sections.title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps

sources.section_title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps

sources.source_text: The definite article with nouns... French uses le for masculine nouns and la for feminine nouns. Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound. The plural les is used for both masculine and feminine.

sections.title: The indefinite and partitive articles with nouns

sources.section_title: The indefinite and partitive articles with nouns
sources.source_text: The indefinite articles are un (masculine singular) (a), une (feminine singular) (a), and des (both masculine and feminine plural) (some).
The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article. de + le = du; de + l’ = de l’; de + la = de la; de + les = des.

The noun endings very often indicate their gender... Nouns ending in -age, -eau, and -ment tend to be masculine... Nouns ending in -ure, -ence, -ance, -sion, -tion, -té, -ouille, -eille, -ie, -ette, -eur tend to be feminine.
In most cases, an -s is added to a noun to make it plural... Nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z do not change... Nouns ending in -eu, -eau usually take an -x... Nouns ending in -al usually change to -aux.
Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender. For geographical nouns, an -e ending usually indicates the feminine. Other endings tend to be masculine.

To express in or to with a geographical name, the preposition varies. With cities, the preposition à is used... With countries, regions, states, and provinces, the article and/or the preposition change according to gender and number.
From is expressed by de (d’) for continents, feminine countries, provinces, regions, and states. For masculine and plural entities, the definite article is retained (du, des).

sources.source_text: There are many types of pronouns in French. Let’s start with the subject pronouns you have already used when conjugating verbs.
Another type of pronoun is the direct object pronoun (le pronom objet direct).
Now that you have mastered the pronom objet direct, let’s take a look at the pronom objet indirect (indirect object pronoun).
Y is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb.
En is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb.

When a direct and indirect pronoun appear in the same sentence, the indirect object pronoun comes first, unless the direct and indirect pronouns are in the third person, in which case the direct object pronoun comes first.
There are many ways to use disjunctive pronouns, also known as stressed or tonic pronouns.

sources.source_text: Sometimes you need to be very specific when identifying things. To do so, you use demonstrative adjectives (this, that, these, those).
Possessive adjectives modify nouns and are used to express relationship and ownership. They agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives. They agree in gender and number with the noun they replace, not with the possessor.
Remember that the most common way of expressing possession is by using être à + the disjunctive pronoun.

Compound demonstrative pronouns are used to compare elements of the same nature or to indicate a choice between two objects or two people.
The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and is often the subject of the verb être. It refers to an idea previously introduced.

concepts.description: A conjunction meaning 'provided that' or used to express hope in a single clause.

sources.source_text: Pourvu que has the sense of provided that. ... When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning.

concepts.name: Preposition de
concepts.description: Used with venir to form immediate past, and with tenir to mean 'to take after'.

concepts.name: Preposition à
concepts.description: Used to indicate destination, attachment, etc.

sources.source_text: Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going.

concepts.name: Prepositions
concepts.description: Use of prepositions before relative pronouns such as à, de, pour, avec, sans, etc.

concepts.name: Present conditional

sources.source_text: For most verbs, the present of the subjunctive is formed...

concepts.name: Present tense
concepts.description: The present indicative tense of French verbs, covering various uses including general statements, ongoing actions, close future, habitual actions, past connected to present, historical/dramatic present, and actions in progress.

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
sources.source_text: The present indicative is used in a number of ways
The present tense of -ir and -re verbs
Let’s start with être: je suis / I am / nous sommes / we are...

concepts.name: Pronominal verbs
concepts.description: Verbs preceded by me, te, se, nous, vous, se in infinitive and conjugated forms.

sources.source_text: Pronominal verbs are verbs that are preceded in the infinitive and in conjugated forms by the pronouns me, te, se, nous, vous, se.

sources.section_title: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé
sources.source_text: All pronominal verbs are conjugated with être in the passé composé.

concepts.name: Pronominal verbs with infinitive
concepts.description: Reflexive pronoun agrees with subject and precedes infinitive.

sources.section_title: Pronominals in the imperative and the infinitive
sources.source_text: When pronominal verbs are used in the infinitive, the reflexive pronoun is always in the same person and number as the subject, and it precedes the infinitive.

concepts.name: Pronoun en
concepts.description: Indirect object pronoun replacing inanimate objects preceded by de.

concepts.name: Pronoun y
concepts.description: Indirect object pronoun replacing inanimate objects preceded by à or sometimes sur.

concepts.name: Pronunciation of final consonants in certain numbers
concepts.description: Special pronunciation of final consonants in cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, and mute consonant rule before consonant-initial words.

sources.source_text: Although consonants are generally silent in French, they are pronounced in the following numbers: cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix.

concepts.name: Reciprocal verbs
concepts.description: Action two or more people perform with or for each other.

sources.source_text: It describes an action two or more people perform with or for each other.

sources.section_title: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé
sources.source_text: When reciprocal verbs take a direct object, the past participle agrees with the subject. When reciprocal verbs take an indirect object in French, the past participle does not agree.

concepts.name: Reflexive verbs
concepts.description: Action reflected back on the subject.

sources.source_text: The action of a reflexive verb is, for the most part, reflected back on the subject, the action being done to oneself.

concepts.name: Regret or reproach
concepts.description: Using the past conditional to express regret or reproach about past actions.

sources.source_text: The passé du conditionnel can express regret or reproach.

concepts.name: Regular -er verbs
concepts.description: Verbs belonging to the first group, ending in -er in the infinitive, which follow a standard conjugation pattern.

concepts.name: Regular conjugation
concepts.description: Conjugation patterns that follow predictable rules, such as Type 1 -ir verbs and regular -re verbs.

sources.source_text: Type 1 verbs drop the -ir of the infinitive, add an -iss- to the plural form, and then insert the appropriate ending.

concepts.name: Regular past participle formation
concepts.description: Past participle endings for regular verbs: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u.

sources.source_text: Regular past participles take the following endings: -er verbs take -é, -ir verbs take -i, -re verbs take -u.

concepts.name: Relative clauses
concepts.description: The subjunctive may be used after relative pronouns when there is doubt about existence.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
sources.source_text: The relative pronouns qui and que can sometimes be followed by the subjunctive. If there is some doubt about the existence of someone or the possible realization of something...

concepts.name: Relative pronouns
concepts.description: Pronouns that link a dependent clause to a main clause, referring to persons or things.

concepts.name: Reporting verbs
concepts.description: Verbs used in the main clause of indirect speech

sources.section_title: Main clause verbs in indirect speech
sources.source_text: Here are some typical main clause verbs

concepts.name: Savoir vs. connaître
concepts.description: Distinction between knowing facts/how to do something (savoir) and being acquainted with (connaître).

sources.source_text: When learning the verb savoir, you also need to become acquainted with the verb connaître, in order to understand when to use one or the other.

concepts.name: Spelling changes in -er verbs
concepts.description: Certain -er verbs undergo spelling or stem changes in the present tense to maintain pronunciation, including verbs ending in -cer, -ger, -e+consonant+er, -é+consonant+er, and -e+l+er.

sources.section_title: -er verbs with spelling and stem changes
sources.source_text: -er verbs with spelling and stem changes

concepts.name: Subject pronoun
concepts.description: Pronoun used as the subject of a verb.

concepts.name: Subject pronouns
concepts.description: The French subject pronouns: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles.

sources.source_text: je I / tu you (singular familiar) / il he, it (masculine) / elle she, it (feminine) / on one, we, they / nous we / vous you (singular formal and all plurals) / ils they (masculine or mixed masculine and feminine) / elles they (feminine)

concepts.name: Subjective pronominal
concepts.description: Idiomatic or historical use of pronominal form; neither reflexive nor reciprocal.

sources.source_text: These verbs are neither reflexive nor reciprocal. For idiomatic or historical reasons, they just happen to use the pronominal forms.

concepts.name: Subjunctive
concepts.description: Use of subjunctive after relative pronouns to express doubt or after superlative antecedents.

concepts.name: Subjunctive mood
concepts.description: The subjunctive is a mood, not a tense. It refers to someone's opinion or deals with hypothetical actions.

sources.source_text: The subjunctive is a mood, not a tense. The mood of a verb determines how one views an event.

concepts.name: Subjunctive with indefinite expressions
concepts.description: Use of the present subjunctive after indefinite expressions equivalent to whatever, whenever, wherever, whoever.

sources.source_text: The present subjunctive is used with the indefinite expressions that are the French equivalents of whatever, whenever, wherever, and whoever.

concepts.name: Superlative
concepts.description: The subjunctive is used after superlatives and adjectives with superlative meaning.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea...

concepts.name: Tense concordance
concepts.description: la concordance des temps

sources.section_title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps

concepts.name: The verb manquer
concepts.description: The verb manquer and its meanings depending on preposition or lack thereof.

sources.source_text: The verb manquer Note how the preposition (or lack of preposition) changes the meaning of the verb manquer (to miss)

concepts.name: Time
concepts.description: Expressions and adverbs relating to time (today, tomorrow, yesterday, etc.)

concepts.name: Time expressions
concepts.description: Vocabulary items related to time, such as days, parts of day, frequency adverbs.

concepts.description: The various contexts in which the present tense is used in French.

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
sources.source_text: The present indicative is used in a number of ways

concepts.name: Verbs ending in -eindre and -aindre
concepts.description: A group of -re verbs with similar conjugation patterns.

sources.source_text: Among the -re verbs, some verbs ending in -eindre or -aindre can be grouped together.

concepts.name: Verbs with avoir and être (six verbs)
concepts.description: Sortir, rentrer, monter, descendre, passer, retourner can use avoir when followed by a direct object, with meaning change.

sources.section_title: Verbs conjugated with avoir or être
sources.source_text: Six verbs among those conjugated with être in the passé composé (sortir, rentrer, monter, descendre, passer, retourner) are conjugated with avoir and follow the avoir agreement when a direct object follows the verb.

concepts.name: Verbs with changing prepositions
concepts.description: Verbs that change meaning depending on the preposition used or lack of preposition.

sources.source_text: Some verbs can be very capricious as they change preposition and meaning.

concepts.name: Wish and desire
concepts.description: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing wish and desire when subjects differ.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing the notion of wish and desire.

concepts.name: active voice
concepts.description: The active voice, where the subject performs the action.

sources.source_text: In the active voice, the subject performs the action.

concepts.name: adjective placement
concepts.description: Position of adjectives relative to the noun.

sources.source_text: In French, most qualificative adjectives follow the noun.

concepts.name: adjectives
concepts.description: Qualificative adjectives that modify nouns and agree in gender and number.

sources.source_text: To describe things and people, we use qualificative adjectives.

concepts.name: agent
concepts.description: The agent in a passive construction, introduced by par or de.

sources.section_title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice
sources.source_text: In most cases, the agent is introduced by par.

concepts.name: agreement
concepts.description: Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

sources.source_text: In French, adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

concepts.name: anteriority
concepts.description: Past infinitive marks anteriority.

sources.source_text: The infinitif passé (past infinitive) is used to mark anteriority.
describes an action that will take place and be completed before another future action.

concepts.name: après + past infinitive
concepts.description: Après + infinitif passé marks an action completed before another.

sources.section_title: après + past infinitive / avant de + present infinitive
sources.source_text: One common occurrence of the infinitif passé is after the preposition après

concepts.description: Use of avoir or être in imparfait as auxiliary for plus-que-parfait.

sources.source_text: use the forms of avoir or être in the imparfait + the past participle

concepts.name: avant de + present infinitive
concepts.description: Avant de + infinitif présent marks an action before another.

sources.section_title: après + past infinitive / avant de + present infinitive
sources.source_text: the infinitif présent follows avant de

concepts.description: Faire + infinitive expresses having something done or causing something to happen.

sources.source_text: This causative form with faire is used to express the idea of having something done by someone or of causing something to happen.

concepts.description: Vocabulary related to names, birth, marriage, death, addresses, identity documents, and marital status.

concepts.name: definite article
concepts.description: Use of le, la, l', les

sources.source_text: French uses le for masculine nouns and la for feminine nouns. Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound. The plural les is used for both masculine and feminine.

concepts.name: depuis
concepts.description: Preposition used to express duration from a past point until interruption.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: interrupted continuous action
sources.source_text: To express the idea that an action had been going on for a period of time before being interrupted, use the imparfait with depuis.

concepts.name: depuis duration
concepts.description: Depuis with present vs imparfait to express duration from past to present or past to past.

sources.source_text: Ils dînent dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années. / Ils dînaient dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années quand ils ont décidé d'essayer le restaurant d'en face.

concepts.name: description and background
concepts.description: Use of imparfait to describe past situations, states, and background circumstances.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: background and description
sources.source_text: It is used for background and description. It describes a situation that existed in the past, a state of mind or being.

concepts.name: elision
concepts.description: Dropping vowel before vowel or mute h

sources.source_text: Le and la are shortened to l’ before a singular noun or adjective that begins with a vowel sound.

concepts.name: expressions of position
concepts.description: Infinitive after expressions like être debout à, être assis à, etc.

sources.source_text: The infinitive is used after expressions of position. The preposition à precedes the infinitive.

concepts.name: expressions of spending time
concepts.description: Infinitive after expressions like passer son temps à, gaspiller sa vie à, etc.

sources.section_title: Infinitive after expressions of spending time
sources.source_text: The infinitive is used after expressions of spending time.

concepts.name: futur antérieur
concepts.description: The future perfect tense, used for actions completed before another future action, probability of past, and after 'si' meaning 'whether'.

concepts.name: futur simple
concepts.description: The simple future tense in French, used for future events, probability, narration, and polite commands.

concepts.name: future in narration
concepts.description: Use of futur simple to express a future idea from the standpoint of the past.

sources.source_text: In a narration, the futur simple can be used to express a future idea from the standpoint of the past.

concepts.name: future tense
concepts.description: Tenses expressing future time: futur simple and futur antérieur.

sources.source_text: French has two other future constructions: the futur simple and the futur antérieur.

concepts.name: gender of nouns
concepts.description: Masculine and feminine noun classification

sources.source_text: All nouns in French have a gender: masculine or feminine.

concepts.name: geographical names
concepts.description: Use of articles and prepositions with countries, cities, etc.

sources.source_text: Countries, continents, states, provinces, and regions also have a gender.

concepts.name: gerund
concepts.description: Gérondif: en + present participle, expresses relationship between two actions.

sources.source_text: When the present participle is introduced by en, it is referred to as the gérondif (gerund).

concepts.name: gerund meanings
concepts.description: The gerund can express simultaneity, manner, condition, or causality.

sources.source_text: It can express simultaneity, manner, condition, or causality.

concepts.name: habitual action
concepts.description: Past actions that were repeated or habitual.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action
sources.source_text: Another use of the imparfait is to express habitual, repetitive action.

concepts.name: health and pharmacy vocabulary
concepts.description: Vocabulary related to health, pharmacy, and medical conditions.

concepts.name: immediate past
concepts.description: Using venir de + infinitive in the imparfait to describe an action that had just happened.

sources.section_title: Immediate past in the imparfait (venir de + infinitive)
sources.source_text: The immediate past can also be used in the imparfait to describe an action that had just happened.

concepts.name: imparfait
concepts.description: French imperfect tense used for description, habitual action, background, and interrupted actions in the past.

sources.source_text: The uses of the imparfait (imperfect) are some of the most difficult aspects of French grammar to master.

concepts.name: imperative mood
concepts.description: L’impératif is used to give orders, make suggestions, or give advice.

sources.source_text: The imperative mood (l’impératif) is used to give orders, make suggestions, or give advice.

concepts.name: indefinite article
concepts.description: Use of un, une, des

sources.section_title: The indefinite and partitive articles with nouns
sources.source_text: The indefinite articles are un (masculine singular) (a), une (feminine singular) (a), and des (both masculine and feminine plural) (some).

concepts.name: infinitive mood
concepts.description: The infinitive mood used as subject, for instructions, after prepositions, and after certain verbs.

concepts.name: instructions and notices
concepts.description: Infinitive used for general instructions, prescriptions, public notices, and proverbs.

sources.source_text: The infinitif is also used for general instructions, prescriptions, public notices, and proverbs

concepts.name: interrogation
concepts.description: Interrogative infinitive using question words + infinitive.

sources.source_text: The infinitive is used in the interrogative infinitive.

concepts.name: interrupted action
concepts.description: A continuous past action interrupted by another action.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: interrupted continuous action
sources.source_text: The imparfait is also used to describe a continuous action that was going on in the past when another action (expressed in the passé composé) interrupted it.

concepts.name: irregular future stems
concepts.description: Verbs with irregular stems in the futur simple.

sources.source_text: However, some irregular verbs have irregular stems.

concepts.name: irregular imperative forms
concepts.description: être, avoir, and savoir have irregular imperative forms; vouloir is used only in the vous form.

sources.source_text: Some imperatives are irregular. Let’s take a look at être, avoir, and savoir.

concepts.name: irregular present participles
concepts.description: Three verbs have irregular present participles: être, avoir, savoir.

sources.source_text: Three verbs have an irregular present participle: être -> étant, avoir -> ayant, savoir -> sachant.

concepts.name: irregular stem
concepts.description: A verb stem that does not follow the regular pattern.

sources.source_text: Note that the verb être has an irregular stem in the imparfait.

concepts.name: negation
concepts.description: Negation with infinitive: ne...pas precedes infinitive and is not separated.

sources.source_text: the negation (ne… pas) does not surround the verb but rather precedes it, and is not separated.
When used in the negative, the du, de la, and des all become de, since the quantity of the item doesn’t exist any longer.

concepts.name: negative imperative
concepts.description: Negation is placed around the verb; object pronouns precede the verb following ne (n’).

sources.source_text: In the negative form, the negation is placed around the verb. Note that object pronouns immediately precede the verb (following ne [n’]) in the negative imperative.

concepts.name: on as passive alternative
concepts.description: Using the third-person singular pronoun on to avoid the passive voice.

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: French often prefers to use the third-person singular form on rather than the passive voice construction.

concepts.name: partitive article
concepts.description: Use of du, de la, de l', des to express unspecified quantity

sources.source_text: The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article.

concepts.name: passive voice
concepts.description: The passive voice, where the subject is acted upon.

sources.source_text: In the passive voice, the subject is acted upon.

concepts.name: passé composé
concepts.description: French compound past tense used for completed actions on specific occasions.

sources.source_text: While the passé composé is used to talk about an action that took place on a specific occasion in the past, the imparfait plays a different role.

concepts.name: past anteriority
concepts.description: Action before another past action, often with dependent clause.

sources.source_text: the plus-que-parfait indicates a past action that happened before another past action started.

sources.source_text: When an action precedes another one, avoir and être in the participe présent can be combined with a participe passé.

concepts.name: plural of nouns
concepts.description: Formation of plural nouns

sources.source_text: In most cases, an -s is added to a noun to make it plural.

concepts.name: plus-que-parfait
concepts.description: Compound past tense indicating an action completed before another past action.

sources.source_text: The plus-que-parfait (pluperfect) indicates a past action that happened before another past action started (in English, had done).

concepts.name: polite imperative with future
concepts.description: Using futur simple instead of imperative for a less peremptory tone.

sources.source_text: The futur simple can be used instead of an imperative (command form) to achieve a less peremptory tone.

concepts.name: prepositions with geographical names
concepts.description: Use of à, en, au, aux, de, du, des with places

sources.source_text: To express in or to with a geographical name, the preposition varies.

concepts.name: present infinitive
concepts.description: Infinitif présent used as subject, for general instructions, after verbs of perception, in interrogative infinitive, after expressions of spending time and position.

concepts.name: present participle
concepts.description: Participe présent: verb form ending in -ant, used as verb, noun, or adjective.

sources.source_text: Another participle is the participe présent (present participle).

concepts.description: The present participle can function as a noun (with gender/number agreement), as an adjective (agreeing with noun), or as a verb (invariable).

sources.source_text: Some participes présents can be used as nouns... Many participes présents can be used as adjectives... The participe présent can also be used as a verb.

concepts.description: Use of future tenses to express probability or likelihood.

sources.source_text: The future tense of être and avoir is sometimes used to express probability in the present.

sources.source_text: Pronominal verbs follow the same pattern. Do not forget the pronoun corresponding to the subject.

concepts.name: pronominal verbs
concepts.description: Pronominal verbs have pronouns that change position in the imperative: after the verb in affirmative, before the verb in negative.

sources.source_text: When putting pronominal verbs in the imperative, watch for the pronoun and its position.

concepts.name: pronunciation
concepts.description: How words are pronounced.

sources.source_text: Note that the -ais, -ait, -aient endings are pronounced alike.

concepts.name: reflexive passive
concepts.description: Use of reflexive verbs to express passive meaning.

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: In Chapter 6, you studied one type of pronominal verb called the passive pronominal.

concepts.name: school and education vocabulary
concepts.description: Vocabulary related to school, exams, and learning.

concepts.name: si seulement regret
concepts.description: Use of si seulement + plus-que-parfait to express regret about past.

sources.source_text: The plus-que-parfait, when used with si seulement, expresses a wish or regret about past events.

concepts.name: spelling changes
concepts.description: Orthographic adjustments in certain verbs to maintain pronunciation.

sources.source_text: Verbs with spelling changes in the present tense nous form, such as manger and commencer, retain the spelling change only for the je, tu, il, elle, ils, and elles subject pronouns.

concepts.name: spelling changes in future
concepts.description: Verbs with spelling modifications in the futur simple (e.g., acheter, appeler, employer, essuyer, jeter, nettoyer, préférer).

sources.source_text: Some slight spelling modifications occur with some verbs.

concepts.name: spelling changes in present participle
concepts.description: Some -cer and -ger verbs have spelling changes when forming the present participle.

sources.source_text: Some spelling changes occur with some -cer and -ger verbs.

concepts.name: subject difference
concepts.description: When main and dependent clause subjects differ, use que clause.

sources.source_text: When the subjects are different, a dependent clause introduced by que is required.

concepts.name: suggestion
concepts.description: Using si on + imparfait to make a suggestion or invitation.

sources.source_text: With a si + on construction, the imparfait is used to make a suggestion or to invite someone to do something.

concepts.name: superlative
concepts.description: Superlative forms of adjectives and adverbs.

sources.source_text: To express the ideas of the most, the least, the best, the worst, etc., one uses the superlative.

concepts.description: Use of future tense in both main and dependent clauses after certain conjunctions.

sources.source_text: In a compound sentence in French, if the main clause is in the futur simple, the dependent clause, introduced by some conjunctions, will also be in the futur simple.

concepts.name: time expressions
concepts.description: Words and phrases that signal habitual or repetitive actions in the past.

sources.section_title: Uses of the imparfait: habitual and repetitive action
sources.source_text: souvent, fréquemment, toujours, le mardi, etc.

concepts.name: verb conjugation
concepts.description: The inflection of verbs according to person, number, tense, mood, etc.

sources.source_text: To form the imperfect, take the nous form of the present tense and remove the -ons ending...

concepts.name: verbs of perception
concepts.description: Infinitive used after verbs of perception instead of English present participle.

sources.source_text: The infinitive is used after verbs of perception

concepts.name: verbs with prepositions
concepts.description: Verbs may be followed directly by infinitive or by prepositions à, de, etc.

sources.section_title: Verbs not followed by a preposition
sources.source_text: When a verb is followed by another verb in the infinitive (j’aime danser), the first thing to ask is whether or not it is followed by a preposition.

concepts.name: vocabulary
concepts.description: Geographical and noun vocabulary

concepts.name: wish or regret
concepts.description: Using si seulement + imparfait to express a wish or regret.

sources.source_text: You will encounter the imparfait in other idiomatic constructions, for instance, preceded by si seulement, to express a wish or a regret.

concepts.name: Être as auxiliary
concepts.description: Certain intransitive verbs of movement and all pronominal verbs use être as the auxiliary.

sources.source_text: Some verbs use être instead of avoir in the passé composé. Many of these are intransitive verbs of movement.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Adjectives change meaning based on position
grammar_rules.summary: Some adjectives have different meanings depending on whether they precede or follow the noun.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives like ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier have distinct meanings when placed before or after the noun.
grammar_rules.formation: adjective + noun (figurative meaning) vs noun + adjective (literal meaning)
restrictions: Only certain adjectives have this property.
conditions: Adjective is one of: ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier.
signal_words: ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier
exceptions: Only a small set of adjectives behaves this way (ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier)
Most adjectives keep the same meaning in either position
agreement_rules: The adjective still agrees in gender and number with the noun, whatever its position
Position affects meaning only, never agreement
transformations: un ancien professeur -> un professeur ancien
ma propre chambre -> une chambre propre
un grand homme -> un homme grand
common_traps: Misinterpreting the adjective's meaning based on position.

sources.source_text: Beware: Some adjectives have different meanings, depending on whether they precede or follow the noun.

grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives ending in -e in the masculine form remain unchanged in the feminine form.
grammar_rules.explanation: If an adjective ends with an -e in the masculine form, the feminine form is identical.
restrictions: Applies only to adjectives whose masculine form ends in -e.
The feminine form is identical, so no ending is added.
conditions: Adjective masculine form ends in -e.
exceptions: A few adjectives in -e still have a distinct feminine in -esse (e.g. traître, traîtresse)
agreement_rules: No change in gender.
grammar_rules.word_order: Adjective keeps the same position as the masculine form (noun + adjective).
transformations: un homme calme -> une femme calme
un voisin aimable -> une voisine aimable
un élève fidèle -> une élève fidèle

sources.source_text: If an adjective ends with an -e in the masculine form, the feminine form remains the same.

grammar_rules.summary: Add stressed pronoun after verb with hyphen.
grammar_rules.explanation: For the affirmative imperative, add the stressed pronoun toi, nous, or vous after the verb, connected with a hyphen.
restrictions: Applies only to affirmative commands, not negative ones.
The hyphen between the verb and the stressed pronoun is required.
conditions: The imperative is affirmative, not negative.
The verb is pronominal, so a stressed pronoun (toi, nous, vous) is added after the verb.
exceptions: The pronoun follows the verb only in the affirmative; in the negative it precedes the verb
Only toi, nous, and vous are used after the verb; me and te become moi and toi
agreement_rules: No past participle agreement arises; the added form is a stressed pronoun, not a participle
The pronoun form depends on the subject (toi, nous, vous) but never on gender
transformations: tu te lèves -> lève-toi
nous nous levons -> levons-nous
vous vous levez -> levez-vous
common_traps: Do not forget the hyphen.

sources.section_title: Pronominals in the imperative and the infinitive
sources.source_text: For the affirmative imperative, add the stressed pronoun toi, nous, or vous after the verb, connected with a hyphen.

grammar_rules.summary: The preposition de is commonly used after verbs expressing emotion or opinion.
grammar_rules.explanation: When the passive verb expresses emotion or opinion, de is used instead of par, and the agent plays a less active role.
usage: After verbs of emotion or opinion.
restrictions: Used when the agent is less active.
conditions: The verb expresses emotion or opinion.
exceptions: par is used with most other passive verbs
de is limited to verbs of emotion or opinion whose agent is less active
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees with the subject, as in all passive constructions
The agent introduced by de does not affect agreement
transformations: Il est aimé de tous.
par -> de after verbs of emotion or opinion

sources.section_title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice
sources.source_text: However, the preposition de is commonly used after verbs expressing emotion or opinion.

grammar_rules.summary: In most cases, the agent in a passive sentence is introduced by the preposition par.
grammar_rules.explanation: The preposition par is the default way to introduce the agent (the doer) in a passive construction.
usage: To indicate who performs the action in most passive sentences.
restrictions: Not universal: some passive sentences introduce the agent with de instead of par.
par remains the default choice for most passive sentences with an expressed agent.
conditions: The sentence is in the passive voice.
The agent (doer of the action) is expressed in the sentence.
exceptions: de replaces par after verbs of emotion or opinion
Some fixed passive expressions use de (e.g. aimé de tous)
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees with the subject, never with the agent
The agent introduced by par never triggers agreement
transformations: Il est respecté par ses collègues.
de -> par as the default agent preposition

sources.section_title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice
sources.source_text: In most cases, the agent is introduced by par.

grammar_rules.summary: Agreement with subject generally, but no agreement when followed by direct object or another verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: Most pronominal verbs agree with subject, but exceptions exist.
grammar_rules.formation: s'être (conjugated) + past participle; agrees with subject unless a direct object or another verb follows
restrictions: no agreement if verb followed by direct object or another verb
conditions: The verb is pronominal and used in a compound tense such as the passé composé.
The past participle is not followed by a direct object or by another verb.
exceptions: direct object follows
another verb follows
agreement_rules: agree with subject unless direct object or verb follows
grammar_rules.word_order: reflexive pronoun + être + past participle (+ direct object)
grammar_rules.affirmative_form: Elle s'est offert une nouvelle moto.
transformations: Elle s'est lavée.
Elle s'est lavé les mains.
Ils se sont parlé.
common_traps: Thinking agreement is always required

sources.section_title: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé
sources.source_text: Note that the past participle does not agree with the subject of the pronominal verb when the verb is followed by a direct object or by another verb.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Agreement of pronominal verbs in plus-que-parfait
grammar_rules.summary: All pronominal verbs use être auxiliary and past participle agrees in gender and number with subject.
grammar_rules.explanation: In the plus-que-parfait, pronominal verbs are always conjugated with être. The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.
usage: With all pronominal verbs in plus-que-parfait
restrictions: Applies to all pronominal verbs in the plus-que-parfait, without exception.
The past participle must agree with the subject in gender and number.
conditions: The verb is pronominal.
The tense is the plus-que-parfait, which always uses the être auxiliary.
exceptions: No agreement when the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object (e.g. se parler)
Agreement is with a preceding direct object rather than the subject when such an object exists
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees with subject in gender and number
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + reflexive pronoun + être (imparfait) + past participle
transformations: Elle s'était levée tôt.
Ils s'étaient réveillés.
présent: elle s'est levée -> plus-que-parfait: elle s'était levée
common_traps: Forgetting to agree past participle with pronominal verbs

sources.source_text: In the plus-que-parfait, all pronominal verbs are conjugated with être and agree in gender and number with the subject.

grammar_rules.summary: With avoir, past participle agrees with direct object if it precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: In passé composé with avoir, past participle agrees in gender and number with a preceding direct object noun or pronoun.
grammar_rules.formation: direct object + avoir + past participle (agrees with DO)
usage: when direct object is before the verb
restrictions: only if direct object precedes
conditions: direct object noun or pronoun precedes the verb
exceptions: No agreement when the direct object follows the verb
No agreement with indirect object pronouns (lui, leur)
The participle is invariable when the object is the pronoun en
agreement_rules: agrees with direct object in gender and number
grammar_rules.affirmative_form: Il a pris la bonne décision.
transformations: Il l'a prise.
common_traps: If direct object follows verb, no agreement.

sources.source_text: In the passé composé of verbs conjugated with avoir, the past participle agrees with the direct object of the verb, but only in sentences where the direct object noun or pronoun precedes the verb.

grammar_rules.summary: Use the preposition à after aller to indicate destination; note contraction with le/les.
grammar_rules.explanation: The verb aller (to go) is followed by the preposition à to say where one is going. When à is followed by the definite articles le or les, they contract to au and aux respectively.
grammar_rules.formation: aller + à + place; à + le = au; à + les = aux
usage: To express going to a place.
restrictions: Only applies to destinations that require à; some places may use en or other prepositions.
conditions: Aller expresses movement toward a destination.
The destination is a place that takes à rather than en or another preposition.
exceptions: No contraction with la or l'.
agreement_rules: In compound tenses the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject (elle est allée)
The destination phrase after à triggers no agreement
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + aller conjugated + pas + à + place
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + aller conjugated + à + place? or inversion
transformations: à le -> au
à les -> aux
common_traps: Forgetting contraction with le/les.

sources.source_text: Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.

grammar_rules.summary: Aller is used in many common expressions such as Ça va?, Comment allez-vous?, etc.
grammar_rules.explanation: Aller appears in several common idiomatic expressions to ask about well-being or comment on appearance.
restrictions: Limited to fixed idioms built on aller, such as Ça va? and Comment allez-vous?.
The meaning is idiomatic and does not express literal movement.
conditions: The expression is a fixed idiom built on aller.
The context is a greeting, a question about health, or a comment on fit, as in Ça va? and Ce tailleur vous va bien.
exceptions: Expressions like aller bien à quelqu'un take an indirect object instead of expressing movement
Comment allez-vous uses the vous form even for one person in formal address
agreement_rules: In compound tenses the past participle agrees with the subject (elle est allée)
Fixed expressions such as Ça va are invariable
grammar_rules.word_order: interrogative word + verb + hyphen + subject pronoun (Comment allez-vous ?)
transformations: Comment allez-vous?
Ça va?
aller bien à quelqu'un -> Ce tailleur vous va bien.

sources.source_text: Aller is used in many common expressions.

grammar_rules.summary: The expression au cas où (in case) is used with the present or past conditional.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expresses a possible future or past situation that triggers an action.
restrictions: conditional tense required
conditions: Au cas où introduces a clause expressing a possible contingency (in case).
The clause verb is in the present or past conditional.
exceptions: The subjunctive is not used after au cas où
agreement_rules: With être as auxiliary, the past participle of the past conditional agrees with the subject
The expression au cas où itself triggers no agreement
grammar_rules.word_order: au cas où + subject + conditional verb
transformations: au cas où + subjonctif -> au cas où + conditionnel
Au cas où il pleuvrait, prends ton parapluie.
common_traps: Do not use subjunctive after au cas où.

sources.source_text: The présent or passé du conditionnel are also used with the expression au cas où (in case).

grammar_rules.summary: The passive voice can be replaced by reflexive verbs se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire.
grammar_rules.explanation: These reflexive constructions express passive meaning without using the passive voice.
usage: To avoid the passive voice in French.
restrictions: Limited to the reflexive verbs se laisser, se faire, se voir, and s'entendre dire.
The construction is a reflexive paraphrase rather than a true passive with a par + agent phrase.
conditions: The sentence would otherwise be expressed in the passive voice.
The verb is one of se laisser, se faire, se voir, or s'entendre dire.
exceptions: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject
se faire and se laisser take a following infinitive, not a past participle
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees with the subject when the reflexive pronoun is a direct object
No agreement occurs when the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object
grammar_rules.word_order: reflexive pronoun + se laisser/se faire/se voir + infinitive [+ past participle]
transformations: Il a été renvoyé. -> Il s'est fait renvoyer.
passive -> se faire / se laisser / se voir + infinitive

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: The voix passive can be replaced by the active voice in French with the following reflexive verbs: se laisser, se faire, se voir, s'entendre dire.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Avoir and être are irregular in the passé simple
grammar_rules.summary: Avoir and être have irregular stems and endings in the passé simple.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir uses stem eu- and être uses stem fu- in the passé simple.
grammar_rules.formation: avoir: eus, eus, eut, eûmes, eûtes, eurent; être: fus, fus, fut, fûmes, fûtes, furent
usage: Common in literature and formal writing.
restrictions: Limited to avoir and être; other verbs follow their own irregular or regular patterns.
The stems eu- and fu- must be memorized and not confused.
conditions: The verb is avoir or être.
The tense is the passé simple.
exceptions: No other verb shares the stems eu- and fu-
The first- and second-person plural forms carry a circumflex (eûmes, eûtes, fûmes, fûtes)
agreement_rules: The passé simple agrees in person and number with the subject (eus/fus, eûmes/fûmes)
The passé simple has no participle and therefore no gender agreement
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + irregular stem (eu-/fu-) + passé simple ending
transformations: avoir: j'eus, tu eus, il eut, nous eûmes, vous eûtes, ils eurent
être: je fus, tu fus, il fut, nous fûmes, vous fûtes, ils furent
common_traps: Do not confuse eu- and fu- forms.

sources.section_title: Avoir and être in the passé simple
sources.source_text: Avoir (to have) and être (to be) are irregular in the passé simple.

grammar_rules.summary: The expression avoir beau + infinitive is translated as 'although' or 'however'.
grammar_rules.explanation: It expresses concession: despite doing something or being something, the result is contrary to expectation.
restrictions: The expression is idiomatic and cannot be translated literally as 'to have beautiful'.
It expresses concession only, not possession or beauty.
conditions: The clause expresses concession, translatable as although or however much.
Avoir beau is followed by an infinitive.
exceptions: The construction is fixed: beau cannot be replaced by another adjective
The infinitive follows beau directly, with no preposition
It never means 'to have beautiful'
agreement_rules: beau is invariable in this expression and never agrees with the subject
The following infinitive triggers no agreement
grammar_rules.word_order: Subject + avoir (conjugated) + beau + infinitive + rest of sentence.
transformations: avoir beau + infinitive -> although / however + verb
Il a beau pleuvoir -> Although it is raining.
common_traps: Do not translate literally; it is not 'to have beautiful'.

sources.source_text: The expression avoir beau + infinitive can usually be translated by although or however.

grammar_rules.summary: Expression to indicate pain or trouble doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir mal à + body part indicates pain. Avoir du mal à + infinitive indicates difficulty doing something.
grammar_rules.formation: avoir mal à + article + body part; avoir du mal à + infinitive
restrictions: Avoir mal à requires a body part, while avoir du mal à requires an infinitive.
The two constructions differ in meaning: physical pain versus difficulty doing something.
conditions: The expression refers to physical pain: avoir mal à + body part (J'ai mal à la tête).
The expression refers to difficulty: avoir du mal à + infinitive.
exceptions: With a following verb, à becomes du mal à (avoir du mal à + infinitive)
The body part takes a definite article, not a possessive (j'ai mal à la tête)
agreement_rules: The body part takes a definite article and the expression does not agree with the possessor
avoir agrees with its subject in person and number (j'ai mal, nous avons mal)
grammar_rules.word_order: avoir + mal + à + article + body part
transformations: avoir mal à + article + partie du corps -> J'ai mal à la tête.
avoir du mal à + infinitive -> Nous avons du mal à accepter sa décision.
à + le -> au, à + les -> aux

sources.source_text: When referring to the state of one’s body, French uses avoir mal à (having an ache or pain). J’ai mal à la tête. Il a mal au bras. When avoir mal à is followed by a verb, it means to have trouble doing something. Nous avons du mal à accepter sa décision. Elle a du mal à monter l’escalier.

grammar_rules.summary: Place ne...pas around the conjugated verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: To make a sentence negative, place ne before the conjugated verb and pas after it. If the verb starts with a vowel or mute h, ne becomes n'. Examples: Elle ne travaille pas le lundi. Je n'habite pas à Strasbourg.
restrictions: ne becomes n' only before a vowel or mute h.
Both ne and pas are normally kept in writing, even though ne is often dropped in spoken French.
conditions: The sentence is made negative.
The verb is conjugated, with ne before it and pas after it; ne becomes n' before a vowel or mute h.
exceptions: ne becomes n' before vowel or mute h
agreement_rules: ne is invariable and carries no gender or number
The agreement rules of the tense used still apply (e.g. with avoir and a preceding direct object)
transformations: Elle travaille le lundi. -> Elle ne travaille pas le lundi.
j'habite -> je n'habite pas
ne + vowel or mute h -> n'
common_traps: Do not forget the ne, even in spoken French; remember elision.

sources.source_text: To make a sentence negative, you simply place ne... pas around the verb.

grammar_rules.summary: Faire + infinitive expresses having something done or causing something to happen.
grammar_rules.explanation: The subject causes another person to perform the action.
restrictions: The object of faire may be placed before or after the infinitive depending on whether pronouns are used.
Faire remains invariable before the infinitive.
conditions: The subject causes another person to perform the action.
Faire is followed directly by an infinitive.
exceptions: No preposition links faire to the infinitive
With a pronoun object, the pronoun precedes faire (je le fais réparer)
agreement_rules: The past participle of faire is invariable in this construction (elle a fait réparer la voiture)
The infinitive never agrees; only the auxiliary carries the tense
transformations: English 'have something done' -> French faire + infinitive
common_traps: The object of faire may be placed before or after the infinitive depending on pronouns.

sources.source_text: This causative form with faire is used to express the idea of having something done by someone or of causing something to happen.

grammar_rules.summary: Use faire + infinitive to express having something done or causing something to happen.
grammar_rules.explanation: The causative form is formed with the verb faire followed by an infinitive. It expresses the idea of having something done by someone or causing something to happen.
usage: To have something done by someone else.
restrictions: The agent may be introduced by par or à.
The past participle of faire is invariable in compound tenses.
The causative must not be confused with simple faire plus a noun.
conditions: The subject has something done by someone else or causes something to happen.
Faire is followed by an infinitive, with the agent optionally introduced by par or à.
exceptions: The agent may be introduced by par or à.
agreement_rules: The past participle of faire in compound tenses is invariable.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + faire conjugated + infinitive?
transformations: Active sentence: Elle écrit la lettre. -> Causative: Elle fait écrire la lettre par sa secrétaire.
common_traps: Confusing causative with simple faire + noun.

sources.source_text: It is formed with the verb faire followed by an infinitive.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Ce + relative at beginning for emphasis
grammar_rules.summary: Ce qui, ce que, ce à quoi, ce dont are frequently placed at the beginning of a sentence to stress a point; preposition is repeated in second clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Ce qui est amusant, c’est les marchés aux puces. Ce qu’elle adore, c’est acheter des vieilles chaises. Ce dont il a envie, c’est de cet automate. Ce à quoi il s’intéresse, c’est à l’aromathérapie.
restrictions: The preposition must be repeated in the second clause (ce dont il a envie, c'est de...).
Only ce qui, ce que, ce dont, and ce à quoi occur in this fronted pattern.
conditions: The sentence begins with ce qui, ce que, ce dont, or ce à quoi.
The second clause is introduced by c'est and repeats the preposition used in the first clause.
exceptions: The preposition required by the verb is repeated in the second clause after c'est
The pattern uses ce qui for subjects and ce que for direct objects
agreement_rules: c'est is invariable; the relative pronoun ce shows no gender or number
When the complement is plural, careful usage allows ce sont
grammar_rules.word_order: ce relative at start, then c’est
transformations: preposition repeated after c’est

sources.section_title: Ce que, ce qui, ce dont, ce à quoi
sources.source_text: Ce qui est amusant, c’est les marchés aux puces.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Ce dont for verbs with de
grammar_rules.summary: Ce dont is used when the verb or expression requires the preposition de, meaning what.
grammar_rules.explanation: Elle ne comprend pas ce dont il a peur. Fais-moi voir ce dont tu te sers. La police veut savoir ce dont elle se souvient. Je m’intéresse à ce dont vous avez parlé ce matin.
grammar_rules.formation: ce dont + subject + verb (verb with de)
usage: object of verb with de referring to idea
restrictions: Only verbs or expressions requiring de can use ce dont (avoir peur de, se servir de, se souvenir de, parler de).
Ce dont replaces a thing or an idea rather than a specific person.
conditions: verb requires de
exceptions: Verbs taking à use ce à quoi instead of ce dont
ce dont replaces the whole de + antecedent, so no noun antecedent is expressed
agreement_rules: ce dont is invariable, with no gender or number
The verb in the clause agrees with its own subject
transformations: parler de -> ce dont vous avez parlé
avoir peur de -> ce dont il a peur
se souvenir de -> ce dont elle se souvient

sources.section_title: Ce que, ce qui, ce dont, ce à quoi
sources.source_text: Elle ne comprend pas ce dont il a peur.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Ce que as direct object of idea
grammar_rules.summary: Ce que is used as the direct object of the dependent clause when referring to an idea.
grammar_rules.explanation: Savez-vous ce qu’il fait ces jours-ci? Tu comprends ce que ce journaliste écrit? Ils ont fait ce qu’il ne fallait pas faire. Elle écrit ce qu’elle vit.
usage: direct object of dependent clause referring to idea
restrictions: no gender or number
conditions: no specific antecedent
exceptions: With a specific antecedent, que replaces ce que
ce que never varies in gender or number
que is elided to qu' before a vowel
agreement_rules: ce que is invariable, with no gender or number
The verb in the clause agrees with its own subject
transformations: faire -> Savez-vous ce qu'il fait ces jours-ci?
écrire -> ce que ce journaliste écrit
ce que + vowel -> ce qu'

sources.section_title: Ce que, ce qui, ce dont, ce à quoi
sources.source_text: Savez-vous ce qu’il fait ces jours-ci?

grammar_rules.rule_name: Ce qui as subject of idea
grammar_rules.summary: Ce qui is used as the subject of a dependent clause when referring to an idea, not a specific noun.
grammar_rules.explanation: J’aime ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier. Il ne sait pas ce qui a provoqué leur réaction. Qui sait ce qui est arrivé? J’aimerais savoir ce qui lui plairait.
usage: subject of dependent clause referring to idea
restrictions: no gender or number
conditions: no specific antecedent
exceptions: With a specific antecedent, qui replaces ce qui
ce qui never varies in gender or number
qui is never elided before a vowel
agreement_rules: ce qui is invariable, with no gender or number
The verb after ce qui is third-person singular
transformations: être fabriqué -> ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier
arriver -> ce qui est arrivé
provoquer -> ce qui a provoqué leur réaction

sources.section_title: Ce que, ce qui, ce dont, ce à quoi
sources.source_text: J’aime ce qui est fabriqué dans cet atelier.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Ce à quoi for verbs with à
grammar_rules.summary: Ce à quoi is used when the verb requires the preposition à, meaning what.
grammar_rules.explanation: J’ignore ce à quoi il s’abonne. C’est exactement ce à quoi je m’attendais de sa part. Ils ne savent pas ce à quoi tu t’opposes. Je voudrais savoir ce à quoi elle aspire.
grammar_rules.formation: ce à quoi + subject + verb (verb with à)
usage: object of verb with à referring to idea
restrictions: Only verbs requiring à can use ce à quoi (s'abonner à, s'attendre à, s'opposer à, aspirer à).
Ce à quoi replaces a thing or an idea rather than a specific person.
conditions: verb requires à
exceptions: Verbs taking de use ce dont instead of ce à quoi
ce à quoi replaces the whole à + antecedent, so no noun antecedent is expressed
agreement_rules: ce à quoi is invariable, with no gender or number
The verb in the clause agrees with its own subject
transformations: s'abonner à -> ce à quoi il s'abonne
s'attendre à -> ce à quoi je m'attendais
s'opposer à -> ce à quoi tu t'opposes

sources.section_title: Ce que, ce qui, ce dont, ce à quoi
sources.source_text: J’ignore ce à quoi il s’abonne.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Choice between futur simple and futur antérieur in dependent clauses
grammar_rules.summary: When both clauses use futur simple, actions are simultaneous; use futur antérieur in dependent clause to mark anteriority.
grammar_rules.explanation: Sometimes you have a choice between the futur simple and the futur antérieur. When both clauses use the futur simple, it is implied that both actions take place simultaneously. If you want to mark an anteriority, use the futur antérieur.
grammar_rules.formation: main clause futur simple + conjunction + (futur simple for simultaneous / futur antérieur for anterior)
usage: to indicate simultaneity or anteriority in future temporal clauses
restrictions: The choice applies only after conjunctions such as quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, and tant que.
The futur antérieur is required in the dependent clause to mark anteriority.
conditions: after conjunctions like quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, tant que
exceptions: The futur antérieur is required when anteriority must be explicit
After quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, and tant que the future is used rather than the present
agreement_rules: The futur antérieur takes avoir or être; with être the past participle agrees with the subject
The futur simple itself shows no gender agreement
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause in futur simple + conjunction + dependent clause verb (futur antérieur for anteriority)
transformations: quand il acceptera -> quand il aura accepté (anteriority)
Quand il aura fini, il téléphonera.
common_traps: using futur simple when anteriority is intended

sources.source_text: Sometimes you have a choice between the futur simple and the futur antérieur. When both clauses use the futur simple, it is implied that both actions take place simultaneously. If you want to mark an anteriority, use the futur antérieur.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Color adjectives agree in gender and number
grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives describing colors usually agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation: Color adjectives follow normal agreement rules.
grammar_rules.formation: color adjective + -e (feminine) / + -s (plural), agreeing with the noun
restrictions: Agreement applies only to simple color adjectives.
Noun-derived colors (orange, marron, safran) and compound color adjectives are invariable.
conditions: Adjective is a simple color adjective.
exceptions: Color adjectives derived from nouns (orange, marron, safran) and compound color adjectives are invariable.
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with noun.
transformations: un livre vert -> une robe verte
un œil bleu -> des yeux bleus
des robes orange (invariable)

sources.source_text: Adjectives describing colors usually agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Color adjectives from nouns are invariable
grammar_rules.summary: Adjectives of color that are also nouns of fruit or plants remain in the masculine singular form.
grammar_rules.explanation: Orange, marron, safran are invariable because they originate as nouns.
grammar_rules.formation: noun-derived color adjective (orange, marron, safran) = invariable masculine singular form
