Adjectives followed by a complement always come after the noun
conditions: Default placement.
exceptions: Some short, common adjectives precede the noun.
agreement_rules: Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify, whether they follow or precede it.
Placement after the noun does not change the agreement pattern.
transformations: une voiture rouge
un livre intéressant
une femme intelligente
common_traps: Do not place all adjectives before the noun.

sources.source_text: In French, most qualificative adjectives follow the noun.

grammar_rules.summary: After negation, un, une, des change to de or d'.
grammar_rules.explanation: When a verb is negated, the indefinite articles un, une, des become de (or d' before a vowel).
restrictions: Limited to un, une, des and the partitive articles after a negated verb
Not applied after être, which keeps un/une (Il n'est pas un expert)
conditions: Applies to direct objects after negated verbs.
exceptions: After être, un and une are kept in the negative (Ce n'est pas un problème)
Only the article changes to de; the noun itself is not replaced
agreement_rules: After negation the article no longer shows gender or number: un/une/des all become invariable de (d' before a vowel).
The noun keeps its own gender and number; only the article form changes.
transformations: des amis -> pas d'amis

sources.source_text: Note that un, une, and des change to de or d’ when the verb is in the negative form. Tu as des amis à Paris? Non, je n’ai pas d’amis à Paris.

grammar_rules.summary: Place ne (n') before auxiliary and pas after auxiliary.
grammar_rules.explanation: Negative form of passé composé.
restrictions: ne and pas surround only the auxiliary, never the past participle
Requires a compound tense with an auxiliary; a simple conjugated verb is negated differently
conditions: The tense is the passé composé.
Ne (n') is placed before the auxiliary and pas after it, not around the past participle.
exceptions: ne and pas surround the auxiliary, never the past participle
Pronominal verbs place the reflexive pronoun between ne and the auxiliary
agreement_rules: Negation does not affect past participle agreement: with être the participle still agrees with the subject in gender and number.
With avoir, the participle still agrees with a preceding direct object in the negative.
grammar_rules.negative_form: Il n'a pas vendu sa voiture.
transformations: Il a vendu sa voiture. -> Il n'a pas vendu sa voiture.
J'ai dîné. -> Je n'ai pas dîné.
common_traps: Placement of ne and pas around auxiliary, not past participle

sources.source_text: In the negative form, ne (n') is placed in front of avoir or être, and pas after avoir or être.

grammar_rules.summary: Negation ne...pas precedes the infinitive and is not separated.
grammar_rules.explanation: Because the infinitive is not conjugated, the negative elements are placed before the infinitive as a unit.
restrictions: Applies only to a non-conjugated infinitive
ne and pas remain together before the infinitive and are never split around it
conditions: The verb to negate is in the infinitive.
Ne and pas precede the infinitive together and are not separated.
exceptions: ne and pas form a unit before the infinitive and are never split
With a conjugated verb, ne and pas normally surround the verb instead
agreement_rules: The infinitive carries no person or number agreement, so ne pas + infinitive stays invariable in form.
ne and pas are invariable negative particles and do not agree with the subject.
transformations: dîner -> ne pas dîner
Il a décidé de ne pas partir.
common_traps: Do not place ne before and pas after the infinitive.

sources.source_text: the negation (ne… pas) does not surround the verb but rather precedes it, and is not separated.

grammar_rules.summary: ni...ni... negates two nouns; ne before verb; articles behave differently.
grammar_rules.explanation: The negation ni...ni... precedes each noun it negates, and ne (n') comes before the verb. If a definite article (le, la, l', les) is used before the nouns in the affirmative, it remains in the negative. If an indefinite or partitive article is used, it disappears in the negative. Examples: Il n'aime ni le café ni le chocolat. Elle ne commande ni eau ni vin.
grammar_rules.formation: ne + verb + ni + noun1 + ni + noun2
restrictions: Requires at least two negated nouns; a single noun uses pas de
Definite articles (le, la, l', les) are kept, while indefinite and partitive articles disappear
ne precedes the verb and ni precedes each negated noun
conditions: Two items are negated together.
Ne (n') precedes the verb and ni precedes each noun; definite articles remain while indefinite and partitive articles disappear.
exceptions: Definite articles (le, la, l', les) are kept after ni
Indefinite and partitive articles disappear after ni
With a single negated noun, pas de replaces ni
agreement_rules: ni is invariable and is repeated before each negated element.
Definite articles (le, la, l', les) remain and keep their gender and number agreement, while indefinite and partitive articles disappear in the negative.
grammar_rules.word_order: ne + verb + ni + noun + ni + noun
transformations: Il aime le café et le chocolat. -> Il n'aime ni le café ni le chocolat.
Elle commande de l'eau et du vin. -> Elle ne commande ni eau ni vin.
common_traps: Remember definite articles stay; indefinite/partitive articles disappear.

sources.source_text: The negation ni… ni… precedes each noun that it negates.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Negative duration: passé composé instead of present
grammar_rules.summary: In negative sentences expressing duration of an action that began in the past and continues to the present, use the passé composé, not the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Exception to the general rule: in negative sentences with depuis, the passé composé is used.
grammar_rules.formation: ne + auxiliary (avoir/être) + pas + past participle + depuis + time
usage: To express that an action has not occurred for a duration (and still hasn't)
restrictions: Only in negative sentences
conditions: Sentence is negative; action has not happened for a duration
exceptions: In affirmative sentences with depuis, the present tense is used
The imparfait is used when the duration runs up to a past point
agreement_rules: Past participle agreement rules apply
grammar_rules.word_order: ne + auxiliary + pas + past participle + depuis + time
grammar_rules.negative_form: Il n'a pas revu sa sœur depuis dix ans.
transformations: Il voit sa sœur depuis dix ans. -> Il n'a pas revu sa sœur depuis dix ans.
Elle apprend le russe depuis deux ans. -> Elle n'a pas appris le russe depuis deux ans.
common_traps: Do not use present tense in negative duration sentences; use passé composé

sources.source_text: There is an important exception to the construction with depuis: In negative sentences, the passé composé is used instead of the present.

grammar_rules.summary: ne follows subject pronoun; pas follows conjugated verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: In the negative form, the ne follows the subject pronoun and the pas follows the conjugated verb.
restrictions: The reflexive pronoun stays between ne and the conjugated verb
In compound tenses ne and pas surround the auxiliary, with the reflexive pronoun before the auxiliary
conditions: The verb is reflexive and the sentence is negative.
Ne follows the subject pronoun and pas follows the conjugated verb.
exceptions: ne precedes the reflexive pronoun, not the verb alone
In compound tenses ne and pas surround the auxiliary, with the pronoun before it
agreement_rules: The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject in person and number (je me, tu te, il se, nous nous, vous vous, ils se).
ne and pas are invariable and do not agree with the subject.
transformations: Tu te couches. -> Tu ne te couches pas.
Je me lave. -> Je ne me lave pas.
common_traps: Do not place ne after the pronoun.

sources.source_text: In the negative form, the ne follows the subject pronoun and the pas follows the conjugated verb.

grammar_rules.summary: ne + pronoun + verb + pas
grammar_rules.explanation: For the negative imperative, use ne in front of the pronoun and pas after the verb. The reflexive pronoun precedes the verb, as in a normal sentence.
restrictions: Only in the negative imperative; the affirmative imperative places the pronoun after the verb
The reflexive pronoun precedes the verb in the negative
No subject pronoun is expressed in the imperative
conditions: The imperative is negative.
The order is ne + reflexive pronoun + verb + pas, with the pronoun before the verb.
exceptions: In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb
ne precedes the pronoun and pas follows the verb
agreement_rules: The reflexive pronoun agrees with the addressee: te (tu), nous (nous), vous (vous).
No third-person imperative exists, so there is no il/ils reflexive agreement.
transformations: Couche-toi! -> Ne te couche pas!
Lève-toi! -> Ne te lève pas!
common_traps: Do not place pronoun after verb in negative imperative.

sources.section_title: Pronominals in the imperative and the infinitive
sources.source_text: For the negative imperative of pronominal verbs, use ne in front of the pronoun and pas after the verb. Note that in the negative the reflexive pronoun precedes the verb, as it would in a normal sentence.

grammar_rules.summary: In the negative imperative, ne...pas surrounds the verb and object pronouns precede the verb (after ne/n’).
grammar_rules.explanation: In the negative form, the negation is placed around the verb; object pronouns immediately precede the verb following ne (n’).
restrictions: Only in the negative imperative; in the affirmative the pronoun follows the verb with a hyphen
Object pronouns immediately precede the verb, after ne/n'
No subject pronoun is expressed in the imperative
conditions: Only in negative imperative
exceptions: In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb with a hyphen
The object pronoun comes between ne and the verb
agreement_rules: The object pronoun agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces (le/la/les).
Imperative forms show no subject-pronoun agreement; they address tu, nous, or vous only.
transformations: Parle-lui! -> Ne lui parle pas!
Prends-le! -> Ne le prends pas!
common_traps: Incorrect pronoun placement after the verb in negative imperative.

sources.source_text: In the negative form, the negation is placed around the verb. Note that object pronouns immediately precede the verb (following ne [n’]) in the negative imperative.

grammar_rules.rule_name: No futur simple after 'si' in future condition
grammar_rules.summary: In French, futur simple is never used after 'si' implying a future condition; present tense is used instead.
grammar_rules.explanation: In French, the futur antérieur is never used after si implying a future condition. Use the present instead. (Note: this also applies to futur simple.)
grammar_rules.formation: si + present tense, main clause futur simple/imperative
usage: to express a condition for a future action
restrictions: only when 'si' means 'if' introducing a condition
conditions: Si means if and introduces a future condition.
The present tense is used in the si clause instead of the futur simple or futur antérieur.
exceptions: The futur antérieur is also excluded after si when si means 'if'
si meaning 'whether' may be followed by the future
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement; the si clause uses the present tense instead of the futur simple.
si is an invariable conjunction and triggers no agreement change.
grammar_rules.word_order: si + present tense clause, main clause in futur simple or imperative
transformations: Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
Si tu peux, téléphone-moi.
common_traps: using future tense after 'si' in conditional sentences

sources.source_text: In French, the futur antérieur is never used after si implying a future condition. Use the present instead.

grammar_rules.summary: When two object pronouns occur together, the indirect comes first unless both are third person, in which case direct comes first.
grammar_rules.explanation: Order: me/te/nous/vous before le/la/les; le/la/les before lui/leur; en always in second position.
grammar_rules.formation: me/te/nous/vous + le/la/les; le/la/les + lui/leur; indirect + en
restrictions: me, te, nous, vous come before le, la, les
le, la, les come before lui, leur
en always comes in second position, after the other object pronoun
conditions: Two object pronouns appear together in the same sentence.
The order is me/te/nous/vous before le/la/les before lui/leur, with en always in second position.
exceptions: me, te, nous, vous precede le, la, les
le, la, les precede lui, leur
en comes in second position, after the other object pronoun
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees with preceding direct object pronoun, not with en or indirect pronouns.
transformations: Il me le donne.
Je le lui donne.
Il m'en donne.
common_traps: Remember that third person direct object comes before third person indirect object.

sources.source_text: When a direct and indirect pronoun appear in the same sentence, the indirect object pronoun comes first, unless the direct and indirect pronouns are in the third person, in which case the direct object pronoun comes first.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Other negations (personne, jamais, plus, rien, guère)
grammar_rules.summary: Use ne...personne, ne...jamais, ne...plus, ne...rien, ne...guère.
grammar_rules.explanation: In addition to ne...pas, other negative particles can be used in the same construction: ne...personne (nobody), ne...jamais (never), ne...plus (no longer), ne...rien (nothing), ne...guère (hardly). Examples: Il n'attend personne. Tu ne voyages jamais en hiver. Il n'a plus de patience. Elle ne répond rien. Ce n'est guère raisonnable.
restrictions: ne is required before the verb in standard written French
personne, rien, and jamais can also function as subjects (Personne ne vient), in which case they precede ne
guère is restricted to formal or literary French
conditions: The sentence uses a negative particle other than pas (personne, jamais, plus, rien, guère).
Ne (n') precedes the verb, as in the ne...pas construction.
exceptions: personne, rien, and jamais can act as subjects, in which case they precede ne
guère is formal and rare in spoken French
plus meaning 'no longer' is distinct from plus meaning 'more'
agreement_rules: The negative particles personne, jamais, plus, rien, and guère are invariable.
When personne or rien is the subject, the verb agrees with it in the third-person singular (Personne n'est venu).
transformations: Il attend. -> Il n'attend personne.
Il voyage. -> Il ne voyage jamais.
Il a de la patience. -> Il n'a plus de patience.
common_traps: Do not confuse plus (no longer) with plus (more); note guère is formal.

sources.source_text: Aside from ne... pas, there are other negations, constructed in the same way.

grammar_rules.summary: Où replaces dans lequel, sur lequel, par lequel, etc., when referring to a place.
grammar_rules.explanation: C’est le magasin dans lequel je fais mes courses. C’est le magasin où je fais mes courses. La région dans laquelle ils habitent est très calme. La région où ils habitent est très calme.
restrictions: Only when the antecedent expresses a place
Cannot be preceded by a preposition; à où and de où do not occur
conditions: antecedent expresses a place
exceptions: où cannot be preceded by a preposition; dans lequel or sur lequel is required there
où is not used when the antecedent is a person
agreement_rules: où is invariable and does not agree in gender or number with its antecedent.
Unlike lequel, où carries no gender or number marking.
transformations: où = dans lequel, sur lequel, par lequel, etc.

sources.source_text: C’est le magasin où je fais mes courses.

grammar_rules.summary: Où is also used when the antecedent expresses time, meaning when.
grammar_rules.explanation: Tu te souviens de l’année où il est arrivé dans la région? Le jour où il a été élu, tout le monde était content. L’instant où nous sommes partis, il a commencé à pleuvoir. Le dix-neuvième siècle fut un siècle où il y eut de nombreuses inventions.
restrictions: Only when the antecedent expresses time (e.g. l'année, le jour, l'instant, le siècle)
Où here means 'when' and does not replace a place prepositional phrase
conditions: antecedent expresses time
exceptions: où meaning 'when' cannot be replaced by quand in this relative construction
où is not used when the antecedent is a person
agreement_rules: où is invariable when the antecedent expresses time; it marks no gender or number agreement.
The time antecedent (année, jour, instant, siècle) transfers no agreement to où.
transformations: l'année où il est arrivé
le jour où il a été élu
l'instant où nous sommes partis

sources.source_text: Tu te souviens de l’année où il est arrivé dans la région?

grammar_rules.summary: In negative, du/de la/de l'/des become de (or d').
grammar_rules.explanation: Because quantity doesn't exist, partitive article is replaced by de.
grammar_rules.formation: du/de la/de l'/des → de (or d' before vowel/mute h)
usage: to express negation of existence of mass/plural items
restrictions: Exception: after être, partitive remains
conditions: after ne...pas
exceptions: C'est du fromage → Ce n'est pas du fromage (être retains partitive)
agreement_rules: In the negative, du/de la/de l'/des all become invariable de (d' before a vowel), so the article no longer shows gender or number.
After être the partitive article remains and keeps its gender and number agreement (Ce n'est pas du fromage).
transformations: du pain → pas de pain
des amis → pas d'amis
common_traps: Do not use de after être in negative.

sources.source_text: When used in the negative, the du, de la, and des all become de, since the quantity of the item doesn’t exist any longer.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Partitive article: du, de la, de l', des
grammar_rules.summary: Use partitive article to express unspecified quantity: du, de la, de l', des.
grammar_rules.explanation: Partitive article is required in French where English often omits 'some'.
grammar_rules.formation: de + le = du; de + l' = de l'; de + la = de la; de + les = des
usage: to indicate an unspecified amount of a mass noun
to indicate some of a plural noun
restrictions: Limited to mass nouns and plural count nouns whose quantity is unspecified
Becomes de (or d' before a vowel) in negative sentences, except after être
Not used after quantity expressions, which take de alone (beaucoup de, trop de)
conditions: used with non-count nouns and plural count nouns when quantity is unknown
exceptions: In negative sentences, du/de la/de l'/des become de (except after être).
agreement_rules: agrees with noun gender and number
grammar_rules.negative_form: du/de la/de l'/des → de (or d' before vowel/mute h)
transformations: de + le = du
de + les = des
common_traps: Do not use de after être in negative; keep partitive: Ce n'est pas du fromage.

sources.source_text: The partitive article is used when the exact quantity of an item is unknown... It is formed by combining de and the definite article. de + le = du; de + l’ = de l’; de + la = de la; de + les = des.

grammar_rules.summary: A pronominal verb construction can express passive meaning.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pronominal verbs (like se dire, se traduire, se voir, se boire) can have passive meaning.
usage: To express passive meaning in a more natural French way.
restrictions: Limited to pronominal verbs such as se dire, se traduire, se voir, se boire
No agent is expressed with this passive meaning
conditions: A pronominal verb such as se dire, se traduire, se voir, or se boire is used.
The subject undergoes the action rather than performing it.
exceptions: Limited to pronominal verbs such as se dire, se traduire, se voir, and se boire
No agent is expressed with this passive meaning
agreement_rules: In compound tenses the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject (Ces livres se sont bien vendus).
The reflexive pronoun se agrees with the subject in person and number.
transformations: dire -> ça se dit
voir -> ça se voit
traduire -> comment ça se traduit

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: In Chapter 6, you studied one type of pronominal verb called the passive pronominal. This construction is another example of the voix passive.

grammar_rules.summary: Subject not person/animal; verb in 3rd person singular with se; expresses passive meaning.
grammar_rules.explanation: With passive pronominal verbs, the subject does not perform the action but is subjected to it. It is in the third-person singular, with se.
restrictions: Subject is not a person or animal.
conditions: The subject is a thing, not a person or an animal.
The verb is in the third-person singular with se and expresses passive meaning.
exceptions: The subject is never a person or an animal
The verb is always third-person singular with se
No agent phrase is used with this construction
agreement_rules: The verb is third person and agrees with the grammatical subject, not with an agent.
The reflexive pronoun se matches the subject in person and number.
transformations: ça se dit
ça ne se dit pas

sources.source_text: With the passive pronominal verbs, the subject is not a person or an animal. The subject does not perform the action of the verb but rather is subjected to it. It is in the third-person singular, with se.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Passive used to avoid specifying agent
grammar_rules.summary: The passive voice is used to avoid mentioning who performed the action.
grammar_rules.explanation: When the agent is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately omitted, the passive voice is used.
grammar_rules.formation: être (conjugated) + past participle, without par + agent
restrictions: Used only when the agent is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately omitted
If the agent must be named, the active voice or an explicit par-phrase is used instead
conditions: The agent is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately omitted.
The sentence is put in the passive voice.
exceptions: If the agent must be named, the active voice or an explicit par-phrase is used
The passive is not used when the agent is the focus of the message
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject of the passive sentence.
Omitting the agent (par + noun) does not affect participle agreement with the subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + être (conjugated) + past participle, with no par + agent phrase
transformations: On a construit la maison. -> La maison a été construite.
On a volé les tableaux. -> Les tableaux ont été volés.

sources.source_text: The voix passive is also used to avoid specifying the agent of the action.

grammar_rules.summary: The passive voice is used to emphasize the subject (the receiver of the action).
grammar_rules.explanation: By placing the receiver of the action as the subject, the passive voice draws attention to it.
grammar_rules.formation: receiver of the action as subject + être (conjugated) + past participle (+ par + agent)
restrictions: Used only when the receiver of the action is the focus of the sentence
Not used when the agent is the more important element of the message
conditions: The receiver of the action is placed in subject position.
The speaker wants to draw attention to that receiver.
exceptions: Not used when the agent is the more important element
The passive here does not imply an unknown agent; the agent may still appear with par
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject of the passive sentence.
The agent, when expressed, is introduced by par and does not control agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: receiver of the action as subject + être (conjugated) + past participle (+ par + agent)
transformations: Le président a signé la loi. -> La loi a été signée par le président.
Les élèves ont écrit la lettre. -> La lettre a été écrite par les élèves.

sources.source_text: The voix passive is used to emphasize the subject.

grammar_rules.summary: The passive voice is formed with être in the required tense plus the past participle of the main verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: In the passive voice, the subject is acted upon. The verb être is conjugated in the appropriate tense, and the past participle agrees with the subject.
usage: To express that the subject undergoes the action.
restrictions: Limited to transitive verbs that can take a direct object
The past participle agrees with the subject, not with the agent
Never formed with avoir as the auxiliary
conditions: The subject undergoes the action rather than performing it.
Être is conjugated in the required tense and followed by the past participle, which agrees with the subject.
exceptions: Limited to transitive verbs that can take a direct object
The past participle agrees with the subject, not with the agent
Never formed with avoir as the auxiliary
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + être (conjugated in the required tense) + past participle agreeing with the subject
transformations: La maison est construite.
La maison a été construite.
Les maisons sont construites.

sources.source_text: The passive voice is formed with être in the tense required + the past participle of the main verb.

grammar_rules.summary: The passé composé is formed with auxiliary (avoir or être) + past participle.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to talk about past events; refers to a single action in the past.
restrictions: Requires an auxiliary (avoir or être); a single conjugated verb is not a passé composé
Most verbs take avoir, while a limited set of verbs and all pronominal verbs take être
Only the auxiliary is negated, with ne...pas surrounding it
conditions: A single completed action in the past is described.
The auxiliary avoir or être is followed by the past participle of the main verb.
exceptions: Most verbs take avoir, while a limited set of verbs and all pronominal verbs take être
Only the auxiliary is negated, with ne...pas surrounding it
A single conjugated verb is not a passé composé
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject when the auxiliary is être.
With avoir, the past participle agrees only with a preceding direct object.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: rising intonation, inversion, or est-ce que
transformations: avoir + participe passé: j'ai vendu
être + participe passé: je suis allé

study.frequency_note: Most common past tense in spoken French

sources.source_text: It is built of two parts: the auxiliary or helping verb, avoir or être, + a past participle.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Past conditional for regret or reproach
grammar_rules.summary: The past conditional expresses regret or reproach about past actions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to indicate what should have been done or what one would have liked.
restrictions: Limited to unrealized past actions, not to present or future ones
Typically used with verbs such as devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, and aimer plus an infinitive
conditions: The speaker expresses regret or reproach about a past action.
The past conditional is used, often with aurais dû, aurait aimé, or aurait voulu plus an infinitive.
exceptions: Limited to unrealized past actions, not to present or future ones
Typically used with verbs such as devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, and aimer plus an infinitive
agreement_rules: The past participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is être; with avoir it agrees with a preceding direct object.
The regret or reproach meaning does not change compound-tense agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: auxiliary (avoir/être) in conditionnel présent + past participle (+ infinitive after devoir/vouloir/aimer)
transformations: j'aurais dû partir
j'aurais aimé venir
il aurait voulu savoir

sources.source_text: The passé du conditionnel can express regret or reproach.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Past conditional for unconfirmed past information (journalistic)
grammar_rules.summary: The past conditional is used like the present conditional as a conditionnel journalistique to express unconfirmed past information.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often translated with 'reportedly' or 'allegedly'.
restrictions: Limited to journalistic reporting of information not confirmed by authorities
Not used for verified factual statements, where the indicative is required
conditions: The statement is unconfirmed or alleged past information (conditionnel journalistique).
The past conditional is used, translatable as reportedly or allegedly.
exceptions: Not used for verified factual reporting, which takes the indicative
Typically third-person, reporting what others are said to have done
agreement_rules: The past participle follows normal compound-tense agreement: with être it agrees with the subject, with avoir with a preceding direct object.
The journalistic (unconfirmed) value does not change the agreement rules.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + auxiliary in conditionnel présent + past participle
transformations: il aurait volé le tableau
elle se serait installée à Lyon
le président l'aurait gracié
common_traps: Do not confuse with factual past reporting.

sources.source_text: The passé du conditionnel is used like the present du conditionnel as a conditionnel journalistique to express a statement not necessarily confirmed by authorities.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Past conditional with si clause in plus-que-parfait
grammar_rules.summary: The past conditional is usually found in sentences where the si clause is in the plus-que-parfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expresses hypothetical situations in the past.
grammar_rules.formation: si + plus-que-parfait, main clause in past conditional
restrictions: The si clause must be in the plus-que-parfait; the past conditional never appears after si
Used only for hypothetical past situations that did not actually occur
conditions: si clause must be in plus-que-parfait
exceptions: The past conditional never appears in the si clause
For present or future hypotheses, si + imparfait with the present conditional is used instead
agreement_rules: Both clauses keep normal compound-tense agreement: participles with être agree with the subject, participles with avoir agree with a preceding direct object.
The plus-que-parfait si clause shows the same agreement rules as the main clause.
grammar_rules.word_order: si + plus-que-parfait clause, main clause in past conditional
transformations: Si j'avais su, j'aurais agi autrement.
Si elle était partie plus tôt, elle aurait pris le train.
common_traps: Do not use past conditional in the si clause.

sources.source_text: The passé du conditionnel is usually found in sentences where the si (dependent) clause is in the plus-que-parfait.

grammar_rules.summary: Infinitif passé = avoir or être infinitive + past participle of main verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs conjugated with être in compound tenses, the past participle agrees with the subject.
restrictions: The auxiliary stays in the infinitive (avoir/être) and is never conjugated
Agreement with the subject occurs only when the auxiliary is être
conditions: Agreement of past participle with subject when using être.
exceptions: Agreement with the subject occurs only with être, not with avoir
The auxiliary is never conjugated; it stays in the infinitive
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees with subject when auxiliary is être.
transformations: avoir + participe passé: avoir mangé
être + participe passé: être parti(e)
common_traps: Remember agreement with être.

study.frequency_note: Common in written and formal French

sources.source_text: It is formed with the infinitive of avoir or être and the past participle of the main verb. (Note that, for verbs conjugated with être, the past participle of the infinitif passé agrees with the subject of the sentence.)

grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in future, change the dependent verb to conditionnel.
grammar_rules.explanation: Future recounted in the present conditional.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb conditionnel
usage: When reporting future statements with a past main clause
restrictions: Applies only when the main clause is in a past tense such as the passé composé
Requires the direct speech to be in the future tense
Not applied when the main clause is in the present, which keeps the future form
conditions: Direct speech is in future tense
Main clause is in passé composé
exceptions: When the main clause is in the present, the future is kept in the dependent clause
The conditionnel here marks a tense shift, not a hypothesis
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement after the tense shift.
The shift from future to conditionnel does not alter agreement of the dependent verb with its subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause in passé composé + que + dependent verb in conditionnel
transformations: Future → Conditionnel

sources.section_title: Future recounted in the present conditional
sources.source_text: If the direct speech is in the future, the dependent clause verb is changed into the conditionnel in the indirect speech.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Past main clause: passé composé → plus-que-parfait
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in passé composé, change the dependent verb to plus-que-parfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Passé composé recounted in the plus-que-parfait.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb plus-que-parfait
usage: When reporting passé composé statements with a past main clause
restrictions: Applies only when the main clause is in a past tense such as the passé composé
Requires the direct speech to be in the passé composé
Not applied when the main clause is in the present, which keeps the passé composé
conditions: Direct speech is in passé composé
Main clause is in passé composé
exceptions: When the main clause is in the present, the passé composé is kept in the dependent clause
The plus-que-parfait marks anteriority relative to the past main clause
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement; the shift to plus-que-parfait does not change agreement.
Participles still agree with the subject when the auxiliary is être and with a preceding direct object when the auxiliary is avoir.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause (passé composé) + que + dependent verb (plus-que-parfait)
transformations: Passé composé → Plus-que-parfait

sources.section_title: Passé composé recounted in the plus-que-parfait
sources.source_text: If the direct speech is in the passé composé, the verb in the dependent clause is changed into the plus-que-parfait.

grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in passé composé and direct speech is in present, change the dependent verb to imparfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Present recounted in the imparfait.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause passé composé + dependent verb imparfait
usage: When reporting present tense statements with a past main clause
restrictions: Applies only when the main clause is in a past tense such as the passé composé
Requires the direct speech to be in the present tense
Not applied when the main clause is in the present, which keeps the present form
conditions: Direct speech is in present tense
Main clause is in passé composé
exceptions: When the main clause is in the present, the present is kept in the dependent clause
The imparfait marks the shift into indirect speech, not a habitual past meaning
agreement_rules: The tense shift from present to imparfait preserves subject-verb agreement in person and number.
Imparfait endings continue to mark person and number in the dependent clause.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause (passé composé) + que + dependent verb (imparfait)
transformations: Present → Imparfait

sources.source_text: If the direct speech is in the present tense, the dependent clause verb is changed into the imparfait.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Past participle agreement with preceding direct object (que)
grammar_rules.summary: In compound tenses, if the direct object is placed before the verb, the past participle agrees in gender and number with that direct object, including when que refers back to it.
grammar_rules.explanation: C’est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces. La pièce qu’il a écrite n’a jamais été jouée. Montrez-moi la photo que vous avez prise. Les chaises qu’ils ont restaurées sont comme neuves.
grammar_rules.formation: direct object + avoir/être + past participle agreeing with object
restrictions: Limited to compound tenses where the direct object precedes the verb
Requires the relative pronoun que to refer back to that preceding direct object
No agreement occurs when the direct object follows the verb
conditions: compound tense
direct object before verb
exceptions: No agreement when the direct object follows the verb
No agreement with en or with indirect object pronouns
Agreement is with the direct object, not with the subject
agreement_rules: past participle agrees with preceding direct object
grammar_rules.word_order: preceding direct object + que + subject + auxiliary + past participle
transformations: C'est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces.
La pièce qu'il a écrite n'a jamais été jouée.
Montrez-moi la photo que vous avez prise.

sources.source_text: C’est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces.

grammar_rules.summary: Past participle agrees with subject in gender and number.
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs conjugated with être (non-pronominal), past participle agrees with subject.
grammar_rules.formation: être (conjugated) + past participle + -e/-s agreeing with the subject
restrictions: Limited to non-pronominal verbs conjugated with être
Does not apply to verbs conjugated with avoir unless a direct object precedes the participle
Pronominal verbs follow their own agreement rules instead
conditions: verb uses être
exceptions: pronominal verbs have specific rules
agreement_rules: agrees with subject in gender and number
transformations: Elle est arrivée en retard.
Elles sont nées en 1990.
common_traps: Forgetting to add -e or -s

sources.source_text: The past participle of verbs conjugated with être agrees in gender and number with the subject.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Pendant vs pour for past duration
grammar_rules.summary: Use pendant (or omit it) to express duration in the past. Do not use pour for duration in the past.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pendant means 'for' or 'during' and is used with the passé composé to indicate how long an action lasted. It may be omitted. Pour is never used for duration in the past.
usage: To express duration of a completed past action
restrictions: Only for past completed actions
conditions: Passé composé or other past tense
exceptions: pendant may be omitted entirely (Il a habité cinq ans à Londres)
pour is never used for duration in the past
agreement_rules: Pendant is invariable and does not agree with the noun expressing duration.
The past participle still agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is être (Elle est restée pendant deux ans).
grammar_rules.affirmative_form: Il a habité pendant cinq ans à Londres.
transformations: pendant may be omitted: Il a habité cinq ans à Londres.
common_traps: Do not use pour for duration in the past

sources.section_title: Using adverbs with the passé composé
sources.source_text: To express time with the passé composé, pendant (for, during) is commonly used (although it can actually be omitted). However, pour (for) is never used to talk about duration in the past.

grammar_rules.summary: Penser and croire in the affirmative are followed by the indicative; in negative or interrogative, the subjunctive may be used to express uncertainty.
grammar_rules.explanation: Affirmative: Je pense qu'il vient (indicative). Negative: Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne (subjunctive) may indicate doubt. The choice can convey different degrees of certainty.
grammar_rules.formation: Affirmative: penser/croire + que + indicative. Negative/interrogative: ne pas penser/croire + que + subjunctive (optional).
restrictions: Subjunctive in negative/interrogative is optional and indicates more uncertainty.
conditions: Negative or interrogative form of penser/croire.
exceptions: The affirmative takes the indicative, not the subjunctive
In the negative and interrogative the subjunctive is optional and signals greater uncertainty
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement in person and number, whether indicative or subjunctive.
The choice of mood does not change agreement: subjunctive forms also agree with their subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: affirmative: penser/croire + que + indicative; negative: ne + penser/croire + pas + que + subjunctive
transformations: Je pense qu'il vient. -> Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne.
Je crois que Daniel est coupable. -> Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable.
common_traps: Using subjunctive after affirmative penser/croire.

sources.source_text: The verbs penser (to think) and croire (to believe) in the affirmative are followed by the indicative mood. However, in the negative and interrogative, the subjunctive can be used to underline the uncertainty of the event. Je ne crois pas que Daniel est coupable. / Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable.

grammar_rules.summary: When an action precedes another, use avoir or être in the present participle combined with a past participle. The past participle agrees with the subject if the verb is conjugated with être.
grammar_rules.explanation: Forms: ayant vu, ayant compris, ayant joué, ayant traversé, étant allé(e)(s), étant parti(e)(s), nous étant promené(e)s, nous étant retrouvé(e)s.
restrictions: Used only when one action precedes another
Agreement with the subject occurs only when the auxiliary is être
The auxiliary appears in the present participle (ayant/étant), never conjugated
conditions: action precedes another
exceptions: agreement with être
agreement_rules: past participle agrees with subject if auxiliary is être
transformations: ayant vu
étant allé(e)(s)
n'ayant pas compris
common_traps: forgetting agreement with être

sources.source_text: When an action precedes another one, avoir and être in the participe présent can be combined with a participe passé. Note that the past participle agrees with the subject of the sentence if the verb is conjugated with être.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Placement of short adverbs in passé composé
grammar_rules.summary: Short adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency are placed between the auxiliary (avoir/être) and the past participle in the passé composé.
grammar_rules.explanation: In compound tenses, short adverbs like beaucoup, trop, assez, bien, mal, souvent, rarement, toujours, etc., appear between the auxiliary and the past participle.
usage: To modify a verb in the passé composé with a short adverb
restrictions: Applies to short adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency
conditions: Passé composé tense
exceptions: The adverb goes between the auxiliary and the past participle, not after the participle
Longer adverbs and time expressions stand outside the auxiliary + participle block
agreement_rules: Short adverbs (beaucoup, trop, assez, bien, souvent, toujours) are invariable and never agree with the subject.
Past participle agreement is unchanged: with être it agrees with the subject, with avoir with a preceding direct object.
transformations: Elle a beaucoup étudié.
Il a trop mangé.
Nous avons souvent voyagé.
common_traps: Do not place the adverb after the past participle

sources.section_title: Using adverbs with the passé composé
sources.source_text: In the passé composé, shorter adverbs of quantity, quality, and frequency are placed between avoir or être and the past participle.

grammar_rules.summary: Most nouns add -s to form plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: Basic plural formation.
restrictions: Does not apply to nouns already ending in -s, -x, or -z, which stay unchanged
Does not apply to nouns in -al, which form -aux
Does not apply to nouns in -eau or -eu, which take -x
conditions: The noun is a regular noun that does not already end in -s, -x, or -z.
The plural is formed by adding -s; -eu and -eau take -x and -al becomes -aux.
exceptions: nouns ending in -s, -x, -z unchanged; -eu, -eau → -x; -al → -aux
agreement_rules: Plural nouns require plural agreement of determiners and adjectives (les livres intéressants).
The plural -s is not pronounced but agreement is marked in writing.
transformations: maison → maisons
livre → livres
common_traps: Remember liaison after plural article.

sources.source_text: In most cases, an -s is added to a noun to make it plural.

grammar_rules.summary: Cent takes -s when multiplied by a number greater than 1 and not followed by another number (deux cents); no -s when followed by another number (deux cent trois).
grammar_rules.explanation: Add an -s to cent greater than one hundred (deux cents, trois cents), except when cent is followed by another number (deux cent trois).
grammar_rules.formation: cent (100), deux cents (200), trois cents (300); but deux cent trois (203).
restrictions: No -s when cent is followed by another number (deux cent trois)
No -s when cent stands alone or is not multiplied (cent, cent un)
conditions: No -s when cent is followed by another number.
exceptions: No -s when cent is followed by another number (deux cent trois)
No -s when cent stands alone or is not multiplied (cent, cent un)
agreement_rules: Cent agrees in number when it is multiplied and not followed by another number.
grammar_rules.word_order: multiplier + cent + -s (only when not followed by another number)
transformations: deux cents
trois cents
deux cent trois
common_traps: Do not add -s to cent when followed by another number.
related_concepts: Plural of cent, mille, million, milliard

sources.source_text: Add an -s to cent greater than one hundred (deux cents, trois cents), except when cent is followed by another number.

grammar_rules.summary: Mille never takes -s; million and milliard take -s when greater than one.
grammar_rules.explanation: Never add an -s to mille (one thousand). In French, an -s is added to million and milliard greater than un (one).
grammar_rules.formation: mille (1000), deux mille (2000); un million, deux millions; un milliard, deux milliards.
restrictions: mille is invariable and never takes -s
million and milliard take -s only when greater than un
million and milliard are nouns and require de before a following noun (deux millions de personnes)
conditions: Mille is invariable; million/milliard agree in number.
exceptions: mille never takes -s, unlike million and milliard
million and milliard take de before a following noun (deux millions de personnes)
agreement_rules: Mille: no agreement; million/milliard: plural -s when > 1.
grammar_rules.word_order: number + mille (invariable); number + million/milliard + -s (when greater than un)
transformations: mille -> deux mille (no -s)
un million -> deux millions
un milliard -> deux milliards
common_traps: Do not add -s to mille.
related_concepts: Plural of cent, mille, million, milliard

sources.source_text: Never add an -s to mille (one thousand). In French, an -s is added to million and milliard greater than un (one).

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they modify
grammar_rules.summary: Possessive adjectives express relationship/ownership and agree in gender and number with the noun, not the possessor.
grammar_rules.explanation: Possessive adjectives modify nouns and agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.formation: Masculine singular: mon, ton, son, notre, votre, leur; feminine singular: ma, ta, sa, notre, votre, leur; plural: mes, tes, ses, nos, vos, leurs.
restrictions: Agreement is with the possessed noun, not with the possessor
son/sa/ses can mean his, her, or its; only context disambiguates
The masculine forms mon, ton, son replace ma, ta, sa before feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or mute h
conditions: A possessive adjective modifies a noun to express relationship or ownership.
The form agrees in gender and number with the possessed noun; mon, ton, son precede a feminine singular noun beginning with a vowel or mute h.
exceptions: Mon, ton, son are used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or mute h (e.g., mon amie, ton amitié, son honnêteté).
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.
transformations: mon livre / ma maison / mes livres
ma amie -> mon amie
common_traps: Son, sa, ses can mean his or her; context usually disambiguates.

sources.source_text: Possessive adjectives modify nouns and are used to express relationship and ownership. They agree in gender and number with the noun they modify.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive pronouns replace noun + possessive adjective
grammar_rules.summary: Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives and agree with the noun replaced.
grammar_rules.explanation: Possessive pronouns (le mien, la mienne, etc.) replace a noun modified by a possessive adjective.
grammar_rules.formation: le mien / la mienne / les miens / les miennes / le tien / la tienne / les tiens / les tiennes / le sien / la sienne / les siens / les siennes / le nôtre / la nôtre / les nôtres / le vôtre / la vôtre / les vôtres / le leur / la leur / les leurs.
usage: Replacing a noun to avoid repetition
restrictions: Always preceded by a definite article (le, la, les)
Agreement is with the replaced noun, not with the possessor
à and de contract with the article (au mien, du mien); à le mien and de le mien do not occur
conditions: Preceded by definite article (le, la, les).
exceptions: When preceded by à or de, contractions occur: au mien, du mien, etc.
agreement_rules: Agree in gender and number with the noun replaced, not with the possessor.
transformations: mon livre -> le mien
mes livres -> les miens
à le mien -> au mien
common_traps: Forgetting to contract à/de with the article (au lieu de "à le mien", use "au mien").

sources.source_text: Possessive pronouns replace nouns used with possessive adjectives. They agree in gender and number with the noun they replace, not with the possessor.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Possessive pronouns with aussi and non plus
grammar_rules.summary: Use possessive pronouns with aussi (affirmative) and non plus (negative) to confirm statements.
grammar_rules.explanation: The possessive pronoun is used with aussi to confirm an affirmative statement and with non plus to confirm a negative statement.
grammar_rules.formation: le mien aussi / le mien non plus
restrictions: aussi is used only in affirmative contexts
non plus is used only in negative contexts
conditions: An affirmative statement is confirmed with aussi.
A negative statement is confirmed with non plus.
exceptions: aussi is used only in affirmative contexts and non plus only in negative ones
The pronoun still agrees with the replaced noun, not with the possessor
agreement_rules: Possessive pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces.
transformations: ma voiture -> la mienne aussi
ma voiture -> la mienne non plus
common_traps: Using aussi in negative contexts or non plus in affirmative contexts.

sources.section_title: Possessive pronouns with aussi and non plus
sources.source_text: The possessive pronoun is also often used with aussi and non plus to confirm an affirmative or negative statement.

grammar_rules.summary: When used in a single clause, pourvu que expresses hope and is followed by the subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pourvu que + subjunctive can be used as an exclamation to express a wish or hope.
restrictions: Only in a single clause.
conditions: Pourvu que is used in a single clause as an exclamation.
The verb that follows is in the subjunctive.
exceptions: Only in a single clause; in a two-clause construction it means 'provided that'
The subjunctive is still required in this use
agreement_rules: Pourvu que is invariable; the subjunctive verb agrees with its own subject in person and number.
The exclamatory single-clause use does not change subject agreement.
transformations: Pourvu qu'il vienne!
Pourvu qu'il fasse beau!
common_traps: Confusing the two meanings.

sources.source_text: When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning. It is a handy expression, also followed by the subjunctive, that expresses hopes and desires.

grammar_rules.summary: Pourvu que is a conjunction meaning 'provided that' and is followed by the subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: In a two-clause construction, pourvu que introduces a condition.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause + pourvu que + subjunctive clause.
restrictions: Always followed by the subjunctive
Requires a subordinate clause with its own subject; it is not followed by an infinitive
Occurs only in a two-clause construction (main clause + pourvu que clause)
conditions: Pourvu que introduces a condition in a two-clause construction.
The verb of the subordinate clause is in the subjunctive.
exceptions: In a single clause, pourvu que expresses hope instead of a condition
The subjunctive is required in both uses
agreement_rules: Pourvu que is invariable and introduces a subjunctive clause whose verb agrees with its own subject.
The main clause and the pourvu que clause agree independently with their own subjects.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause + pourvu que + subjunctive clause
transformations: Je viendrai, pourvu que tu sois là.
Nous sortirons pourvu qu'il ne pleuve pas.

sources.source_text: Pourvu que has the sense of provided that.

grammar_rules.summary: Use à to express in/to for cities.
grammar_rules.explanation: Cities generally do not take an article and use à.
usage: to express location or direction to a city
restrictions: Some cities have article: Le Caire, La Havane, etc.
conditions: The place is a city, normally used without an article.
À expresses both location in and direction to that city.
exceptions: Le Caire
La Nouvelle-Orléans
La Havane
Le Havre
La Rochelle
Le Touquet
agreement_rules: à is invariable; city names normally take no article, so no gender or number agreement applies.
Cities that do carry an article keep it and agree accordingly (Le Caire, La Havane).
transformations: aller à Paris
habiter à Tokyo
Le Havre -> au Havre
common_traps: Do not use en/au for cities.

sources.source_text: With cities, the preposition à is used. Cities are usually not preceded by an article.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with countries: en, au, aux
grammar_rules.summary: Use en for feminine countries and masculine starting with vowel; au for masculine; aux for plural.
grammar_rules.explanation: Preposition depends on gender and number of country.
grammar_rules.formation: en + feminine or vowel-starting masculine; au + masculine singular; aux + plural
restrictions: à is not used directly before a country name
en is used only for feminine countries and masculine countries beginning with a vowel
Cities take à, not en or au
conditions: gender and number of country
exceptions: à is not used before country names; cities take à
en is used only for feminine countries and masculine countries beginning with a vowel
agreement_rules: The preposition reflects the country's gender and number: en + feminine or vowel-initial masculine, au + masculine singular, aux + plural.
Contracted forms au (à + le) and aux (à + les) show the country's gender and number.
transformations: aller en France (feminine)
aller au Canada (masculine)
aller aux États-Unis (plural)
common_traps: Do not use à for countries.

sources.source_text: en before feminine countries and regions; en before masculine countries beginning with a vowel; au before singular masculine countries; aux before plural countries.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with islands: à, aux, en
grammar_rules.summary: Usually à for islands, aux for plural; exceptions with en.
grammar_rules.explanation: Island usage varies; à is common.
grammar_rules.formation: à + island; aux + plural; en for some exceptions
restrictions: Usage varies by island, so the pattern is not fully predictable
The exceptions en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe do not take à
Plural island groups take aux, not à
conditions: The place is an island or an island group.
À is used for singular islands, aux for plural islands, and a few islands take en (en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe).
exceptions: en Haïti
en Martinique
en Guadeloupe
agreement_rules: à is used for a single island and aux for plural island groups, reflecting the island's number.
Exceptions with en (en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe) show no gender or number marking in the preposition.
transformations: aller à Cuba
aller aux Baléares (plural)
aller en Martinique (exception)
common_traps: Some islands use en, not à.

sources.source_text: Although usage may vary, the preposition à (aux in the plural) is often used for islands. Some exceptions: en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Preposition with states/provinces: en, au, dans le
grammar_rules.summary: Use en for feminine or vowel-starting masculine states; au for masculine; dans le sometimes replaces au.
grammar_rules.explanation: Similar to countries but with variation.
grammar_rules.formation: en + feminine/vowel masculine; au + masculine; dans le + masculine consonant
usage: to express in/to a state or province
restrictions: en applies only to feminine states/provinces or masculine ones beginning with a vowel
au applies to masculine states, not to feminine ones
dans le is used with masculine states beginning with a consonant instead of au
conditions: The place is a state, province, or department.
En is used before feminine nouns and masculine nouns beginning with a vowel, while au or dans le is used before masculine nouns beginning with a consonant.
exceptions: dans le often replaces au before masculine states beginning with a consonant
en applies only to feminine states or masculine states beginning with a vowel
agreement_rules: The preposition reflects the state's gender and number: en + feminine or vowel-initial masculine, au + masculine.
dans le contains the masculine singular article, so the state's masculine gender is marked explicitly.
transformations: au Texas
dans le Midi
common_traps: dans le often replaces au for masculine states starting with consonant.

sources.source_text: However, with provinces, departments, or states, the preposition may vary. Before feminine nouns or masculine nouns starting with a vowel, use en. Au is used in front of masculine states. In front of masculine nouns starting with a consonant, dans le often replaces au.

grammar_rules.summary: The present conditional makes statements or requests more polite.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used with verbs like pouvoir, vouloir, etc.
restrictions: Used for politeness only, not to express a hypothetical condition
Typically limited to verbs such as pouvoir and vouloir followed by an infinitive
conditions: A request or statement is to be made more polite.
The present conditional of a verb such as pouvoir or vouloir is used (Pourriez-vous + infinitif).
exceptions: Not used to express a real hypothesis, which requires a si clause
Typically limited to verbs such as pouvoir and vouloir
agreement_rules: The conditional verb agrees with the subject in person and number (pourriez-vous, est-ce que tu pourrais).
Politeness does not alter subject-verb agreement.
transformations: Pouvez-vous m'aider? -> Pourriez-vous m'aider?
Voulez-vous venir? -> Voudriez-vous venir?

sources.source_text: The présent du conditionnel is used to make a statement or a request more polite.

grammar_rules.summary: The present conditional expresses unconfirmed or alleged information, known as conditionnel journalistique.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used in press or news to indicate that information is reported but not confirmed.
restrictions: Limited to press or news reporting of information that is not confirmed
Not used for verified facts, which take the indicative
conditions: The information is reported but not confirmed (conditionnel journalistique).
The present conditional is used in press or news style, translatable as reportedly or allegedly.
exceptions: Not used for verified facts, which take the indicative
Limited to press and news register
agreement_rules: The conditional verb agrees with the subject in person and number.
The journalistic use does not change agreement rules.
transformations: il serait impliqué dans l'affaire
le contrat serait signé
elle se rendrait à Paris
common_traps: Do not confuse with factual reporting.

sources.source_text: The présent du conditionnel is also used to express unconfirmed or alleged information. In this case it is called the conditionnel journalistique.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present conditional for wish or suggestion
grammar_rules.summary: The present conditional expresses a wish or a suggestion.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to soften requests or express desires.
restrictions: Used to soften a wish or suggestion, not to express a real condition
Typically limited to verbs such as aimer, vouloir, and être
conditions: A wish or a suggestion is expressed.
The present conditional is used to soften the request or state the desire.
exceptions: Not used for a hypothetical condition, which requires a si clause
Typically limited to verbs such as aimer, vouloir, and être
agreement_rules: The conditional verb agrees with the subject in person and number (je voudrais, tu aimerais).
The wish or suggestion meaning does not change subject-verb agreement.
transformations: j'aimerais venir
je voudrais un café
je parierais que oui

sources.source_text: The présent du conditionnel is used to express a wish or a suggestion.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present conditional with si clause in imparfait
grammar_rules.summary: When the main clause is in the present conditional, the si clause is in the imparfait.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expresses hypothetical situations in the present or future.
grammar_rules.formation: si + imparfait, main clause in present conditional
restrictions: The si clause must be in the imparfait; the conditional never appears after si
Used only for hypothetical present or future situations, not for unreal past conditions
conditions: si clause must be in imparfait
exceptions: The conditional never appears in the si clause
Past unreal conditions use si + plus-que-parfait with the past conditional
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement; the imparfait si clause agrees with its own subject.
The hypothetical condition does not alter person and number agreement in either clause.
grammar_rules.word_order: si + imparfait clause + main clause in present conditional
transformations: Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais.
Si tu venais, nous serions contents.
common_traps: Do not use present conditional in the si clause.

sources.source_text: The présent du conditionnel is used when a condition is implied. When the main clause is in the présent du conditionnel, the si clause is in the imparfait.

grammar_rules.summary: Pronominal verbs follow the same pattern, but include the reflexive pronoun corresponding to the subject.
grammar_rules.explanation: Example with se promener: me promenant, te promenant, se promenant, nous promenant, vous promenant, se promenant.
restrictions: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject
The pronoun precedes the participle and cannot be omitted
conditions: The verb is pronominal.
The present participle keeps the reflexive pronoun matching the subject (me promenant, se promenant).
exceptions: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject
The pronoun cannot be omitted
agreement_rules: The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject in person and number (me promenant, nous promenant).
The participle itself stays invariable; only the pronoun marks the person.
transformations: se promener -> me promenant
se promener -> se promenant
se promener -> nous promenant
common_traps: don't forget the pronoun

sources.source_text: Pronominal verbs follow the same pattern. Do not forget the pronoun corresponding to the subject. Let's look at the present participle of se promener.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present participle used as a noun
grammar_rules.summary: Some present participles can be used as nouns; when used as a noun, they change according to gender and number.
grammar_rules.explanation: Examples: un gagnant/une gagnante, un perdant/une perdante.
grammar_rules.formation: present participle as noun with gender/number agreement
restrictions: Agreement applies only when the participle functions as a noun, not as a verb
Not every present participle can be used as a noun
conditions: The present participle functions as a noun (un gagnant, une gagnante).
It then changes for gender and number.
exceptions: Only some present participles function as nouns (gagnant, perdant)
When the same participle is used as a verb it stays invariable
agreement_rules: agrees in gender and number
grammar_rules.word_order: determiner + present participle used as noun (+ gender/number ending)
transformations: gagnant -> un gagnant / une gagnante
perdant -> un perdant / une perdante
common_traps: do not leave invariable when used as noun
related_concepts: present participle as noun, adjective, verb

sources.source_text: Some participes présents can be used as nouns. When used as a noun, the present participle changes according to gender and number.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present participle used as a verb
grammar_rules.summary: When used as a verb, the present participle is invariable.
grammar_rules.explanation: Examples: La police l'a aperçu entrant dans un laboratoire médical. Étant blessé au genou, il n'a pas pu jouer.
restrictions: Invariable only in verbal use, not when it functions as an adjective or noun
The verbal use is not preceded by en, which would form the gérondif instead
conditions: The present participle is used verbally, as in La police l'a aperçu entrant dans un laboratoire.
It remains invariable in that use.
exceptions: When used as an adjective or a noun, the participle does agree
The verbal use is not preceded by en, which would form the gérondif
agreement_rules: invariable
transformations: La police l'a aperçu entrant dans un laboratoire médical.
Étant blessé au genou, il n'a pas pu jouer.
common_traps: do not make it agree
related_concepts: present participle as noun, adjective, verb

sources.source_text: The participe présent can also be used as a verb. Note that when used as a verb, the present participle is invariable.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present participle used as an adjective
grammar_rules.summary: Many present participles can be used as adjectives; they agree with the noun they modify.
grammar_rules.explanation: Examples: des matchs épuisants, un commentateur fascinant, un sport exigeant, une pièce amusante.
grammar_rules.formation: verb stem + -ant, agreeing in gender and number with the noun
restrictions: Agreement occurs only in adjectival use, not when the participle is a verb
Some participles are fixed as adjectives and may differ in spelling from the verbal form (e.g. fatigant)
conditions: The present participle modifies a noun as an adjective (des matchs épuisants, une pièce amusante).
It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
exceptions: When used as a verb, the participle stays invariable
Some participles are fixed as adjectives with a different spelling (fatigant)
agreement_rules: agrees in gender and number with noun
grammar_rules.word_order: noun + present participle used as adjective (agreeing)
transformations: des matchs épuisants
un commentateur fascinant
une pièce amusante
common_traps: do not forget agreement
related_concepts: present participle as noun, adjective, verb

sources.source_text: Many participes présents can be used as adjectives. When used as an adjective, the participe présent agrees with the noun it modifies.

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can be used to express a near future event.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often used with time expressions indicating future, like demain soir.
grammar_rules.formation: Present tense verb + future time expression
restrictions: Usually with explicit future time reference
conditions: Event is imminent or planned
exceptions: Usually requires an explicit future time expression (demain soir)
Not used for a distant future, which takes the futur simple or aller + infinitive
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the future time expression is invariable.
The near-future value does not change present-tense agreement.
transformations: Je pars demain.
Nous partons en fin de semaine.
common_traps: Using future tense unnecessarily

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can describe past events dramatically.
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to make narrative more vivid.
restrictions: Limited to narration of past events, not to present time
A past-time context is normally established by the surrounding narrative
Mainly a stylistic device in writing and storytelling
conditions: Past events are narrated to make the account more vivid.
The present tense is used in place of a past tense.
exceptions: A past-time context must be clear from the surrounding narrative
Mainly a stylistic device in writing and storytelling
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number, even when narrating past events.
The historical present keeps normal present-tense agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + present tense verb in narrative sequence
transformations: Il entra dans la salle. -> Il entre dans la salle.
Il avance et entre dans la pièce.

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
sources.source_text: To describe past events more dramatically

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present tense for general statements and ongoing actions
grammar_rules.summary: The present indicative can express general truths and actions happening now, translatable as simple present, present progressive, or emphatic present.
grammar_rules.explanation: The same French present tense corresponds to three English forms: simple present, present progressive, and emphatic present.
restrictions: The English translation varies, but the French form itself does not change
Does not express a completed action, which requires a past tense
Ongoing meaning does not require an equivalent of the English progressive
conditions: A general truth or statement of fact is expressed.
An action happening at the moment of speaking is described.
exceptions: The French form does not change, even though English has three translations
Does not express a completed action, which requires a past tense
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number in all three English translations.
The three possible English renderings (does, is doing, does do) do not affect French subject agreement.
transformations: Can be translated as 'is doing', 'does', or 'does do'
common_traps: Using only one English translation

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
sources.source_text: To make a general statement and to describe ongoing actions in the present. It can be translated in three different ways.

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense expresses habitual or repeated actions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often accompanied by adverbs of frequency or time expressions like tous les jours, d'habitude.
restrictions: Habitual meaning is normally signalled by a frequency or time expression (tous les jours, d'habitude)
Does not by itself express a single completed action
conditions: The action is habitual or repeated.
Time expressions such as tous les jours, d'habitude, or souvent accompany it.
exceptions: Habitual meaning is normally signalled by a frequency expression (tous les jours, d'habitude)
Does not by itself express a single completed action
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; adverbs of frequency are invariable.
Habitual meaning does not change agreement.
transformations: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
J'achète du pain tous les matins.

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can narrate historical events for immediacy.
grammar_rules.explanation: Common in journalistic or literary style.
restrictions: Limited to journalistic or literary style
The narrated events are past, so a past-time context must be clear
Not used for future or hypothetical events
conditions: A historical event or fact is being narrated.
The present tense is used for immediacy in journalistic or literary style.
exceptions: Limited to journalistic or literary style
The events are past, so a past-time context must be clear
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number, even when the event narrated is historical.
The stylistic use does not alter present-tense agreement.
transformations: En 1789, la Révolution commence.
L'auteur publie son premier roman en 1830.

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present tense for past action connected to present
grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can describe a past action that has immediate relevance or consequence in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Often used with verbs like revenir, rentrer, and expressions like à peine.
restrictions: The action must be just completed or still relevant to the present
Not used for actions with no present connection, which require a past tense
Often signalled by expressions such as à peine
conditions: Action just completed or still relevant
exceptions: Not used for actions with no present connection, which require a past tense
Often signalled by expressions such as à peine
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; signal words like à peine and déjà are invariable.
The past-with-present-relevance value does not change agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: present-tense verb + past-time marker (à peine, déjà)
transformations: Je reviens à peine du marché.
Il commence déjà à travailler.
common_traps: Using past tense instead

sources.section_title: When is the present tense used in French?
sources.source_text: To describe a past action closely connected to the present

grammar_rules.rule_name: Present tense in main clause: no tense change
grammar_rules.summary: If the main clause verb is in the present tense, the dependent clause verb remains in the same tense as in direct speech.
grammar_rules.explanation: No change of tense occurs.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause present + dependent clause same tense
usage: When reporting speech with present tense main clause
restrictions: Applies only when the main clause verb is in the present tense
Does not apply when the main clause is in a past tense, which triggers a tense shift
conditions: Main clause verb is in present tense
exceptions: When the main clause is in a past tense, a tense shift occurs in the dependent clause
Only a present-tense main clause produces no change
agreement_rules: Each clause keeps its own subject-verb agreement; no tense shift means no agreement change.
The dependent clause verb continues to agree with its own subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause (present) + que + dependent verb in the same tense as direct speech
transformations: No transformation

sources.section_title: Balancing tenses: la concordance des temps
sources.source_text: If the verb in the main clause is in the present tense, the verb in the dependent clause remains in the same tense as it is in the direct speech.

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of avoir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir is an irregular verb. Its present tense forms are: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
grammar_rules.formation: j'ai / tu as / il/elle a / nous avons / vous avez / ils/elles ont
usage: To express possession, age, states, idiomatic expressions.
restrictions: Irregular: the forms do not follow regular -er, -ir, or -re endings
Applies only to the present indicative, not to other tenses
The idiomatic expressions with avoir are fixed and cannot be replaced by être
conditions: The verb is avoir.
The present indicative forms are j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
exceptions: Irregular: the forms do not follow regular -er, -ir, or -re endings
Applies only to the present indicative, not to other tenses
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
transformations: avoir -> j'ai, tu as, il/elle a
avoir -> nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont
common_traps: The -s of nous, vous, ils, elles is pronounced z when followed by a vowel.

sources.source_text: j’ai / I have / nous avons / we have / tu as / you have / vous avez / you have / il/elle a / he/she has / ils/elles ont / they have

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of pouvoir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pouvoir expresses ability and capability. Its present forms are: je peux, tu peux, il/elle peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils/elles peuvent.
grammar_rules.formation: je peux / tu peux / il/elle peut / nous pouvons / vous pouvez / ils/elles peuvent
restrictions: Irregular stem (peu-/pouv-); regular endings do not apply
In formal inversion the first-person singular is puis-je, not peux-je
conditions: The verb is pouvoir.
The present forms are je peux, tu peux, il/elle peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils/elles peuvent; formal inversion uses puis-je.
exceptions: In formal inversion, first-person singular becomes 'puis-je'.
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number: je peux, tu peux, il/elle peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils/elles peuvent.
In formal inversion the first-person singular becomes puis-je, but agreement remains first-person singular.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject pronoun + pouvoir (present) + infinitive; formal inversion: puis-je + infinitive
transformations: pouvoir -> je peux / nous pouvons
peux-je -> puis-je (formal inversion)
common_traps: Use 'puis-je' instead of 'peux-je' for formal inversion.

sources.source_text: Pouvoir (can, may) expresses ability and capability. je peux / I can / nous pouvons / we can / tu peux / you can / vous pouvez / you can / il/elle peut / he/she can / ils/elles peuvent / they can

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of vouloir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Vouloir expresses wishes and desires. Its present forms are: je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent.
grammar_rules.formation: je veux / tu veux / il/elle veut / nous voulons / vous voulez / ils/elles veulent
restrictions: Irregular stem (veul-/voul-); regular -ir endings do not apply
Politeness is normally expressed with the conditional (je voudrais), not the present
The present je veux can sound abrupt in requests
conditions: The verb is vouloir.
The present forms are je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent.
exceptions: Irregular stem (veul-/voul-); regular -ir endings do not apply
Politeness is normally expressed with the conditional (je voudrais), not the present
