agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number: je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent.
transformations: vouloir -> je veux / nous voulons
vouloir -> ils/elles veulent

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of être in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Être is an irregular verb. Its present tense forms are: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
grammar_rules.formation: je suis / tu es / il/elle est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils/elles sont
usage: To express identity, nationality, profession, state, etc.
restrictions: Irregular forms; they must be memorized rather than derived from a pattern
Applies only to the present indicative, not to other tenses
conditions: The verb is être.
The present forms are je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
exceptions: Irregular forms that must be memorized rather than derived
Applies only to the present indicative, not to other tenses
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.

être -> vous êtes / ils/elles sont
common_traps: The -s of vous is pronounced as a z when followed by the vowel ê- in êtes.

grammar_rules.summary: In the affirmative imperative of pronominal verbs, the pronoun follows the verb; me becomes moi, te becomes toi.
grammar_rules.explanation: When putting pronominal verbs in the affirmative imperative, the pronoun follows the verb form. Me (m’) and te (t’) become moi and toi.
usage: Give affirmative commands with pronominal verbs
restrictions: Only in the affirmative imperative; in the negative the pronoun precedes the verb
The transformation me to moi and te to toi occurs only in the affirmative imperative
No subject pronoun is expressed in the imperative
conditions: Affirmative imperative
exceptions: In the negative imperative the pronoun precedes the verb
me and te become moi and toi only in the affirmative imperative
agreement_rules: The pronoun agrees with the addressee: toi (tu), nous (nous), vous (vous).
The imperative has no third-person form, so there is no il/ils pronoun agreement.
transformations: me → moi
te → toi
common_traps: Using me/te instead of moi/toi after the verb.

sources.source_text: The pronoun follows the verb form in the affirmative imperative; me (m’) and te (t’) become moi and toi.

grammar_rules.summary: In the negative imperative of pronominal verbs, the pronoun precedes the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: However, the pronoun precedes the verb in the negative imperative.
usage: Give negative commands with pronominal verbs
restrictions: Only in the negative imperative; the affirmative places the pronoun after the verb
The pronoun precedes the verb and follows ne
No subject pronoun is expressed in the imperative
conditions: Negative imperative
exceptions: In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb
The pronoun comes after ne and before the verb
agreement_rules: The pronoun agrees with the addressee (te, nous, vous) and precedes the verb.
No third-person imperative agreement exists.

Promenons-nous! -> Ne nous promenons pas!

sources.source_text: However, the pronoun precedes the verb in the negative imperative.

grammar_rules.summary: All pronominal verbs use être; reflexive pronoun before auxiliary.
grammar_rules.explanation: Formation: reflexive pronoun + être + past participle.
restrictions: Only pronominal verbs take être here; non-pronominal verbs may take avoir
Agreement with the subject has exceptions, such as a preceding direct object
The reflexive pronoun must match the subject and precede the auxiliary
conditions: verb is pronominal
exceptions: Agreement with the subject has exceptions, such as a preceding direct object
Non-pronominal verbs may take avoir instead of être
agreement_rules: generally agrees with subject, but see exceptions

grammar_rules.interrogative_form: reflexive pronoun + être + subject + past participle

Elle s'est promenée.
Nous ne nous sommes pas reposés.

Agreement exceptions

sources.source_text: All pronominal verbs are conjugated with être. The reflexive pronouns precede the auxiliary verb (être).

grammar_rules.summary: Reflexive pronoun agrees with subject and precedes infinitive.
grammar_rules.explanation: When pronominal verbs are used in the infinitive, the reflexive pronoun is always in the same person and number as the subject, and it precedes the infinitive.
usage: After verbs like aller, venir de, devoir, pouvoir, aimer, etc.
restrictions: Applies only when a subject is present for the pronoun to agree with
The pronoun precedes the infinitive and cannot be omitted
conditions: The pronominal verb is used in the infinitive, typically after aller, venir de, devoir, pouvoir, or aimer.
The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject and precedes the infinitive.
exceptions: The pronoun precedes the infinitive and cannot be omitted
In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb instead
agreement_rules: Pronoun must agree with subject.

Il doit se lever tôt.
Je viens de m'ennuyer.

sources.section_title: Pronominals in the imperative and the infinitive
sources.source_text: When pronominal verbs are used in the infinitive, the reflexive pronoun is always in the same person and number as the subject, and it precedes the infinitive.

grammar_rules.summary: En replaces inanimate object preceded by de. It precedes the verb; no past participle agreement.
grammar_rules.explanation: En is an indirect object pronoun replacing things/ideas introduced by de.
restrictions: Does not replace people (use disjunctive pronouns).
conditions: The replaced object is inanimate and introduced by de.
En precedes the verb and causes no past participle agreement.
exceptions: No past participle agreement occurs with en
en does not replace people; disjunctive pronouns are used instead
en replaces de + noun, while y replaces à + noun
agreement_rules: No past participle agreement with en.
grammar_rules.word_order: en + verb (or en + auxiliary + past participle)
transformations: de + noun -> en
Il a des amis. -> Il en a.
Je ne veux pas en parler.
common_traps: Do not confuse with y (à vs de).

sources.source_text: En is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb. It usually replaces an inanimate object (thing or idea) preceded by de.

grammar_rules.summary: Y replaces inanimate object preceded by à or sur. It precedes the verb; no past participle agreement.
grammar_rules.explanation: Y is an indirect object pronoun that replaces things/ideas introduced by à (sometimes sur).
usage: Replace sur + inanimate noun in some cases.
restrictions: Does not replace people (use disjunctive pronouns).
conditions: The replaced object is inanimate and introduced by à (sometimes sur).
Y precedes the verb and causes no past participle agreement.
exceptions: No past participle agreement occurs with y
y does not replace people; disjunctive pronouns are used instead
y replaces à + noun, while en replaces de + noun
agreement_rules: No past participle agreement with y.
grammar_rules.word_order: y + verb (or y + auxiliary + past participle)
transformations: à + noun -> y
Je pense à Paris. -> J'y pense.
Il n'y a pas de problème.
common_traps: Do not use y for people; use disjunctive pronouns after preposition.

sources.source_text: Y is an indirect object pronoun that precedes the verb. It usually replaces an inanimate object (thing or idea). The object replaced by y is considered indirect because it is preceded by a preposition, usually the preposition à, but sometimes sur.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Pronunciation of final consonants in certain numbers
grammar_rules.summary: Final consonants in cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix are pronounced; -p in sept is silent but -t pronounced; -x in six and dix pronounced like s; final consonant mute before consonant-initial word for cinq, six, huit, dix.
grammar_rules.explanation: Although consonants are generally silent in French, they are pronounced in the following numbers: cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. With sept, the -p- is silent, but the final -t is pronounced. The final -x in six and dix is pronounced like an s. When the numbers cinq, six, huit, and dix are followed by a word beginning with a consonant, their final consonant is mute (silent).
grammar_rules.formation: cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix + pronounced final consonant (sept: -p silent, -t pronounced; six/dix: -x = [s])
usage: Pronunciation of numbers cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix.
restrictions: For cinq, six, huit, and dix the final consonant is silent before a word beginning with a consonant
sept has a silent -p but a pronounced final -t
Covers only the listed numbers, not numbers in general
conditions: For cinq, six, huit, dix, final consonant is mute before a word beginning with a consonant.
exceptions: For cinq, six, huit, and dix the final consonant is silent before a word beginning with a consonant
sept has a silent -p but a pronounced final -t
agreement_rules: The numbers cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, and dix are invariable and take no gender or number agreement.
Their pronounced or silent final consonants do not change the invariable written form.
grammar_rules.word_order: number + noun (final consonant pronounced before a vowel-initial word, mute before a consonant-initial word)
transformations: six -> [sis] before vowel, [si] before consonant
sept -> -p silent, final -t pronounced
dix -> final -x pronounced like s
common_traps: Do not pronounce final -p in sept; pronounce final -t.
related_concepts: Pronunciation of final consonants in certain numbers

sources.source_text: Although consonants are generally silent in French, they are pronounced in the following numbers: cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. With sept, the -p- is silent, but the final -t is pronounced. The final -x in six and dix is pronounced like an s. When the numbers cinq, six, huit, and dix are followed by a word beginning with a consonant, their final consonant is mute (silent).

grammar_rules.rule_name: Que as direct object relative pronoun
grammar_rules.summary: Que is used as the direct object of the dependent clause when it already has a subject.
grammar_rules.explanation: Que refers to both people and things and means whom, which, that.
restrictions: Requires the dependent clause to have its own subject
Que is elided to qu' before a vowel or mute h
Cannot serve as the subject; subject function requires qui
conditions: dependent clause has its own subject
exceptions: Requires the dependent clause to have its own subject
que is elided to qu' before a vowel or mute h
Cannot serve as the subject; subject function requires qui
agreement_rules: Que is invariable; it does not agree in gender or number with its antecedent.
Unlike lequel, que carries no gender or number marking, whether the antecedent is a person or a thing.
transformations: le cadre que vous lui montrez
que -> qu' before vowel
common_traps: The -e of que is dropped before a vowel (qu')

grammar_rules.summary: Three ways: rising intonation, inversion, est-ce que.
grammar_rules.explanation: As in present tense, questions can be formed three ways.
grammar_rules.formation: rising intonation / inversion (auxiliary + subject pronoun + past participle) / est-ce que
restrictions: In inversion the subject follows the auxiliary, not the past participle
Inversion requires a pronoun subject
conditions: The tense is the passé composé.
The question is formed by rising intonation, by inversion, or with est-ce que.
exceptions: In inversion the subject follows the auxiliary, not the past participle
Inversion requires a pronoun subject
agreement_rules: The auxiliary agrees with the subject in person and number in all three question patterns.
Past participle agreement is unchanged by inversion or by est-ce que.
grammar_rules.word_order: For inversion: auxiliary + subject + past participle
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Vous avez aimé la pièce? / Avez-vous aimé la pièce? / Est-ce que vous avez aimé la pièce?

Avez-vous aimé la pièce? (inversion)
Est-ce que vous avez aimé la pièce?

sources.source_text: As in the present tense, there are three ways to make a question.

grammar_rules.summary: Qui is used after a preposition to refer only to people.
grammar_rules.explanation: Voici le collègue avec qui j’écris le rapport. Je vous présente la personne sans qui je n’aurai pas pu réussir.
usage: object of preposition referring to people
restrictions: only for people
cannot be used with parmi
conditions: preposition precedes qui
exceptions: qui after a preposition cannot be used with parmi
Only people are referred to; for things the lequel forms are used
Prepositions such as avec, sans, and pour require qui, not que
agreement_rules: Qui is invariable and takes no gender or number agreement with its antecedent.
Qui is used for people after a preposition, unlike lequel, which marks gender and number.
transformations: avec qui j'écris le rapport
sans qui je n'aurai pas pu réussir

sources.source_text: Voici le collègue avec qui j’écris le rapport.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Qui as object of verb with intervening subject
grammar_rules.summary: Qui can be the object of the verb in the dependent clause; a subject noun or pronoun comes between qui and the verb.
grammar_rules.explanation: Je ne sais pas qui il est. Le président n’a pas dit qui il nommerait à ce poste. Nous ignorons qui elle renverra. Le policier a révélé qui il avait attrapé.
restrictions: Requires a subject noun or pronoun between qui and the verb
Distinct from qui as subject, where qui directly precedes the verb
conditions: subject pronoun/noun between qui and verb
exceptions: Requires a subject noun or pronoun between qui and the verb
Distinct from qui as subject, where qui directly precedes the verb
agreement_rules: Qui is invariable; it does not agree in gender or number with its antecedent.
The intervening subject governs its own verb agreement (qui il est, qui elle renverra).
transformations: Je ne sais pas qui il est.
Nous ignorons qui elle renverra.

sources.source_text: Je ne sais pas qui il est.

grammar_rules.summary: Qui is used as the subject of a dependent clause, referring to people or things.
grammar_rules.explanation: Qui may refer to people or things and may mean who, whom, which, what, or that. When qui is the subject, it precedes the verb in the dependent clause.
restrictions: qui is never elided before a vowel or mute h
The verb after qui agrees with the antecedent, not with the speaker
Not used as a direct object in this construction
conditions: Qui functions as the subject of a dependent clause.
The antecedent may be a person or a thing, and the verb after qui agrees with that antecedent.
exceptions: qui is never elided before a vowel or mute h
The verb after qui agrees with the antecedent
Not used as a direct object in this construction
agreement_rules: verb after qui agrees with antecedent
transformations: J'écoute la personne qui parle.
les livres qui sont sur la table
common_traps: The -i of qui is never dropped before a vowel

grammar_rules.summary: The expression quitte à + infinitive is translated as 'even if it means'.
grammar_rules.explanation: It expresses acceptance of a possible negative consequence in order to achieve something else.
usage: To express 'even if it means (doing something)'
restrictions: Always followed by an infinitive, never by a conjugated clause
Used in a main clause construction to express a concession
Not to be confused with the verb quitter (to leave)
conditions: The speaker accepts a possible negative consequence in order to achieve something else (even if it means).
Quitte à is followed by an infinitive.
exceptions: Always followed by an infinitive, never a conjugated clause
Used in a main clause construction expressing concession
Not to be confused with the verb quitter (to leave)
agreement_rules: quitte à is invariable and does not agree with the subject.

sources.source_text: The expression quitte à + infinitive can usually be translated by even if it means.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Quoi after prepositions for indefinite things
grammar_rules.summary: Quoi is used after a preposition to refer to an indefinite thing or object.
grammar_rules.explanation: Tu sais à quoi il pense?
usage: object of preposition referring to indefinite things
restrictions: indefinite things only
conditions: preposition precedes quoi
exceptions: Refers only to indefinite things, not to people
qui is used instead when a person is meant

sources.source_text: Tu sais à quoi il pense?

grammar_rules.summary: Action between two or more people; used in plural only.
grammar_rules.explanation: Reciprocal verbs describe an action two or more people perform with or for each other. Since two or more people are involved, reciprocal verbs can only be used in the plural (with se, nous, vous).
restrictions: Cannot be used in singular.
conditions: Two or more people perform the action with or for each other.
The subject is plural, so only the plural pronouns se, nous, and vous are used.
exceptions: Cannot be used in the singular
The pronoun agrees with a plural subject
The meaning is 'each other', not reflexive
agreement_rules: Pronoun agrees with plural subject.

se voir -> ils se voient
se connaître -> vous vous connaissez
common_traps: Do not use singular forms for reciprocal meaning.

sources.source_text: The second type of pronominal verb is called reciprocal. It describes an action two or more people perform with or for each other. Since two or more people are involved, reciprocal verbs can only be used in the plural (with se, nous, vous).

grammar_rules.summary: Agreement with subject if direct object; no agreement if indirect object.

exceptions: No agreement when the reciprocal pronoun is an indirect object
Agreement occurs only when the reciprocal pronoun is a direct object
A plural subject is required for reciprocal meaning
agreement_rules: agrees with subject if direct object; no agreement if indirect object

sources.source_text: When reciprocal verbs take a direct object, the past participle agrees with the subject. When reciprocal verbs take an indirect object in French, the past participle does not agree.

grammar_rules.summary: Drop -re, add endings -s, -s, - (nothing), -ons, -ez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation: For regular -re verbs, remove the -re ending and add: je -s, tu -s, il/elle - (no ending), nous -ons, vous -ez, ils/elles -ent. Example: vendre -> je vends, tu vends, il vend, nous vendons, vous vendez, ils vendent.

restrictions: Limited to regular -re verbs; irregular -re verbs such as prendre follow other patterns
The third-person singular has no ending

grammar_rules.summary: Past participle endings for regular verbs: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u.

grammar_rules.summary: The relative clause is often inserted into the main clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: La commode qui est dans la vitrine, a appartenu à Talleyrand. L’homme que vous voyez au fond de l’atelier est un des meilleurs artisans du pays.

The inserted relative clause does not change the word order of the main clause

grammar_rules.summary: Savoir is used before an infinitive or dependent clause to express knowing how to or knowing a fact.
grammar_rules.explanation: Savoir can be translated as 'can' when followed by an infinitive. It is the only verb that can be used before a dependent clause or an infinitive to mean 'know'.

restrictions: Only savoir, not connaître, can be followed by a dependent clause or infinitive meaning 'know'
Cannot take a direct object noun; connaître is required there
When translated as 'can', it expresses learned ability rather than permission

exceptions: Only savoir, not connaître, can be followed by a dependent clause or infinitive meaning 'know'
Cannot take a direct object noun; connaître is required there
When translated as 'can', it expresses learned ability rather than permission

grammar_rules.rule_name: Savoir in present conditional equivalent to pouvoir
grammar_rules.summary: In formal French, savoir in the present conditional is the equivalent of pouvoir (can, to be able to) in the present or simple future.

grammar_rules.explanation: When 'should' means 'ought to', French uses the conditionnel présent of devoir for present/future advice, and the conditionnel passé of devoir for advice about the past (should have).

Requires a following infinitive

Conditionnel présent is used for present or future advice and conditionnel passé for past advice

grammar_rules.summary: Use 'si on' + imparfait to make a suggestion or invitation.
grammar_rules.explanation: With a si + on construction, the imparfait is used to make a suggestion or to invite someone to do something. The informal on refers to two or more people and is conjugated in the third-person singular.

conditions: on refers to a group
exceptions: Only in informal register
on takes third-person singular conjugation even though it refers to a group

sources.source_text: With a si + on construction, the imparfait is used to make a suggestion or to invite someone to do something. The informal on refers to two or more people and is conjugated in the third-person singular.

grammar_rules.summary: Use 'si seulement' + imparfait to express a wish or regret.
grammar_rules.explanation: You will encounter the imparfait in other idiomatic constructions, for instance, preceded by si seulement, to express a wish or a regret.
restrictions: Used only for present or future wishes and regrets, not for past events
The imparfait must follow si seulement; the conditional is not used after it
conditions: Si seulement introduces the clause.
The imparfait follows and the sentence expresses a wish or a regret.
exceptions: Used only for present or future wishes and regrets, not for past events
The imparfait must follow si seulement; the conditional is not used after it
agreement_rules: The imparfait verb agrees with the subject in person and number after si seulement.
si seulement is an invariable expression and does not affect agreement.
transformations: Si seulement j'avais plus de temps !
Si seulement il pouvait venir !

sources.source_text: You will encounter the imparfait in other idiomatic constructions, for instance, preceded by si seulement, to express a wish or a regret.

grammar_rules.summary: Expresses a wish or regret about past events.
grammar_rules.explanation: The plus-que-parfait used after 'si seulement' expresses regret or a wish about something that did not happen in the past.
usage: To express regret about past events
restrictions: Limited to regrets or wishes about the past, not about the present or future
The plus-que-parfait must follow si seulement; the conditional never follows it
conditions: Regret or wish about past
exceptions: Limited to regrets or wishes about the past
The plus-que-parfait must follow si seulement; the conditional never follows it
agreement_rules: The plus-que-parfait auxiliary agrees with the subject in person and number after si seulement.
The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject when the auxiliary is être.
grammar_rules.word_order: si seulement + plus-que-parfait; negative: si seulement + ne + plus-que-parfait + pas
transformations: Si seulement j'avais su !
Si seulement elle était venue plus tôt !
Si seulement nous n'avions pas oublié les billets !

sources.source_text: The plus-que-parfait, when used with si seulement, expresses a wish or regret about past events.

grammar_rules.summary: Certain short, common adjectives precede the noun; these must be memorized.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives such as long, beau, nouveau, bon, mauvais, vieux, jeune precede the noun.
usage: For a limited set of common adjectives.
restrictions: Specific adjectives: long, beau, nouveau, bon, mauvais, vieux, jeune.
conditions: Adjective is one of the listed ones.
signal_words: long, beau, nouveau, bon, mauvais, vieux, jeune
exceptions: Limited to the listed adjectives (long, beau, nouveau, bon, mauvais, vieux, jeune)
All other adjectives follow the noun
agreement_rules: Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun whether they precede or follow it.
long, beau, nouveau, bon, mauvais, vieux, jeune take feminine and plural forms when the noun is feminine or plural (une longue histoire, de vieux amis).
transformations: un long voyage
un beau jardin
un nouveau livre
un bon repas
un mauvais choix
un vieux château
un jeune homme
adjective + noun
common_traps: Do not place other adjectives before the noun.

sources.source_text: Some adjectives precede the noun. You just need to memorize them.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Some irregular passé simple stems based on past participle
grammar_rules.summary: For some verbs, the passé simple stem is based on the past participle, but this is not a fixed rule.
grammar_rules.explanation: Irregular verbs have unpredictable passé simple forms; sometimes the stem resembles the past participle.
grammar_rules.formation: irregular stem (often based on the past participle) + passé simple endings
usage: Learn third-person singular and plural forms for reading newspapers and novels.
restrictions: Not a fixed rule; many irregular stems must be memorized
Covers only some irregular verbs, not all of them
In practice limited to the third-person singular and plural forms needed for reading
conditions: The verb is irregular and used in the passé simple.
The stem sometimes resembles the past participle, but this is not a fixed rule.
exceptions: Not a fixed rule; many irregular stems must be memorized.
agreement_rules: The passé simple verb agrees with its subject in person and number through its endings.
Irregular stems do not affect agreement; endings such as -s, -t, -rent mark person and number.
grammar_rules.word_order: passé simple stem (often from the past participle) + passé simple ending
transformations: mettre (mis) -> je mis
prendre (pris) -> je pris
dire (dit) -> je dis
faire (fait) -> je fis
conduire (conduit) -> je conduisis
common_traps: Assuming regularity based on past participle.

sources.section_title: The passé simple of irregular verbs
sources.source_text: For some verbs the stem of the passé simple is based on the past participle, but this is not a fixed rule.

grammar_rules.summary: Certain endings change: -eur → -euse, -(i)er → -(i)ère, -teur → -trice, -ien → -ienne.
grammar_rules.explanation: Some suffixes have specific feminine forms.
usage: to form feminine of certain masculine nouns
restrictions: Applies only to nouns ending in the listed suffixes (-eur, -(i)er, -teur, -ien)
-eur nouns split between -euse and -trice, so the pattern is not fully predictable
Does not apply to nouns that already end in -e in the masculine
conditions: noun ending in specific suffix
exceptions: -eur nouns split between -euse and -trice, so the pattern is not fully predictable
Does not apply to nouns that already end in -e in the masculine
agreement_rules: Feminine nouns take feminine agreement of determiners and adjectives (une danseuse, une institutrice).
The ending determines the feminine form: -eur → -euse, -(i)er → -(i)ère, -teur → -trice, -ien → -ienne.
transformations: danseur → danseuse
épicier → épicière
instituteur → institutrice
citoyen → citoyenne
common_traps: Not all -eur nouns follow; some have -euse, others -trice.

sources.source_text: Nouns with certain endings form the feminine in other ways: -eur → -euse; -(i)er → (i)ère; -teur → -trice; -ien → -ienne.

grammar_rules.summary: Certain adjectives have a special masculine singular form before a noun starting with a vowel.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives fou, vieux, nouveau, beau have special forms fol, vieil, nouvel, bel when preceding a masculine singular noun beginning with a vowel sound.
grammar_rules.formation: fou -> fol, vieux -> vieil, nouveau -> nouvel, beau -> bel
usage: Before masculine singular nouns starting with a vowel.
restrictions: Only before masculine singular nouns starting with a vowel sound.
conditions: Noun begins with vowel sound.
exceptions: Used only before masculine singular nouns beginning with a vowel sound, not before consonants
The special forms do not replace the plural forms (beaux, vieux, nouveaux)
agreement_rules: The special forms fol, vieil, nouvel, bel are masculine singular only and agree with a masculine singular noun.
The regular forms fou, vieux, nouveau, beau are used before a consonant or in other positions.
transformations: un fol espoir
un vieil ami
un nouvel appartement
un bel homme
fou -> fol, vieux -> vieil, nouveau -> nouvel, beau -> bel
common_traps: Use special forms only before masculine singular nouns starting with a vowel.

grammar_rules.summary: Nouns ending in -s, -x, -z unchanged; -eu, -eau → -x; -al → -aux; exceptions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Irregular plural patterns.
usage: to form plural of irregular nouns
restrictions: Applies only to nouns ending in -s/-x/-z, -eu/-eau, or -al
Exceptions such as bal, festival, and pneu do not follow the -aux or -x patterns
Some nouns have wholly irregular plurals (œil to yeux)
conditions: noun ending in specific suffix
exceptions: bal → bals
genou → genoux
pneu → pneus
festival → festivals
œil → yeux
bijou → bijoux
agreement_rules: Plural nouns take plural agreement of determiners and adjectives (les journaux intéressants).
Nouns ending in -s, -x, -z keep the same written form in the plural but still trigger plural agreement.
transformations: château → châteaux
journal → journaux
common_traps: Some -al nouns do not change to -aux.

sources.source_text: Nouns ending in -s, -x, or -z do not change in the plural. Nouns ending in -eu, -eau usually take an -x in the plural. Nouns ending in -al usually change to -aux.

grammar_rules.summary: In verbs ending in -cer, the c changes to ç before the letter o to keep the soft pronunciation.
grammar_rules.explanation: The cedilla (ç) is added to c before o in the nous form to preserve the /s/ sound.
restrictions: Only before o
conditions: Verb ends in -cer
exceptions: The cedilla is added only before o (nous form), not before e or i
-ger verbs take an extra e before o instead of a cedilla
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the c → ç spelling change affects only the written stem.
The cedilla appears only in the nous form before o (nous prononçons).
grammar_rules.word_order: nous + stem with ç + ons (ç before o)
transformations: prononcer -> nous prononçons
commencer -> nous commençons
c -> ç before o
-cer: stem + -çons
common_traps: Forgetting to add cedilla before o

sources.source_text: the -c- becomes -ç- before the letter o. The cedilla (ç) under the c is needed to keep the soft pronunciation.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like acheter add an accent grave (è) in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The silent e becomes è in the stem for je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles to maintain pronunciation.
grammar_rules.formation: j'achète, tu achètes, il/elle achète, ils/elles achètent; nous achetons, vous achetez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural
restrictions: Not in nous or vous
conditions: Verb pattern: e + consonant + er
exceptions: The accent grave is not added in the nous and vous forms
The change appears in all other persons
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the accent change affects only the stem spelling.
The accent grave appears in the je/tu/il/ils forms but not in nous/vous (nous achetons, vous achetez).
grammar_rules.word_order: è in the stem before the ending (je/tu/il/ils); e in nous/vous
transformations: acheter -> j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, ils achètent
acheter -> nous achetons, vous achetez
e -> è in all but nous and vous
common_traps: Adding accent in nous/vous forms incorrectly

sources.source_text: An accent grave is added in all but the first- and the second-person plural.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like épeler double the l in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The consonant l is doubled in je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles forms.
grammar_rules.formation: j'épelle, tu épelles, il/elle épelle, ils/elles épellent; nous épelons, vous épelez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural
restrictions: Not in nous or vous
conditions: Verb pattern: e + l + er
exceptions: The l is doubled only in je, tu, il/elle/on, and ils/elles
nous and vous keep a single l (nous épelons, vous épelez)
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the doubled l affects only the stem spelling.
The doubling occurs in the je/tu/il/ils forms but not in nous/vous (nous épelons, vous épelez).
grammar_rules.word_order: doubled ll in the stem (je/tu/il/ils); single l in nous/vous
transformations: épeler -> j'épelle, tu épelles, il épelle, ils épellent
épeler -> nous épelons, vous épelez
appeler -> j'appelle, nous appelons
common_traps: Forgetting to double the l

sources.source_text: sometimes take two ls in all but the first- and second-person plural.

grammar_rules.summary: In verbs ending in -ger, the g becomes ge before the letter o to keep the soft pronunciation.
grammar_rules.explanation: The e is added after g before o in the nous form to preserve the /ʒ/ sound.
restrictions: Only before o
conditions: Verb ends in -ger
exceptions: The extra e is added only before o (nous form)
-cer verbs take a cedilla before o instead
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the g → ge spelling change affects only the written stem.
The added e appears only in the nous form before o (nous voyageons).
grammar_rules.word_order: nous + stem with ge + ons (ge before o)
transformations: voyager -> nous voyageons
manger -> nous mangeons
g -> ge before o
-ger: stem + -geons
common_traps: Forgetting to add e after g before o

sources.source_text: the -g- becomes -ge- before the letter o.

grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like répéter change é to è in all forms except nous and vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The acute accent (é) becomes grave accent (è) in the stem for je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles.
grammar_rules.formation: je répète, tu répètes, il/elle répète, ils/elles répètent; nous répétons, vous répétez
usage: Present tense, all persons except first and second plural
restrictions: Not in nous or vous
conditions: Verb pattern: é + consonant + er
exceptions: The é does not change in the nous and vous forms
The grave accent appears in all other persons
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the é → è change affects only the stem spelling.
The accent grave appears in the je/tu/il/ils forms but not in nous/vous (nous répétons, vous répétez).
grammar_rules.word_order: è in the stem before the ending (je/tu/il/ils); é in nous/vous
transformations: répéter -> je répète, tu répètes, il répète, ils répètent
répéter -> nous répétons, vous répétez
é -> è in all but nous and vous
common_traps: Confusing é and è

sources.source_text: The é aigu changes to an è grave in all but the first- and second-person plural.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Spelling changes for -cer and -ger verbs in passé simple
grammar_rules.summary: Use cedilla (ç) for -cer verbs and add extra -e- for -ger verbs when ending starts with -a.
grammar_rules.explanation: When the passé simple ending starts with -a, verbs ending in -cer use a cedilla and verbs ending in -ger add an extra -e- before the ending.
usage: Applies to all forms with endings beginning with -a: -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent.
restrictions: Only for -cer and -ger verbs.
conditions: Ending begins with -a.
exceptions: Applies only to endings beginning with -a (-a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent)
No cedilla or extra e is needed with endings beginning with -i
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the cedilla or added e affects only the written stem.
The spelling change occurs only in forms whose ending begins with -a (-a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent).
transformations: commencer -> je commençai, nous commençâmes, ils commencèrent
manger -> je mangeai, nous mangeâmes, ils mangèrent
common_traps: Forgetting the cedilla or the extra -e-.

sources.source_text: Verbs like commencer and manger have a spelling change. When the passé simple ending starts with -a, use the cedilla (ç) for verbs ending in -cer and add an extra -e- for verbs ending in -ger.

grammar_rules.summary: Some verbs have slight spelling modifications in the future stem (e.g., acheter -> j'achèterai, appeler -> j'appellerai, employer -> j'emploierai).
grammar_rules.explanation: Some slight spelling modifications occur with some verbs. These are seen throughout all persons of the future conjugation.
restrictions: Applies only to verbs whose stems change by accent, consonant doubling, or y to i
The changes appear in all persons of the future conjugation, not only some
Regular verbs keep the infinitive stem unchanged
conditions: The verb has a stem whose spelling changes in the future (acheter, appeler, employer, etc.).
The change appears in all persons of the futur simple.
exceptions: Applies only to verbs whose stems change by accent, consonant doubling, or y to i
The changes appear in all persons of the future conjugation
Regular verbs keep the infinitive stem unchanged
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; stem spelling modifications do not change the future endings.
The modified stem is used in all persons of the futur simple.
transformations: acheter -> j'achèterai
appeler -> j'appellerai
employer -> j'emploierai
essuyer -> j'essuierai
jeter -> je jetterai
nettoyer -> je nettoierai
préférer -> je préférerai
common_traps: forgetting accent changes (e.g., acheter -> achèterai)
doubling consonants (appeler -> appellerai)
changing y to i (employer -> emploierai)

sources.source_text: Some slight spelling modifications occur with some verbs.

grammar_rules.summary: Some -cer and -ger verbs change spelling in the present participle: -cer becomes -çant, -ger becomes -geant.
grammar_rules.explanation: Examples: commencer -> commençant, influencer -> influençant, manger -> mangeant, nager -> nageant.
grammar_rules.formation: For -cer: replace c with ç before -ant; for -ger: insert e before -ant
restrictions: only some -cer and -ger verbs
conditions: The verb is a -cer or -ger verb of the type that changes spelling.
The present participle shows -çant or -geant (commençant, mangeant).
exceptions: -cer verbs use ç (commençant) while -ger verbs insert e (mangeant)
The change is limited to -cer and -ger verbs; other verbs add -ant directly
agreement_rules: The present participle is invariable; the c → ç or g → ge change affects only the written stem.
The spelling change appears before -ant (commençant, mangeant).
grammar_rules.word_order: -cer: stem + ç + ant; -ger: stem + ge + ant
transformations: commencer -> commençant
influencer -> influençant
manger -> mangeant
nager -> nageant
-cer -> -çant, -ger -> -geant
common_traps: forgetting to change c to ç or g to ge

sources.source_text: Some spelling changes occur with some -cer and -ger verbs: commencer -> commençant, influencer -> influençant, manger -> mangeant, nager -> nageant.

grammar_rules.summary: The subject pronouns in French are je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles.
grammar_rules.explanation: Subject pronouns replace subject nouns. The third-person pronouns apply to people, animals, or things.
grammar_rules.formation: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles
usage: Used as the subject of a verb.
restrictions: on is always third-person singular in agreement even when it means 'we'
ils refers to masculine or mixed groups; elles refers to feminine groups only
je and tu refer to persons, not to things
conditions: A subject noun is replaced by a subject pronoun.
The pronoun is je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, or elles, agreeing with the replaced noun.
exceptions: on is always third-person singular in agreement even when it means 'we'
ils refers to masculine or mixed groups; elles refers to feminine groups only
je and tu refer to persons, not to things
agreement_rules: The verb agrees in person and number with the subject pronoun (je parle, nous parlons).
Third-person pronouns agree in gender and number with the noun they replace (il/elle, ils/elles).
grammar_rules.word_order: subject pronoun + verb (je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles)
transformations: je -> I
tu -> you (singular familiar)
il -> he, it (masculine)
elle -> she, it (feminine)
on -> one, we, they, people
nous -> we
vous -> you (singular formal and all plurals)
ils -> they (masculine, or mixed masculine and feminine)
elles -> they (feminine)
je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles

sources.source_text: je I; tu you (singular familiar); il he, it (masculine); elle she, it (feminine); on one, we, they, people; nous we; vous you (singular formal and all plurals); ils they (masculine, or mixed masculine and feminine); elles they (feminine)

grammar_rules.summary: Idiomatic pronominal verbs; learn with se; not reflexive or reciprocal.
grammar_rules.explanation: These verbs are neither reflexive nor reciprocal. For idiomatic or historical reasons, they just happen to use the pronominal forms. Learn their infinitives with the pronoun se.
grammar_rules.formation: se + verb, learned with the pronoun (neither reflexive nor reciprocal)
restrictions: Neither reflexive nor reciprocal; the pronoun does not refer back to the subject in a reflexive sense
The pronoun must agree with the subject when the verb is conjugated
Cannot be used without the pronominal pronoun
conditions: The verb is pronominal for idiomatic or historical reasons, neither reflexive nor reciprocal.
It is learned with the pronoun se (s'apercevoir, s'enfuir, se souvenir, etc.).
exceptions: Neither reflexive nor reciprocal, despite the pronominal form
The pronoun must still agree with the subject
agreement_rules: Pronoun agrees with subject.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + pronominal pronoun (se/me/te/nous/vous) + verb; negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas
transformations: s'apercevoir -> je m'aperçois
s'emparer -> je m'empare
s'en aller -> je m'en vais
s'enfuir -> je m'enfuis
s'envoler -> je m'envole
s'écrouler -> je m'écroule
s'évanouir -> je m'évanouis
se moquer -> je me moque
se souvenir -> je me souviens
common_traps: Do not interpret as reflexive.

sources.source_text: The last type of pronominal verb is called subjective. These verbs are neither reflexive nor reciprocal. For idiomatic or historical reasons, they just happen to use the pronominal forms. Try to learn their infinitives with the pronoun se.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Subjunctive after relative pronoun with doubt
grammar_rules.summary: After qui or que, subjunctive may be used if there is doubt about existence or realization.
grammar_rules.explanation: Il cherche un artisan qui puisse restaurer ce fauteuil Louis XV. Connaîtriez-vous un antiquaire qui vende des pièces rares?
restrictions: Only when there is doubt about the existence or realization of the antecedent
Not used when the existence of the antecedent is certain, where the indicative is required
Applies to qui and que clauses, not to other subordinate clause types
conditions: doubt about existence or possible realization
exceptions: Not used when the existence of the antecedent is certain
Applies to qui and que clauses, not to other subordinate clause types
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with the antecedent of the relative pronoun in person and number.
The relative pronoun qui is the subject of the subjunctive clause and governs its agreement.
transformations: Il cherche un artisan qui puisse restaurer ce fauteuil Louis XV.
Connaîtriez-vous un antiquaire qui vende des pièces rares ?
Je cherche quelqu'un qui sache la vérité.

sources.source_text: Il cherche un artisan qui puisse restaurer ce fauteuil Louis XV.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Subjunctive after relative with superlative antecedent
grammar_rules.summary: When antecedent of qui or que is a superlative (le plus, le moins, le seul, l’unique, le premier, le dernier), subjunctive may be used.
grammar_rules.explanation: Paolo est le meilleur artisan qui vende des objets à Burano. C’est le seul marché aux puces que je connaisse dans cette ville.
restrictions: Restricted to superlative or exclusive antecedents (le plus, le moins, le seul, l'unique, le premier, le dernier)
Not used when the antecedent is an ordinary noun whose existence is certain
conditions: antecedent is superlative or exclusive
exceptions: Not used when the antecedent is an ordinary noun whose existence is certain
Restricted to superlative or exclusive antecedents (le plus, le moins, le seul, l'unique, le premier, le dernier)
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb in the relative clause agrees with its subject (the relative pronoun) in person and number.
The superlative antecedent does not itself control agreement; it only licenses the subjunctive.
transformations: Paolo est le meilleur artisan qui vende des objets à Burano.
C'est le seul marché aux puces que je connaisse dans cette ville.
C'est la seule personne qui puisse m'aider.

sources.source_text: Paolo est le meilleur artisan qui vende des objets à Burano.

grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives like premier, dernier, seul, unique, etc. trigger the subjunctive in the relative clause.
usage: Expressing a subjective evaluation or uniqueness.
restrictions: Applies only when a relative clause follows the superlative or superlative-like adjective
Not used with an ordinary adjective that conveys no uniqueness or evaluation
conditions: A superlative or a superlative-idea adjective (premier, dernier, seul, unique) modifies the antecedent.
The relative clause that follows uses the subjunctive.
exceptions: Applies only when a relative clause follows the superlative-like adjective
Not used with an ordinary adjective that conveys no uniqueness or evaluation
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with its subject in person and number after a superlative antecedent.
Adjectives such as premier, dernier, seul, unique license the subjunctive but do not affect agreement.
transformations: C'est le meilleur restaurant que je connaisse.
C'est la seule solution qui puisse marcher.
C'est l'unique personne qui sache la vérité.
C'est la pire chose qui puisse arriver.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea, such as: premier (first), dernier (last), seul (only), unique (unique), etc.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Subjunctive in relative clauses with doubt
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive may be used after relative pronouns when there is doubt about the existence or realization of the antecedent.
grammar_rules.explanation: If the existence of the person/thing is uncertain, use the subjunctive.
restrictions: Requires a relative pronoun (qui or que); it does not apply to other conjunctions
Used only when existence or realization is uncertain, not when it is certain
conditions: Doubt about existence or realization.
exceptions: Requires a relative pronoun (qui or que)
Not used when the existence or realization is certain
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with the relative pronoun subject in person and number.
Uncertainty about the existence of the antecedent does not alter agreement.
transformations: Je cherche quelqu'un qui puisse m'aider.
Y a-t-il quelqu'un qui sache la réponse ?
Je voudrais trouver quelque chose qui me plaise.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
sources.source_text: The relative pronouns qui and que can sometimes be followed by the subjunctive. If there is some doubt about the existence of someone or the possible realization of something, the subjunctive may be used after the relative pronoun.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Subjunctive with indefinite expressions (whatever, whenever, wherever, whoever)
grammar_rules.summary: The present subjunctive is used after the indefinite expressions quoi que, quel que, où que, and qui que.
grammar_rules.explanation: When English 'whatever' is followed by subject + verb, use the neuter 'quoi que' + present subjunctive. When 'whatever' is followed by a noun, use 'quel que' (agreeing in gender and number) + subjunctive of être + noun. 'Où que' expresses wherever, and 'qui que' expresses whoever, both followed by the subjunctive.
grammar_rules.formation: quoi que + subject + subjunctive verb; quel/quelle/quels/quelles que + subject + subjunctive of être + noun; où que + subject + subjunctive; qui que + subject + subjunctive
restrictions: Only the fixed expressions quoi que, quel que, où que, and qui que trigger the subjunctive
quoi que requires a following clause with subject + verb, while quel que requires the subjunctive of être + noun
quel que agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows it
conditions: The clause is introduced by quoi que, quel que, où que, or qui que.
The verb is in the present subjunctive, and quel que agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows.
exceptions: Only quoi que, quel que, où que, and qui que trigger the subjunctive
quoi que requires a clause with subject + verb, while quel que requires the subjunctive of être + noun
quel que agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows it
agreement_rules: Quel que agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows it.
grammar_rules.word_order: Indefinite expression followed by subject + verb in subjunctive.
transformations: Quoi que tu fasses, je te soutiendrai.
Quel que soit le problème, nous trouverons une solution.
Quelle que soit la décision, elle sera respectée.
Où que tu ailles, je te suivrai.
Qui que vous soyez, vous êtes le bienvenu.
common_traps: Confusing quoi que (whatever + verb) with quel que (whatever + noun).

sources.source_text: The present subjunctive is used with the indefinite expressions that are the French equivalents of whatever, whenever, wherever, and whoever.

grammar_rules.summary: Superlative is formed by preceding the comparative with the definite article; before a group, use de + definite article.
grammar_rules.explanation: To form the superlative, use le/la/les + plus/moins + adjective. When specifying the group, add de + definite article.
usage: To express the most, least, best, worst.
restrictions: The definite article must agree in gender and number with the noun
When a group is named, de + definite article is required; other prepositions are not used
Not formed with the indefinite article
conditions: The most, least, best, or worst of a quality is expressed.
The definite article precedes plus/moins plus the adjective, and de + definite article introduces the group.
exceptions: The definite article must agree in gender and number with the noun
When a group is named, de + definite article is required
Not formed with the indefinite article
agreement_rules: Article and adjective agree with noun.
grammar_rules.word_order: definite article + plus/moins + adjective + (de + definite article + group)
transformations: le plus grand
la moins chère
les plus beaux
le meilleur restaurant de la ville
definite article + plus/moins + adjective (+ de + definite article + group)
common_traps: Remember to add de + definite article after superlative when mentioning the group.

sources.source_text: To form the superlative in French, simply precede the comparative form by the definite article. Note that before naming a group or entity, the superlative is followed by de  the definite article.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir de means to take after someone.
grammar_rules.explanation: tenir de + person means to resemble or take after that person.
usage: To express resemblance to a family member.
restrictions: Only the preposition de is possible; à changes the meaning of tenir
Requires a person as complement, expressing resemblance to that person
conditions: Tenir is used with the preposition de before a person.
The meaning is resembling or taking after that person, usually a family member.
exceptions: Only the preposition de is possible; à changes the meaning of tenir
Requires a person as complement, expressing resemblance to that person
agreement_rules: Tenir agrees with its subject in person and number (elle tient de sa mère).
The preposition de is invariable and does not agree with the person mentioned.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + de + person
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + de + person?
transformations: Elle tient de sa mère.
De qui tient-elle ?
Il tient de son père.
tenir de + personne -> to take after someone
common_traps: Using à instead of de.

sources.source_text: De qui tient-elle? Whom does she take after? Elle tient de sa mère. She takes after her mother.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir à means to be attached to something or to insist on doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: When used with the preposition à, tenir means to be attached to (someone or something) or to insist on (doing something).
restrictions: Only the preposition à is possible here; de gives tenir a different meaning
The complement may be a noun, a pronoun, or an infinitive, but not a que-clause
conditions: Tenir is used with the preposition à.
The meaning is being attached to someone or something, or insisting on doing something.
exceptions: Only the preposition à is possible here; de gives tenir a different meaning
The complement may be a noun, a pronoun, or an infinitive, but not a que-clause
agreement_rules: Tenir agrees with its subject in person and number (elle tient à ses bijoux).
The preposition à is invariable and contracts only with a following article (à + les = aux).
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + à + object/infinitive
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + à + object/infinitive?
transformations: Elle tient à ses bijoux.
Ils tiennent à leurs habitudes.
Marc tient à vous voir.
tenir à + nom/infinitif -> to be attached to / to insist on
common_traps: Confusing à with de.

sources.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning. Elle tient à ses bijoux. She is attached to her jewels. Ils tiennent à leurs habitudes. They are attached to their habits. Marc tient à vous voir. Marc insists on seeing you.

grammar_rules.summary: When tout precedes the gerund, it underscores a tension or contradiction between two actions.
grammar_rules.explanation: Examples: Tout en étant un bon joueur, il ne marquait jamais de but. Tout en faisant semblant d'écouter le professeur, il jouait avec son iPod. Tout en pleurant, il riait. Tout en prétendant le contraire, elle voulait être élue.
restrictions: Only in the tout en + present participle construction; a plain gerund expresses simple simultaneity
tout is invariable in this construction and does not agree in gender or number
conditions: Tout precedes the gerund (tout en + participe présent).
The sentence underscores a tension or contradiction between two simultaneous actions.
exceptions: Only in the tout en + present participle construction; a plain gerund expresses simple simultaneity
tout is invariable in this construction and does not agree
agreement_rules: tout is invariable before the gerund, and the present participle is also invariable.
The construction shows no gender or number agreement with the subject.
transformations: Tout en étant un bon joueur, il ne marquait jamais de but.
Tout en faisant semblant d'écouter le professeur, il jouait avec son iPod.
Tout en pleurant, il riait.
Tout en prétendant le contraire, elle voulait être élue.
common_traps: do not interpret as simple simultaneity

sources.source_text: When tout precedes the gerund, it underscores a tension, a contradiction between two actions.

grammar_rules.summary: Use tu with friends, family, children, animals; use vous with strangers or to maintain distance/respect. Contemporary trend is toward familiarity among peers.
grammar_rules.explanation: Tu is informal; vous is formal or plural.
grammar_rules.formation: tu + 2nd person singular verb form / vous + 2nd person plural verb form
usage: Addressing friends, family, children, animals with tu.
Addressing strangers or showing respect with vous.
restrictions: Let the native speaker initiate first exchange with tu.
conditions: The addressee is a friend, family member, child, or animal, so tu is used.
The addressee is a stranger or someone to be treated with respect, so vous is used.
exceptions: vous is also the plural form, used for any group regardless of familiarity
The tu/vous choice varies by region, generation, and social setting, so the rule is not absolute
agreement_rules: tu takes second-person singular verb agreement; vous takes second-person plural agreement even when addressing one person politely.
The pronoun choice determines the verb form, not the real number of addressees.
grammar_rules.word_order: tu/vous + verb in the matching person form
transformations: tu -> friends, family, children, animals
vous -> strangers, or to maintain distance and respect
Tu as raison. (informal singular)
Vous avez raison. (formal or plural)
common_traps: Using tu when vous is appropriate can be perceived as rude.

sources.source_text: Use tu and its verb forms to talk to friends, family members, children, and animals. Use vous when you are addressing a stranger or someone you don’t know well, or to maintain a certain degree of distance or respect.

grammar_rules.summary: Drop -ir, add -iss- to plural forms, then add appropriate endings.
grammar_rules.explanation: For Type 1 -ir verbs, remove the -ir ending from the infinitive. In the plural forms (nous, vous, ils/elles), add -iss- before the ending. The endings are: je -is, tu -is, il -it, nous -issons, vous -issez, ils -issent.
usage: Present tense conjugation of regular -ir verbs
restrictions: Limited to -ir verbs that take -iss- in the plural; Type 2 verbs do not
The -iss- appears only in the nous, vous, and ils/elles forms
Not used for irregular -ir verbs such as sortir or partir
conditions: Verbs ending in -ir that follow this pattern
exceptions: Limited to -ir verbs that take -iss- in the plural
The -iss- appears only in the nous, vous, and ils/elles forms
Type 2 -ir verbs such as sortir do not take -iss-
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number.
The -iss- infix appears only in the plural forms (nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent).
transformations: finir -> je finis, tu finis, il finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent
choisir -> je choisis, tu choisis, il choisit, nous choisissons, vous choisissez, ils choisissent
réussir -> je réussis, tu réussis, il réussit, nous réussissons, vous réussissez, ils réussissent
stem + -is / -is / -it / -issons / -issez / -issent
common_traps: Do not forget the -iss- in plural forms.

sources.source_text: Type 1 verbs drop the -ir of the infinitive, add an -iss- to the plural form, and then insert the appropriate ending.

grammar_rules.summary: Drop -ir, add endings without -iss-; irregular.
grammar_rules.explanation: For Type 2 -ir verbs, remove the -ir ending and add the appropriate endings directly, without inserting -iss-. These verbs are irregular. Example: sortir -> je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons, vous sortez, ils sortent.
usage: Present tense conjugation of irregular -ir verbs
restrictions: Limited to irregular -ir verbs that do not take -iss-
No -iss- is inserted in the nous and vous forms
The pattern varies by verb and must be memorized
conditions: Verbs ending in -ir that do not take -iss-
exceptions: Limited to irregular -ir verbs that do not take -iss-
No -iss- is inserted in the nous and vous forms
The pattern varies by verb and must be memorized
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number.
No -iss- infix is added in the plural forms (nous sortons, vous sortez, ils sortent).
transformations: sortir -> je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons, vous sortez, ils sortent
partir -> je pars, tu pars, il part, nous partons, vous partez, ils partent
dormir -> je dors, tu dors, il dort, nous dormons, vous dormez, ils dorment
stem + -s / -s / -t / -ons / -ez / -ent (varies)
common_traps: Do not add -iss- in nous and vous forms.

sources.source_text: Type 2 -ir verbs drop the -ir of the infinitive, then add the appropriate ending, without the -iss- in the nous and vous forms.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of futur antérieur for completed future action
grammar_rules.summary: Futur antérieur expresses an action that will be completed before another future action.
grammar_rules.explanation: The futur antérieur describes an action that will take place and be completed before another future action.
grammar_rules.formation: futur simple of avoir/être + past participle
usage: to express completion before a future point
restrictions: Requires another future action or point of reference to anchor the anteriority
Not used for actions simultaneous with or later than the reference point
conditions: The action will be completed before another future action or future point.
Signal words such as d'ici, avant, quand, or dès que mark the sequence.
exceptions: Requires another future action or point of reference to anchor the anteriority
Not used for actions simultaneous with or later than the reference point
agreement_rules: The auxiliary agrees with the subject in person and number; the past participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is être.
With avoir, the past participle agrees only with a preceding direct object.
grammar_rules.word_order: quand/dès que + futur antérieur clause + main clause in futur simple
transformations: Quand j'aurai fini mes devoirs, je sortirai.
Dès que tu seras arrivé, appelle-moi.
D'ici demain, il aura terminé le projet.
common_traps: using futur simple when anteriority is intended

sources.source_text: The futur antérieur describes an action that will take place and be completed before another future action.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of futur simple for future events
grammar_rules.summary: The futur simple describes future events, as in English.
grammar_rules.explanation: As in English, the French future tense is used to describe future events.
usage: to describe future actions or states
restrictions: Not used for an action completed before a future reference point, which requires the futur antérieur
Not used for hypothetical events, which require the conditional
conditions: A future action or state is described.
Time expressions such as demain, plus tard, quand, dès que, or lorsque accompany it.
exceptions: Not used for an action completed before a future reference point, which requires the futur antérieur
Not used for hypothetical events, which require the conditional
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number; the future endings are the same for all verbs.
The negative form ne...pas surrounds the conjugated future verb without affecting agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: subject + futur simple verb + future time expression (demain, plus tard)
transformations: Demain, je passerai te voir.
Plus tard, nous recommencerons.
Quand tu arriveras, nous mangerons.

sources.source_text: As in English, the French future tense is used to describe future events.

grammar_rules.summary: Indicates a past action that happened before another past action, often with dependent clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: The plus-que-parfait expresses anteriority in the past. This anteriority can be implied or stated, and the tense is often combined with a dependent clause that clarifies the sequence.
grammar_rules.formation: avoir/être in the imparfait + past participle
usage: To express an action completed before another past action
Often used with dependent clauses introduced by quand, lorsque, parce que, car, etc.
restrictions: Requires two past actions; a single past action does not call for it
Not used when the two past actions are simultaneous, which calls for the imparfait
The action expressed must be anterior to the other past action
conditions: Anteriority between two past actions
exceptions: Requires two past actions; a single past action does not call for it
Not used when the two past actions are simultaneous, which calls for the imparfait
agreement_rules: The auxiliary agrees with the subject in person and number; with être the past participle also agrees with the subject.
With avoir, the past participle agrees only with a preceding direct object.
grammar_rules.word_order: plus-que-parfait (anterior action) + quand/lorsque/parce que + other past clause
transformations: Quand je suis arrivé, il était déjà parti.
Elle avait déjà mangé lorsque nous sommes rentrés.
Parce qu'il avait oublié son parapluie, il était mouillé.
common_traps: Using passé composé instead of plus-que-parfait for anterior action

sources.source_text: the plus-que-parfait indicates a past action that happened before another past action started. This anteriority can be implied or stated.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after expressions of doubt
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after expressions of doubt.
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like douter, ne pas croire, ne pas penser, etc. are followed by the subjunctive.
restrictions: Only with expressions of doubt or denial; affirmative croire and penser take the indicative
Requires que followed by a clause with its own subject
conditions: The main clause expresses doubt or denial (douter que, ne pas croire que, ne pas penser que).
The dependent que clause follows in the subjunctive.
exceptions: Only with expressions of doubt or denial; affirmative croire and penser take the indicative
Requires que followed by a clause with its own subject
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with its subject in person and number.
The doubt expressed in the main clause does not change agreement in the subordinate clause.
grammar_rules.word_order: expression of doubt + que + subjunctive verb
transformations: Je doute qu'il vienne.
Je ne crois pas qu'elle soit là.
Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai.
Nous doutons qu'il puisse réussir.

sources.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after expressions of doubt.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after expressions of emotion
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expressions of emotion such as regretter, être ravi, être déçu, être content, etc. are followed by que + subjunctive.
restrictions: Only with expressions of emotion followed by que; factual statements take the indicative
Requires a clause with its own subject
conditions: The main clause expresses emotion (regretter, être ravi, être déçu, être content, avoir peur).
The dependent que clause follows in the subjunctive.
exceptions: Only with expressions of emotion followed by que; factual statements take the indicative
Requires a clause with its own subject
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with its subject in person and number.
Emotion expressions such as être ravi or être déçu take their own subject agreement in the main clause.
grammar_rules.word_order: expression of emotion + que + subjunctive verb
transformations: Je suis content que tu sois là.
Elle est ravie que nous venions.
Il a peur que tu partes.
Nous sommes déçus que ce soit fini.

sources.source_text: The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing wish/desire when the subject of the main clause differs from that of the dependent clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: If the subject is the same, an infinitive is used instead. Examples: Je veux acheter... (same subject) vs Je veux que tu achètes... (different subject).
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause verb of wish + que + subjunctive clause (different subjects).
usage: Expressing wish, desire, demand, etc. with different subjects.
restrictions: Only when subjects are different; otherwise use infinitive.
conditions: Main clause subject ≠ dependent clause subject.
exceptions: With the same subject, an infinitive is used instead of a que-clause
The que-clause must have a subject different from the main clause
agreement_rules: The subjunctive verb agrees with its own subject, which differs from the main clause subject (Je veux que tu achètes).
When the subjects are the same, the infinitive replaces the clause and carries no person agreement.
grammar_rules.word_order: main clause verb of wish + que + subjunctive clause (different subjects); same subject: verb of wish + infinitive
transformations: Je veux que tu achètes cet ordinateur.
Je souhaite qu'il vienne.
Nous exigeons que vous partiez.
Elle désire que nous restions.
Je veux acheter cet ordinateur. (same subject -> infinitive)
common_traps: Forgetting to use subjunctive when subjects differ.

sources.section_title: Subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
sources.source_text: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing the notion of wish and desire. It is used when the subject of the main clause is different from the subject of the dependent clause. Compare: Je veux acheter cet ordinateur. / Je veux que tu achètes cet ordinateur.

grammar_rules.summary: On can mean one, we, they, or people in general; it can also replace a passive voice.
grammar_rules.explanation: On has multiple meanings depending on context: indefinite person, general people, informal nous, informal tu, and passive equivalent.
usage: Indefinite person: On voudrait tout réussir.
People in general: En France, on boit du vin.
Informal nous: On va au cinéma cet après-midi?
Informal tu: Alors, on se promène au lieu de faire ses devoirs!
restrictions: on is always third-person singular in agreement, even when it means 'we'
on is never used with plural verb forms
The senses 'we' and 'you' are informal and limited to spoken French
conditions: The subject is indefinite or general rather than a specific person.
On can mean one, we, they, people, an informal nous or tu, or replace the passive voice.
exceptions: on is always third-person singular in agreement, even when it means 'we'
The senses 'we' and 'you' are informal and limited to spoken French
on cannot be used with plural verb forms
agreement_rules: on always takes third-person singular verb agreement, whatever its meaning (on va, on parle).
When on informally replaces nous, the verb still stays third-person singular.
transformations: On voudrait tout réussir.
En France, on boit du vin.
On va au cinéma cet après-midi ?
Alors, on se promène au lieu de faire ses devoirs !
Ici, on parle anglais.
common_traps: Distinguish between the different meanings of on based on context.

sources.source_text: The pronoun on has several meanings.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Using -ci and -là to distinguish between two elements
grammar_rules.summary: To distinguish between two elements, add -ci (this/these) or -là (that/those) to the noun after the demonstrative adjective.
grammar_rules.explanation: The particles -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective to indicate proximity (ci) or distance (là).
usage: Making a distinction between two elements
restrictions: Only used when two elements are contrasted; a single element needs no particle
The particle attaches to the noun, not to the demonstrative adjective
-ci marks proximity and -là marks distance
conditions: Typically used when comparing two items or indicating a choice.
exceptions: Only used when two elements are contrasted; a single element needs no particle
The particle attaches to the noun, not to the demonstrative adjective
-ci marks proximity and -là marks distance
agreement_rules: -ci and -là are invariable particles; they do not agree with the noun.
The demonstrative adjective, not the particle, marks the noun's gender and number (ce livre-ci, cette maison-là).
transformations: ce livre-ci / ce livre-là
cette chemise-ci / cette chemise-là
ces chaussures-ci / ces chaussures-là
Tu préfères ce gâteau-ci ou ce gâteau-là ?
common_traps: Misplacing the particle: it is attached to the noun, not the adjective.

sources.source_text: To make a distinction between two elements, -ci and -là are added to the noun following the demonstrative adjective.

grammar_rules.summary: French often uses the pronoun on (third-person singular) to avoid the passive voice.
grammar_rules.explanation: The impersonal on construction is preferred in many cases where English would use the passive.
restrictions: Only when the agent is unspecified; if the agent matters, a passive with par is used
on requires a third-person singular verb form
conditions: The English sentence would use the passive voice.
French uses the third-person singular on with an active verb instead.
exceptions: Only when the agent is unspecified; if the agent matters, a passive with par is used
on requires a third-person singular verb form
agreement_rules: on takes third-person singular verb agreement (On parle anglais ici).
The verb agrees with on, not with the logical object of the action.
transformations: On parle anglais ici. (English is spoken here.)
On demande un serveur. (A waiter is wanted.)
On vend des fruits au marché. (Fruit is sold at the market.)

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: French often prefers to use the third-person singular form on rather than the passive voice construction.

grammar_rules.summary: devenir, prévenir, survenir, revenir are conjugated like venir.
grammar_rules.explanation: The derivatives of venir follow the same conjugation pattern as venir.
usage: To express becoming, warning, occurring, returning.
restrictions: Limited to venir and its prefixed derivatives (devenir, prévenir, survenir, revenir)
The pattern does not apply to other -ir verbs with different stems
conditions: The verb is venir or one of its derivatives (devenir, prévenir, survenir, revenir).
The tense is the present indicative, conjugated on the same pattern as venir.
exceptions: Limited to venir and its prefixed derivatives (devenir, prévenir, survenir, revenir)
The pattern does not apply to other -ir verbs with different stems
agreement_rules: Verb agrees with the subject in person and number (je viens, nous venons, ils reviennent).
Derivatives such as devenir, prévenir, revenir, and survenir keep the same agreement pattern as venir.
transformations: venir -> je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent
devenir -> je deviens, tu deviens, il devient, nous devenons, vous devenez, ils deviennent
prévenir -> je préviens, tu préviens, il prévient, nous prévenons, vous prévenez, ils préviennent
revenir -> je reviens, tu reviens, il revient, nous revenons, vous revenez, ils reviennent
survenir -> je surviens, tu surviens, il survient, nous survenons, vous survenez, ils surviennent

sources.source_text: The verb venir (to come) and its derivatives, devenir (to become), prévenir (to warn, to inform), survenir (to occur), are all commonly used verbs.

grammar_rules.summary: When qui is subject of dependent clause, the verb agrees with the noun/pronoun qui replaces.
grammar_rules.explanation: C’est moi qui lui ai vendu cette lampe. C’est toi qui es responsable. C’est vous qui avez restauré cette chaise? C’est vous qui êtes le propriétaire?
grammar_rules.formation: c'est + pronoun + qui + verb agreeing with pronoun
restrictions: Agreement is with the antecedent pronoun after qui, not with c'est
The antecedent may be a stressed pronoun (moi, toi, lui), which determines the verb person
Applies to the c'est + pronoun + qui emphasis construction
conditions: The construction is c'est + pronoun + qui.
The verb after qui agrees with that pronoun (c'est moi qui ai, c'est vous qui êtes).
exceptions: Agreement is with the antecedent pronoun after qui, not with c'est
The antecedent may be a stressed pronoun (moi, toi, lui), which determines the verb person
Applies to the c'est + pronoun + qui emphasis construction
agreement_rules: verb agrees with the pronoun after c'est
transformations: C'est moi qui lui ai vendu cette lampe.
C'est toi qui es responsable.
C'est vous qui avez restauré cette chaise ?
C'est nous qui sommes prêts.

sources.source_text: C’est moi qui lui ai vendu cette lampe.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Verbs conjugated with être in passé composé
grammar_rules.summary: A finite list of intransitive movement and state verbs use être.
grammar_rules.explanation: These verbs must be memorized; most are intransitive verbs of movement.
restrictions: finite list
conditions: The verb is on the finite list of intransitive movement and state verbs (aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, etc.).
The tense is the passé composé, and the past participle agrees with the subject.
exceptions: Some of these can use avoir when transitive (see six verbs rule)
agreement_rules: past participle agrees with subject
transformations: Il est arrivé en retard.
Elle est partie tôt.
Nous sommes allés au marché.
Ils sont nés en France.
être + participe passé (agreement with subject)
common_traps: Forgetting agreement
Confusing with avoir

grammar_rules.rule_name: Verbs followed by preposition de before infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: List of verbs requiring de before a following infinitive.
grammar_rules.explanation: These verbs are followed by de + infinitive; must be memorized.
restrictions: The preposition de is required; à is not possible with these verbs
The list must be memorized because the choice is not predictable from meaning
de becomes d' before a vowel
conditions: The main verb is one that requires de (choisir de, finir de, avoir peur de, etc.).
An infinitive follows the preposition de.
exceptions: The preposition de is required; à is not possible with these verbs
de becomes d' before a vowel
agreement_rules: The main verb agrees with its subject in person and number; the infinitive carries no agreement.
The preposition de is invariable and introduces the dependent infinitive.
transformations: accepter de partir
choisir de rester
demander de sortir
oublier de fermer
refuser d'accepter
regretter d'être parti
verb + de + infinitif
common_traps: Do not confuse with à verbs.

sources.source_text: Verbs followed by the preposition de

grammar_rules.rule_name: Verbs followed by preposition à before infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: List of verbs requiring à before a following infinitive.
grammar_rules.explanation: These verbs are followed by à + infinitive; must be memorized.
restrictions: The preposition à is required; de is not possible with these verbs
The list must be memorized because the choice is not predictable from meaning
à contracts with the definite article (au, aux) when followed by a noun
conditions: The main verb is one that requires à (apprendre à, commencer à, réussir à, etc.).
An infinitive follows the preposition à.
exceptions: The preposition à is required; de is not possible with these verbs
à contracts with the definite article (au, aux) when followed by a noun
agreement_rules: The main verb agrees with its subject in person and number; the infinitive carries no agreement.
The preposition à is invariable before an infinitive and does not contract with an article.
transformations: apprendre à nager
commencer à travailler
réussir à finir
tenir à venir
inviter à dîner
hésiter à répondre
aider à porter
verb + à + infinitif
common_traps: Do not confuse with de verbs.
