exceptions_and_traps.title: -er verbs drop -s in tu imperative
exceptions_and_traps.description: For -er verbs, the tu imperative drops the final -s of the present tense form.
related_examples: Parle!

sources.source_text: For the -er verbs, drop the -s of the present tense tu form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: -t- insertion in third person singular inversion
exceptions_and_traps.description: When forming a question by inversion with a third-person singular subject pronoun and a verb ending in a vowel, a -t- is inserted between the verb and the pronoun for pronunciation.
related_examples: Parle-t-elle russe?
Voyage-t-il souvent en Europe?

sources.source_text: If the third-person singular of a verb ends with a vowel, a -t- is inserted to facilitate the pronunciation.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Active vs passive voice
exceptions_and_traps.description: The passive voice is much more common in English than in French; French tends to use the active voice.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Le pays est envahi par les croisés.
related_examples: Le pays est envahi par les croisés.
Les croisés envahissent le pays.

sources.source_text: Be aware that the passive voice is much more common in English than in French. In French, one tends to use the active voice.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Adjective after ce (c') is always masculine singular
exceptions_and_traps.description: The demonstrative pronoun ce (c') is invariable and the adjective following ce is always masculine singular, even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.
related_examples: Cette ville en hiver! C'est si beau!
Les erreurs qu'elle a faites! C'est idiot!

sources.source_text: The adjective following ce (c') is always in the masculine even if it refers to a feminine antecedent.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Adjectives change meaning based on position
exceptions_and_traps.description: Adjectives like ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier have different meanings before or after the noun.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: un grand homme (= un homme illustre)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: un homme grand (= un homme illustre)
related_grammar_rules: Adjectives change meaning based on position

sources.source_text: Beware: Some adjectives have different meanings, depending on whether they precede or follow the noun.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Agent with par vs de
exceptions_and_traps.description: The preposition par is default, but de is used after verbs of emotion or opinion, and the agent plays a less active role.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Ce professeur est apprécié de ses étudiants.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Ce professeur est apprécié par ses étudiants.
related_examples: Ce professeur est apprécié de ses étudiants.
Ce rapport a été fait par un consultant américain.
Le voleur est suivi de ses complices.
Le voleur est suivi par la police.

sources.section_title: The agent with par and with de in the passive voice
sources.source_text: That is, when the voix passive is followed by the preposition de (rather than par), the agent plays a less active role.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Agreement in past conditional with être
exceptions_and_traps.description: In the past conditional, past participle agrees with subject when auxiliary is être, and with preceding direct object when auxiliary is avoir.
related_examples: je serais venu(e)

sources.source_text: The rules of agreement common to all compound tenses still apply.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Ambiguity of son, sa, ses
exceptions_and_traps.description: Son, sa, ses can mean either his or her. Context usually prevents ambiguity; if ambiguity exists, the sentence should be rephrased.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: sa roman (pour « son roman » quand le possesseur est une femme)
related_grammar_rules: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they modify

sources.source_text: Son, sa, ses can mean either his or hers, since they modify the noun (not the owner). The context will usually prevent any ambiguity about the identity of the owner. If there is ambiguity, the sentence needs to be rephrased for clarity.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Après requires past infinitive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use past infinitive after après, not present infinitive.
related_examples: Elle se lave les mains après avoir décortiqué les crevettes.
Gérard fait mariner la viande après avoir épluché un oignon.
Je fais la cuisine après être allé au cinéma.

sources.section_title: après + past infinitive / avant de + present infinitive
sources.source_text: One common occurrence of the infinitif passé is after the preposition après

exceptions_and_traps.title: Article change in negation
exceptions_and_traps.description: After a negated verb, un, une, des become de or d'.
related_examples: Non, je n'ai pas d'amis à Paris.

sources.source_text: Note that un, une, and des change to de or d’ when the verb is in the negative form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Article retention/dropping with ni...ni...
exceptions_and_traps.description: With ni...ni..., definite articles are retained, but indefinite and partitive articles are dropped.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il n'aime ni le café ni le chocolat. / Elle ne commande ni eau ni vin.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il n'aime ni café ni chocolat. / Elle ne commande ni de l'eau ni du vin.
related_examples: Elle ne commande ni eau ni vin.
Il n'aime ni le café ni le chocolat.

sources.source_text: When the definite article le, la, l’, les is used before the noun, the definite article remains... When the indefinite or partitive article is used... the article disappears.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Au cas où does not take subjunctive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Au cas où is followed by the conditional, not the subjunctive, despite its hypothetical meaning.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Au cas où il pleuvrait, prends un parapluie.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Au cas où il pleuve, prends un parapluie.
related_examples: Au cas où ce cadeau ne vous plairait pas, dites-le-moi.
Au cas où il aurait échoué à l'examen, on lui donnera une autre chance.
Au cas où le projet ne serait pas fini cet après-midi, appelez-moi.
Au cas où tu n'aurais pas retrouvé tes clés, Christian s'occupera de toi.

sources.source_text: The présent or passé du conditionnel are also used with the expression au cas où (in case).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Avant de requires present infinitive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use present infinitive after avant de, not past infinitive.
related_examples: Elle se lave les mains avant de décortiquer les crevettes.
Gérard fait mariner la viande avant d'éplucher un oignon.
Je fais la cuisine avant d'aller au cinéma.

sources.section_title: après + past infinitive / avant de + present infinitive
sources.source_text: the infinitif présent follows avant de

exceptions_and_traps.title: Causative vs simple faire + noun
exceptions_and_traps.description: The causative form uses faire + infinitive, not faire + noun. Example: faire faire la robe (have the dress made) vs faire la robe (make the dress).
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: faire + noun when causative is intended
related_examples: Elle fait faire la robe.
Elle fait la robe.

sources.source_text: Elle fait la robe. She is making the dress. Elle fait faire la robe. She is having the dress made.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Cities with article
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some city names include an article and must be used with it.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Le Caire, La Nouvelle-Orléans, La Havane, Le Havre, La Rochelle, Le Touquet
related_examples: Il vivait à La Havane.
Le Touquet est sa station balnéaire préférée.

sources.source_text: Cities are usually not preceded by an article. Note the following exceptions: Le Caire, La Nouvelle-Orléans, La Havane, Le Havre, La Rochelle, Le Touquet.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Color adjectives from nouns are invariable
exceptions_and_traps.description: Color adjectives that are also nouns of fruit or plants (orange, marron, safran) remain in masculine singular.
related_grammar_rules: Color adjectives from nouns are invariable

sources.source_text: Adjectives of color that are also nouns of fruit or plants generally remain in the masculine singular form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Compound color adjectives are invariable
exceptions_and_traps.description: Compound color adjectives (vert clair, gris foncé, etc.) remain in masculine singular.

sources.source_text: When two adjectives are combined to provide more specificity, both adjectives generally remain in the masculine singular form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Compound demonstrative pronouns may be derogatory
exceptions_and_traps.description: Celui-ci/celui-là (and feminine/plural forms) may carry a condescending or derogatory meaning when used to talk about a person who is not present.

sources.source_text: Note that celui-ci (celle-ci) and celui-là (celle-là) may carry a condescending or derogatory meaning when used to talk about a person who is not present. Therefore, be careful if you decide to use it to refer to a person.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Contraction of à + le/les
exceptions_and_traps.description: Remember that à + le = au and à + les = aux, but no contraction with la or l'.
related_examples: Chloé veut aller aux États-Unis.
Je vais au théâtre ce soir.

sources.source_text: Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Could for polite requests vs other uses
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use conditionnel présent of pouvoir for polite requests, not passé composé or imparfait.
related_grammar_rules: Could for future, hypothesis, suggestion, or request
related_examples: Pourrais-tu me prêter le livre dont tu m'as parlé?

sources.source_text: When could refers to an idea of the future, a hypothesis, a suggestion, or a request, the présent du conditionnel of pouvoir is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Could: unique past vs habitual past
exceptions_and_traps.description: Distinguish between a single completed past ability (passé composé) and a habitual or descriptive past ability (imparfait).
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Using imparfait for unique action or passé composé for habitual action
related_grammar_rules: Could for a unique past action
Could for habitual past or description
related_examples: En ce temps-là, les femmes ne pouvaient pas voter.
Il n'a pas pu lui parler.

sources.source_text: When could refers to a single, unique action in the past, the passé composé of pouvoir is used. When could refers to a description or a habitual action, the imparfait of pouvoir is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Depuis tense choice
exceptions_and_traps.description: Depuis with present tense indicates ongoing action to present; with imparfait indicates ongoing action to a past point. Avoid using passé composé with depuis.
related_examples: Elle prenait de la vitamine C depuis des mois quand le médecin lui a dit de prendre aussi du calcium.
Elle prend de la vitamine C depuis des mois.
Ils dînaient dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années quand ils ont décidé d'essayer le restaurant d'en face.
Ils dînent dans ce restaurant thaïlandais depuis des années.

sources.source_text: In Chapter 1, you studied depuis with the present tense. In Chapter 8, you studied depuis with the imparfait.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Devoir: obligation vs probability ambiguity
exceptions_and_traps.description: The meaning of devoir (obligation vs probability) is often determined by voice intonation and gestures.
related_examples: example_ch43_05
example_ch43_08

sources.section_title: The verb devoir (to have to, must)
sources.source_text: The voice intonation will often determine if devoir implies an obligation or a probability. For example, il doit venir ce soir, may mean he is supposed to come tonight or he must come tonight. Pay attention to intonation and gestures.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Direct vs indirect time expressions
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use direct speech time expressions when speaking directly; use indirect speech expressions when narrating or reporting.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Elle est arrivée la veille de mon anniversaire.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Elle est arrivée hier de mon anniversaire.
related_grammar_rules: Direct vs indirect speech time expressions
related_examples: Elle est arrivée la veille de mon anniversaire.

sources.source_text: If you are discussing past and future events, or telling a story, you are more likely to use an indirect style

exceptions_and_traps.title: Distinguishing imparfait and passé composé usage
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use imparfait for description, habitual action, and interrupted continuous action; use passé composé for specific completed events.

sources.source_text: While the passé composé is used to talk about an action that took place on a specific occasion in the past, the imparfait plays a different role.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Dont replaces duquel, de laquelle, etc.
exceptions_and_traps.description: In modern French, dont usually replaces duquel, de laquelle, desquels, and desquelles.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: duquel (often considered more formal or less common)
related_grammar_rules: Lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles after prepositions
related_examples: Il a besoin de ces documents.

sources.source_text: In modern French, dont usually replaces duquel, de laquelle, desquels, and desquelles.

exceptions_and_traps.title: English simple past may require French plus-que-parfait
exceptions_and_traps.description: In English, the simple past is often used for an anterior action. In French, if anteriority is present, the plus-que-parfait must be used instead of passé composé or imparfait.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: French passé composé or imparfait when anteriority is required
related_grammar_rules: English simple past vs French plus-que-parfait
related_examples: Elle a eu une réaction allergique au médicament qu'elle avait pris.
Léa a dû prendre le médicament que le médecin lui avait prescrit.

sources.source_text: Sometimes in English the French plus-que-parfait is translated as a simple tense. However, if there is any anteriority in a series of actions, the plus-que-parfait must be used in French.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Exceptions to ordinal number formation
exceptions_and_traps.description: Premier/première (first) and dernier/dernière (last) do not follow the regular -ième pattern.
related_examples: La première fois que j'ai pris l'avion, j'avais cinq ans.

sources.source_text: Premier/première (first) and dernier/dernière (last) are the exceptions.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Faire weather vs impersonal verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: Most weather descriptions use il fait + adjective, but some specific conditions use il pleut, il neige, il grêle, il bruine. Do not use faire with these verbs.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: il fait beau/froid/chaud; il pleut; il neige; il grêle; il bruine
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: il fait pleut, il fait neige, etc.
related_examples: Il fait beau.
Il pleut.

sources.section_title: The verb faire (to do, to make)
sources.source_text: A few verbs relating to the weather are used in the impersonal il form, without faire.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Family names in plural
exceptions_and_traps.description: Family names used in plural do not take -s.

sources.source_text: In French, no -s is added to a family name used in the plural. You’ll refer to Monsieur et Madame Renaud as les Renaud.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Floor numbering difference between France and America
exceptions_and_traps.description: In France, le premier étage corresponds to the American second floor. The American first or ground floor is called le rez-de-chaussée.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: premier étage = second floor (US), rez-de-chaussée = first floor (US)
related_examples: L'appartement d'Olivier est au dixième étage.

sources.source_text: In France, le premier étage corresponds to the American second floor. The American first or ground floor is called le rez-de-chaussée in France.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Forgetting agreement with être verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: Past participle must agree with subject when using être; common to forget -e/-s.
related_examples: Elle est arrivée en retard.

sources.source_text: The past participle of verbs conjugated with être agrees in gender and number with the subject.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Futur antérieur after 'si' meaning 'whether'
exceptions_and_traps.description: After 'si' meaning 'whether', futur antérieur can be used to imply a completed action. This is different from 'si' meaning 'if'.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Je me demande s'ils auront signé le contrat.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Je me demande s'ils signeront le contrat.
related_examples: Il se demande s'il aura terminé à temps.
Je me demande s'ils auront signé le contrat.
Je me demande si j'aurai tout réglé avant ce soir.

sources.source_text: The futur antérieur is also used after si, implying a completed action. Si means whether in this case.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Futur simple vs futur antérieur in dependent clauses
exceptions_and_traps.description: When both clauses are in futur simple, actions are simultaneous. To mark anteriority, use futur antérieur in the dependent clause.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Elle vous téléphonera dès qu'elle aura fini son roman.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Elle vous téléphonera dès qu'elle finira son roman. (if anteriority intended)
related_grammar_rules: Choice between futur simple and futur antérieur in dependent clauses
related_examples: Elle vous téléphonera dès qu'elle aura fini son roman.
Elle vous téléphonera dès qu'elle finira son roman.

sources.source_text: Sometimes you have a choice between the futur simple and the futur antérieur. When both clauses use the futur simple, it is implied that both actions take place simultaneously. If you want to mark an anteriority, use the futur antérieur.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Future tenses for probability
exceptions_and_traps.description: Futur simple expresses probability in present; futur antérieur expresses probability of past.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il sera distrait. (present probability) / Il aura encore brûlé le gigot. (past probability)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il aura été distrait. (futur antérieur au lieu du futur simple pour une probabilité présente)
related_grammar_rules: Futur antérieur for probability of past action
Futur simple for probability in present
related_examples: Il aura encore brûlé le gigot d'agneau!
Le professeur n'a pas demandé nos devoirs. Il sera distrait.

sources.source_text: The future tense of être and avoir is sometimes used to express probability in the present. / The futur antérieur can also express the probability of a past action.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Immediate future vs future simple
exceptions_and_traps.description: In everyday conversation, the immediate future often replaces the future simple. Learners may overuse the future simple in informal contexts.
related_grammar_rules: Immediate future as substitute for future simple
related_examples: Vous allez partir la semaine prochaine?
Vous allez prendre des vacances?
Vous partirez la semaine prochaine?
Vous prendrez des vacances?

sources.source_text: And in everyday conversation, the immediate future is often used as a substitute for the future tense (le futur simple).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Impersonal expressions: indicative vs subjunctive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some impersonal expressions take the indicative, others take the subjunctive. The lists must be memorized.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il est certain qu'il viendra. (indicative) / Il est possible qu'il vienne. (subjunctive)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il est certain qu'il vienne. (incorrect use of subjunctive after certainty expression)
related_grammar_rules: Impersonal expressions followed by the indicative
Impersonal expressions followed by the subjunctive
related_examples: Il est certain qu'il viendra ce soir.
Il est possible qu'il vienne ce soir.

sources.source_text: Let's compare the use of the indicative and the subjunctive with some impersonal expressions: Il est certain qu'il viendra ce soir. / Il est possible qu'il vienne ce soir.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular comparatives
exceptions_and_traps.description: Bon, bien, mauvais have irregular comparative forms: meilleur, mieux, pire.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Elle est plus bonne que moi.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular feminine forms
exceptions_and_traps.description: Several adjectives have irregular feminine forms (e.g., vietnamien -> vietnamienne, généreux -> généreuse).

sources.source_text: Note several irregular feminine forms of adjectives

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular imperative of être, avoir, savoir
exceptions_and_traps.description: The verbs être, avoir, and savoir have irregular imperative forms that do not follow regular patterns.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: sois, soyons, soyez / aie, ayons, ayez / sache, sachons, sachez
related_grammar_rules: Irregular imperative forms of être, avoir, savoir
related_examples: Aie plus de patience!
Sachez que je suis avec vous!
Sois sage!

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular plural nouns
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some nouns have irregular plurals that do not follow -s, -x, -aux rules.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: des bals, des genoux, des pneus, des festivals, des yeux, des bijoux
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: des bals (following -al rule would be baux, but bal is exception)

sources.source_text: Here again, you’ll find exceptions, such as: un bal des bals; un genou des genoux; un pneu des pneus; un festival des festivals; un œil des yeux; un bijou des bijoux.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular present participles (être, avoir, savoir)
exceptions_and_traps.description: Three verbs have irregular present participles: être -> étant, avoir -> ayant, savoir -> sachant. They do not follow the regular -ant rule.

sources.source_text: Three verbs have an irregular present participle: être -> étant, avoir -> ayant, savoir -> sachant.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular stem of être in imparfait
exceptions_and_traps.description: The verb être has an irregular stem ét- in the imparfait, not the expected stem from the nous present.
related_examples: j'étais
nous étions

sources.source_text: Note that the verb être has an irregular stem in the imparfait.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Irregular stems not predictable from past participle
exceptions_and_traps.description: For some irregular verbs, the passé simple stem is based on the past participle, but this is not a fixed rule; forms must be memorized.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Various irregular forms (e.g., il but, il vint)
related_grammar_rules: Some irregular passé simple stems based on past participle

sources.section_title: The passé simple of irregular verbs
sources.source_text: For some verbs the stem of the passé simple is based on the past participle, but this is not a fixed rule.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Islands with en
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some islands use en instead of à.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe
related_grammar_rules: Preposition with islands: à, aux, en

sources.source_text: Some exceptions: en Haïti, en Martinique, en Guadeloupe.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Liaison after plural subject pronouns
exceptions_and_traps.description: The final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with a following vowel sound, making a z sound.
related_grammar_rules: Conjugation of regular -er verbs in present tense

sources.source_text: The final -s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with verbs beginning with a vowel sound, making a z sound.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Masculine countries ending in -e
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some countries/states ending in -e are masculine, not feminine.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: le Mexique, le Cambodge, le Maine, le Mozambique

sources.source_text: Note that some countries and states ending in -e are masculine: le Mexique, le Cambodge, le Maine, le Mozambique.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Mille never takes -s
exceptions_and_traps.description: Mille (thousand) is invariable; never add -s.

sources.source_text: Never add an -s to mille (one thousand).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Million and milliard take -s when greater than one
exceptions_and_traps.description: Million and milliard take an -s when the number is greater than one.

sources.source_text: In French, an -s is added to million and milliard greater than un (one).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Mon, ton, son used before feminine nouns starting with vowel/mute h
exceptions_and_traps.description: The masculine singular possessive adjectives mon, ton, son are used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or a mute h instead of ma, ta, sa.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: mon amie, ton amitié, son honnêteté
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: ma amie, ta amitié, sa honnêteté
related_grammar_rules: Possessive adjectives agree with the noun they modify
related_examples: Mon amie Suzanne travaille à Rennes.
Son honnêteté est suspecte.
Ton amitié est importante.

sources.source_text: Note that the masculine singular form of the possessive adjective (mon, ton, son) is used before singular feminine nouns beginning with a vowel or a mute h.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Negation with infinitive precedes it
exceptions_and_traps.description: With infinitive, negation ne...pas precedes the infinitive and is not separated.
related_examples: Elle m'a dit de ne pas mettre d'huile.
Il a promis de ne pas ajouter trop d'ail.
Je lui ai conseillé de ne pas mettre le gâteau au four avant midi.
Je lui ai demandé de ne pas faire frire le poisson.

sources.source_text: the negation (ne… pas) does not surround the verb but rather precedes it, and is not separated.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Negative duration: use passé composé, not present
exceptions_and_traps.description: In negative sentences with depuis, the passé composé is used instead of the present tense.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il n'a pas revu sa sœur depuis dix ans.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il ne revoit pas sa sœur depuis dix ans.
related_grammar_rules: Duration with depuis, il y a... que, cela/ça fait... que
Negative duration: passé composé instead of present
related_examples: Il n'a pas revu sa sœur depuis dix ans.
Nous ne sommes pas allées à Madrid depuis dix ans.

sources.source_text: There is an important exception to the construction with depuis: In negative sentences, the passé composé is used instead of the present.

exceptions_and_traps.title: No -iss- in Type 2 -ir verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: Type 2 -ir verbs do not take the -iss- infix in plural forms, unlike Type 1 -ir verbs.
related_examples: nous sortons

sources.source_text: without the -iss- in the nous and vous forms

exceptions_and_traps.title: No future tense after 'si' in future condition
exceptions_and_traps.description: In French, neither futur simple nor futur antérieur is used after 'si' when it means 'if' introducing a future condition. Use present tense instead.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: S'il a le temps, il passera vous voir.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: S'il aura le temps, il passera vous voir.
related_grammar_rules: No futur simple after 'si' in future condition
related_examples: S'il a le temps, il passera vous voir.
Si vous pouvez, envoyez-moi votre CV avant lundi.

sources.source_text: In French, the futur antérieur is never used after si implying a future condition. Use the present instead.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Object pronouns in negative imperative
exceptions_and_traps.description: In negative imperative, object pronouns precede the verb, unlike affirmative imperative where they follow.
related_examples: Ne l'appelle pas dimanche!

sources.source_text: Note that object pronouns immediately precede the verb (following ne [n’]) in the negative imperative.

exceptions_and_traps.title: On as impersonal pronoun
exceptions_and_traps.description: The pronoun on can mean one, we, or they depending on context.

sources.source_text: The pronoun on takes on different meanings. It may mean one, we, or they depending on how it is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Partitive after être in negative
exceptions_and_traps.description: After être in negative, the partitive article remains du/de la/de l'/des instead of changing to de.
related_examples: Ce n'est pas de l'eau potable.
Ce n'est pas de la porcelaine.
Ce n'est pas du fromage de chèvre.

sources.source_text: One exception to this rule is when using the verb être (to be). In the negative, the partitive article is always used with être.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement in perfect participle with être
exceptions_and_traps.description: In the perfect participle construction (ayant/étant + past participle), the past participle agrees with the subject if the auxiliary is être. Example: étant allé(e)(s), étant parti(e)(s).
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: étant allée (feminine singular), étant partis (masculine plural)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: étant allé (without agreement for feminine subject)
related_examples: nous étant promené(e)s
nous étant retrouvé(e)s
étant allé(e)(s)
étant parti(e)(s)

sources.source_text: Note that the past participle agrees with the subject of the sentence if the verb is conjugated with être.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement with object pronouns
exceptions_and_traps.description: The past participle agrees with a preceding direct object pronoun, but never with an indirect object pronoun (including y and en).
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Le journaliste les a prises. (direct object feminine plural)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Le journaliste leur a parlés. (indirect object)
related_grammar_rules: Direct object pronouns in compound tenses
Indirect object pronouns forms and placement

sources.source_text: The past participle agrees in number and gender when the direct object precedes the verb.
the past participle never agrees with an indirect object pronoun

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement with preceding direct object
exceptions_and_traps.description: With avoir, past participle does not normally agree, but agrees with a direct object that precedes the verb.
related_examples: Il a pris la bonne décision.
Il l'a prise.

sources.source_text: In the passé composé of verbs conjugated with avoir, the past participle agrees with the direct object of the verb, but only in sentences where the direct object noun or pronoun precedes the verb.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement with preceding direct object (que)
exceptions_and_traps.description: In compound tenses, if the direct object is placed before the verb, the past participle agrees with it, including when que refers back to a direct object noun.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: la table que nous avons trouvée
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: la table que nous avons trouvé
related_grammar_rules: Past participle agreement with preceding direct object (que)
related_examples: C'est la table en marbre que nous avons trouvée au marché aux puces.

sources.source_text: In the compound tenses, if the direct object is placed before the verb, the past participle agrees in gender and number with that direct object.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Past participle agreement with être in past infinitive
exceptions_and_traps.description: For verbs conjugated with être, the past participle in the infinitif passé agrees with the subject.
related_examples: Elle lit le journal après s'être levée.
Nous nous sommes excusés d'être partis avant le dessert.

sources.source_text: for verbs conjugated with être, the past participle of the infinitif passé agrees with the subject of the sentence.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pendant vs pour for past duration
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use pendant (or omit it) for duration in the past; never use pour.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il a habité pendant cinq ans à Londres.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il a habité pour cinq ans à Londres.
related_grammar_rules: Pendant vs pour for past duration
related_examples: Il a habité pendant cinq ans à Londres.

sources.section_title: Using adverbs with the passé composé
sources.source_text: However, pour (for) is never used to talk about duration in the past.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Penser/croire: affirmative vs negative/interrogative
exceptions_and_traps.description: Affirmative penser/croire is followed by the indicative; negative/interrogative may use the subjunctive to express doubt.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable. (subjunctive, doubt)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Je crois que Daniel soit coupable. (incorrect use of subjunctive after affirmative)
related_grammar_rules: Use of subjunctive after expressions of doubt
related_examples: Je ne crois pas que Daniel est coupable.
Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable.

sources.source_text: The verbs penser (to think) and croire (to believe) in the affirmative are followed by the indicative mood. However, in the negative and interrogative, the subjunctive can be used to underline the uncertainty of the event.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Plural of cent
exceptions_and_traps.description: Cent takes -s when multiplied and not followed by another number; no -s when followed by another number.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: deux cents (200), trois cents (300); but deux cent trois (203)

sources.source_text: Add an -s to cent greater than one hundred (deux cents, trois cents), except when cent is followed by another number.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Polite request with vouloir bien
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use 'vouloir bien' in conditionnel to soften a polite request.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Est-ce que tu veux bien...? (too direct)
related_expressions: Est-ce que tu voudrais bien + infinitif ?
related_examples: Est-ce que tu voudrais bien m'aider à résoudre ce problème?

sources.source_text: Est-ce que tu voudrais bien m’aider à résoudre ce problème? Could you help me solve that problem?

exceptions_and_traps.title: Possessive adjective vs pronoun in 'un de' constructions
exceptions_and_traps.description: Contrary to English, sometimes a possessive adjective rather than a possessive pronoun is required in French, e.g., C'est un de mes collègues (not *un de les miens).
related_grammar_rules: Possessive pronouns replace noun + possessive adjective

sources.source_text: Contrary to English, sometimes a possessive adjective rather than a possessive pronoun is required in French. C'est un de vos associés? C'est un de mes collègues.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pourvu que: 'provided that' vs hope
exceptions_and_traps.description: Pourvu que can mean 'provided that' in a two-clause structure, or express hope in a single clause.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il ne démissionnera pas pourvu que le directeur lui donne une augmentation. (provided that) / Pourvu qu'il y ait un cybercafé! (hope)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Using 'provided that' in a single-clause exclamation or vice versa.
related_examples: Il ne démissionnera pas pourvu que le directeur lui donne une augmentation de salaire.
Pourvu qu'il y ait un cybercafé!

sources.source_text: Pourvu que has the sense of provided that. ... When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning. It is a handy expression, also followed by the subjunctive, that expresses hopes and desires.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Present participle agreement depends on function
exceptions_and_traps.description: The present participle agrees when used as a noun (gender/number) or adjective (with noun), but is invariable when used as a verb.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: noun: un gagnant/une gagnante; adjective: des matchs épuisants; verb: invariable (e.g., entrant)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: using adjective agreement for verb use or vice versa
related_grammar_rules: Present participle used as a noun
Present participle used as a verb
Present participle used as an adjective
related_examples: La police l'a aperçu entrant dans un laboratoire médical.
des matchs épuisants
un commentateur fascinant
un sport exigeant
une pièce amusante
Étant blessé au genou, il n'a pas pu jouer.

sources.source_text: Some participes présents can be used as nouns... Many participes présents can be used as adjectives... The participe présent can also be used as a verb. Note that when used as a verb, the present participle is invariable.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pronominal pronoun placement in imperative
exceptions_and_traps.description: In affirmative imperative, pronoun follows verb (me→moi, te→toi); in negative imperative, pronoun precedes verb.
related_examples: Lève-toi!
Ne te lève pas!

sources.source_text: The pronoun follows the verb form in the affirmative imperative; me (m’) and te (t’) become moi and toi. However, the pronoun precedes the verb in the negative imperative.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pronominal verbs: no agreement with direct object/verb following
exceptions_and_traps.description: Past participle does not agree with subject when the pronominal verb is followed by a direct object or another verb.
related_examples: Elle s'est coupé les ongles.
Elle s'est fait arracher une dent.
Elle s'est offert une nouvelle moto.

sources.section_title: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé
sources.source_text: Note that the past participle does not agree with the subject of the pronominal verb when the verb is followed by a direct object or by another verb.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pronunciation of final consonants in numbers
exceptions_and_traps.description: In cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, final consonants are pronounced; -p in sept is silent; -x in six/dix pronounced like s; before consonant-initial word, final consonant of cinq, six, huit, dix is mute.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: cinq [sɛ̃k], six [sis], sept [sɛt], huit [ɥit], neuf [nœf], dix [dis]; but mute before consonant-initial word for cinq, six, huit, dix.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Silent final consonants in all contexts.
related_grammar_rules: Pronunciation of final consonants in certain numbers

sources.source_text: Although consonants are generally silent in French, they are pronounced in the following numbers: cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix. With sept, the -p- is silent, but the final -t is pronounced. The final -x in six and dix is pronounced like an s. When the numbers cinq, six, huit, and dix are followed by a word beginning with a consonant, their final consonant is mute (silent).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Puis-je for formal inversion
exceptions_and_traps.description: In formal inversion, the first-person singular of pouvoir becomes 'puis-je' instead of 'peux-je'.
related_examples: Puis-je vous aider?

sources.source_text: When asking permission with inversion in formal style, the first-person singular of pouvoir takes a different form. Puis-je vous aider?

exceptions_and_traps.title: Quatre-vingts loses -s before another number
exceptions_and_traps.description: Quatre-vingts has an -s when used alone (80), but the -s drops when followed by another number (e.g., quatre-vingt-un).

sources.source_text: Note that quatre-vingts has an -s. But once you attach another number to quatre-vingts, the -s will drop.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Que becomes qu' before vowel
exceptions_and_traps.description: The -e of que is dropped before a vowel sound, becoming qu'.
related_examples: Les articles qu'il vend sont chers.

sources.source_text: In the following sentences, note that the -e of que is dropped before a vowel (qu’).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Qui as object: subject comes between qui and verb
exceptions_and_traps.description: When qui is the object of the verb in the dependent clause, a subject noun or pronoun comes between qui and the verb form.
related_grammar_rules: Qui as object of verb with intervening subject
related_examples: Je ne sais pas qui il est.

sources.source_text: Note the following sentences where qui is the object of the verb in the dependent clause. In this case, a subject noun or pronoun comes between qui and the verb form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Qui cannot be used with parmi
exceptions_and_traps.description: Qui cannot be used with the preposition parmi (among). Use parmi lesquels/lesquelles instead.
related_grammar_rules: Lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles after prepositions

sources.source_text: Note that qui cannot be used with the preposition parmi (among).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Reciprocal verbs: no agreement with indirect object
exceptions_and_traps.description: For reciprocal pronominal verbs, if the reciprocal pronoun is an indirect object, the past participle does not agree.
related_examples: Ils se sont téléphoné.
Ils se sont écrit de longues lettres.
Vous vous êtes parlé au téléphone.

sources.section_title: Pronominal verbs in the passé composé
sources.source_text: When reciprocal verbs take an indirect object in French, the past participle does not agree.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Reflexive passive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Pronominal verbs can express passive meaning, e.g., se dire, se traduire, se voir, se boire.
related_examples: Comment ça se traduit?
Le vin blanc se boit frais.
Ça ne se dit pas.
Ça se voit.

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: In Chapter 6, you studied one type of pronominal verb called the passive pronominal. This construction is another example of the voix passive.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Savoir in conditional not literal
exceptions_and_traps.description: In formal French, savoir in the present conditional is equivalent to pouvoir, not 'would know'.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Je ne saurais vous répondre. (I cannot answer you.)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Je ne saurais pas la réponse. (I wouldn't know the answer.)
related_grammar_rules: Savoir in present conditional equivalent to pouvoir
related_examples: Je ne saurais vous dire combien j'apprécie votre geste.
Je ne saurais vous répondre.

sources.source_text: In formal French, savoir in the présent du conditionnel is the equivalent of pouvoir (can, to be able to) in the present or the simple future.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Savoir vs. Connaître
exceptions_and_traps.description: Savoir is used for knowing facts or knowing how to do something; it can be followed by an infinitive or clause. Connaître means to be acquainted with and is always followed by a direct object, never a clause.
related_examples: Elle connaît bien Paris.
Elle sait jouer du piano.

sources.source_text: When learning the verb savoir, you also need to become acquainted with the verb connaître, in order to understand when to use one or the other. Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, to be familiar with. It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Should vs should have
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use conditionnel présent of devoir for present advice, conditionnel passé for past advice/regret.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Using présent of devoir for past advice
related_examples: Elle devrait se détendre un peu.
Tu aurais dû lui demander des explications.

sources.source_text: When should means ought to, the conditionnel (présent or passé) is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Silent endings in -er verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: The -e, -es, and -ent endings of regular -er verbs are silent in pronunciation.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: ils parlent [il paʁl] (la terminaison -ent est muette)
related_grammar_rules: Conjugation of regular -er verbs in present tense

sources.source_text: The -e, -es, and -ent endings of the verbs are all silent.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Some French verbs omit preposition even when English requires one
exceptions_and_traps.description: Verbs like attendre (wait for), abandonner (give up), écouter (listen to), entrer (walk in) do not take a preposition in French.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: attendre le train, écouter la conférence
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: attendre pour le train, écouter à la conférence
related_grammar_rules: French verbs without preposition where English requires one
related_examples: Elle attend le train.
Il a abandonné le projet.
Nous écoutons la conférence.
Soudain, ils sont entrés.

sources.section_title: Verbs not followed by a preposition
sources.source_text: In some cases, a French verb does not need a preposition even though its English equivalent requires one.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Special masculine forms before vowel
exceptions_and_traps.description: Certain adjectives (fou, vieux, nouveau, beau) have special masculine singular forms before a vowel (fol, vieil, nouvel, bel).

sources.source_text: Note the special forms of these adjectives when they precede a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel

exceptions_and_traps.title: Spelling change for -cer and -ger verbs in passé simple
exceptions_and_traps.description: Verbs ending in -cer use a cedilla (ç) and verbs ending in -ger add an extra -e- when the passé simple ending begins with -a.
related_grammar_rules: Spelling changes for -cer and -ger verbs in passé simple
related_examples: Elle prononça un discours.
Il partagea sa fortune.

sources.source_text: When the passé simple ending starts with -a, use the cedilla (ç) for verbs ending in -cer and add an extra -e- for verbs ending in -ger.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Spelling changes in imparfait
exceptions_and_traps.description: Verbs with spelling changes in the nous present (e.g., manger, commencer) do not take the extra e or ç in the nous and vous forms of the imparfait.
related_examples: nous nagions
nous protégions

sources.source_text: The extra e or the ç are not needed in the nous and vous forms of the imparfait.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Spelling changes with -cer and -ger verbs in present participle
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some -cer and -ger verbs change spelling when forming the present participle: -cer becomes -çant (e.g., commencer -> commençant), and -ger becomes -geant (e.g., manger -> mangeant).

sources.source_text: Some spelling changes occur with some -cer and -ger verbs: commencer -> commençant, influencer -> influençant, manger -> mangeant, nager -> nageant.

exceptions_and_traps.title: State verbs: imparfait vs passé composé meaning change
exceptions_and_traps.description: Verbs like être, avoir, penser, croire, savoir, espérer, sembler, paraître tend to be used in imparfait for states; in passé composé they may indicate a specific change or event.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il semblait déprimé (state) vs Tout à coup il a semblé comprendre (change)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Tout à coup, il semblait comprendre la situation.
related_grammar_rules: Imparfait vs passé composé with state verbs
related_examples: Il semblait déprimé.
Immédiatement, j'ai su qu'il était innocent.
Je savais qu'il avait raison.
Tout à coup il a semblé comprendre la situation.

sources.section_title: The imparfait versus the passé composé
sources.source_text: However, when these verbs are used in the passé composé, they may take on a different meaning.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Subjunctive after relative pronoun with doubt/superlative
exceptions_and_traps.description: The subjunctive may be used after a relative pronoun if there is doubt about existence or after superlative antecedents.
related_grammar_rules: Subjunctive after relative pronoun with doubt
Subjunctive after relative with superlative antecedent
related_examples: Il cherche un artisan qui puisse restaurer ce fauteuil Louis XV.
Paolo est le meilleur artisan qui vende des objets à Burano.

sources.source_text: The relative pronouns qui and que can sometimes be followed by the subjunctive.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Tenir à vs tenir de
exceptions_and_traps.description: tenir à means to be attached to or insist on; tenir de means to take after. They are easily confused.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: using à instead of de or vice versa
related_examples: Elle tient de sa mère.
Elle tient à ses bijoux.

sources.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning.

exceptions_and_traps.title: The -i of qui is never dropped
exceptions_and_traps.description: Unlike que, qui never loses its final -i before a vowel sound.
related_examples: Nous félicitons l'artiste qui a pris cette photo.

sources.source_text: Note that the -i of qui is never dropped in front of a vowel sound.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Tout + gerund expresses contradiction, not just simultaneity
exceptions_and_traps.description: When tout precedes the gerund, it underscores tension or contradiction between two actions, not simple simultaneity.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Tout en étant un bon joueur, il ne marquait jamais de but.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Interpreting as simple simultaneity: 'While being a good player' without contradiction.
related_examples: Tout en faisant semblant d'écouter le professeur, il jouait avec son iPod.
Tout en pleurant, il riait.
Tout en prétendant le contraire, elle voulait être élue.
Tout en étant un bon joueur, il ne marquait jamais de but.

sources.source_text: When tout precedes the gerund, it underscores a tension, a contradiction between two actions.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Tu vs vous
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use tu for friends, family, children, animals. Use vous for strangers, people you don't know well, or to maintain distance/respect.

sources.source_text: Use tu to talk to friends, family members, children, and animals. Use vous when you are addressing a stranger, someone you don't know well, or to maintain a certain degree of distance or respect.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Use que clause when subjects differ
exceptions_and_traps.description: If the subject of the first verb and the infinitive differ, use que + subordinate clause instead of infinitive.
related_examples: J'espère qu'elle obtiendra ce poste.
Tu veux qu'il apprenne ce métier.

sources.source_text: When the subjects are different, a dependent clause introduced by que is required.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Using on instead of passive
exceptions_and_traps.description: French often prefers the pronoun on to avoid the passive voice.
related_examples: Ici, on parle anglais.
On vous demande au téléphone.

sources.section_title: Avoiding the passive voice in French
sources.source_text: French often prefers to use the third-person singular form on rather than the passive voice construction.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Using present tense with depuis vs English
exceptions_and_traps.description: In English, past tense or present perfect is often used, but French uses present tense with depuis.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: J'habite à Paris depuis cinq ans.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: J'ai habité à Paris depuis cinq ans.

sources.section_title: One more use of the present tense: depuis
sources.source_text: Note that in English, the past tense is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Using y/en for people
exceptions_and_traps.description: Y and en replace inanimate objects. For people, use disjunctive pronouns after the preposition.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: J'en parle (when referring to a person).
related_grammar_rules: Disjunctive pronouns with verbs taking à/de + person

sources.source_text: Disjunctive pronouns are used with certain verbs when the indirect object is a person.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Verbs with être or avoir (six verbs)
exceptions_and_traps.description: Sortir, rentrer, monter, descendre, passer, retourner use avoir when transitive; meaning changes.
related_grammar_rules: Verbs with avoir or être (six verbs)
related_examples: Elle a descendu les poubelles.
Elle a rentré les géraniums dans le salon.
Elle a retourné l'omelette.
Elle a sorti la voiture du garage.
Elle est descendue au rez-de-chaussée.
Elle est rentrée de vacances hier.
Elle est sortie avec des amis.
Ils ont monté les malles au grenier.
Ils sont montés en haut de la Tour Eiffel.
J'ai passé trois semaines à Tokyo.
Je suis passée devant les Galeries Lafayette.
Je suis retournée à Venise pour la troisième fois.

sources.section_title: Verbs conjugated with avoir or être
sources.source_text: Six verbs among those conjugated with être in the passé composé (sortir, rentrer, monter, descendre, passer, retourner) are conjugated with avoir and follow the avoir agreement when a direct object follows the verb. In these cases, the meaning of the verb has changed.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Vouloir only in vous imperative
exceptions_and_traps.description: The verb vouloir is used only in the vous imperative form: veuillez.
related_examples: Veuillez signer le contrat.

sources.source_text: The irregular verb vouloir (to want) is used only in the vous imperative form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Would: repeated past vs specific past refusal
exceptions_and_traps.description: Use imparfait for repeated past actions; use passé composé of vouloir (negative) for specific past refusal.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Je lisais (repeated) / Il n'a pas voulu (refusal)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Using conditionnel for repeated past or imparfait for refusal
related_examples: Nous leur avons demandé de nous accorder un peu de temps; ils n'ont pas voulu le faire.
Quand j'étais étudiant, je lisais les journaux tous les jours.

sources.source_text: When would refers to a repeated action in the past, the imparfait is used. When would refers to a specific action in the past, the passé composé of vouloir is used.

exceptions_and_traps.title: ce vs cet before vowel or mute h
exceptions_and_traps.description: The demonstrative adjective ce adds a -t before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or a mute h, becoming cet.
related_grammar_rules: Demonstrative adjectives agree in gender and number

sources.source_text: Note that the demonstrative adjective ce adds a -t before a masculine singular noun that starts with a vowel or a mute h (cet appartement, cet arbre).

exceptions_and_traps.title: croire à (something abstract) vs croire en (person/God)
exceptions_and_traps.description: 'Croire à' is used for believing in abstract concepts (magic, progress), while 'croire en' is used for faith in a person or God.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: croire à + abstract; croire en + person/God

sources.source_text: Il ne croit pas à la magie. Crois-tu en Dieu?

exceptions_and_traps.title: finir de (finish doing) vs finir par (end up doing)
exceptions_and_traps.description: 'Finir de' means to complete an action; 'finir par' means to eventually do something after a delay or hesitation.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: finir de + infinitive; finir par + infinitive
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: J'ai fini par manger. (au lieu de : J'ai fini de manger.)

sources.source_text: J’ai fini de manger. Il a fini par lui dire la vérité.

exceptions_and_traps.title: jouer à (game) vs jouer de (instrument)
exceptions_and_traps.description: The preposition changes the meaning: 'jouer à' is used for games and sports, while 'jouer de' is used for musical instruments.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: jouer à + game; jouer de + instrument
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: jouer de + game; jouer à + instrument

sources.source_text: Marie et Émile jouent aux échecs. Thierry joue de la guitare.

exceptions_and_traps.title: manquer (miss) vs manquer de (lack)
exceptions_and_traps.description: Without preposition, 'manquer' means to miss (an event). With 'de', it means to lack something.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: J'ai manqué du cours. (au lieu de : J'ai manqué le cours.)

sources.source_text: J’ai manqué le cours. Cette pièce manque d’air.

exceptions_and_traps.title: manquer à quelqu'un (to be missed by someone)
exceptions_and_traps.description: The French construction 'manquer à quelqu'un' means 'to be missed by someone'; the subject and object are reversed compared to English.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Je te manque (if meaning 'I miss you')

sources.source_text: Tu me manques. I miss you (i.e., you are lacking to me)

exceptions_and_traps.title: être à vs possessive pronoun for possession
exceptions_and_traps.description: The most common way of expressing possession is être à + disjunctive pronoun. Possessive pronouns are used to stress ownership or identify different items of similar nature.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Cette valise est à moi. (common) / C'est le mien. (stress)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Cette valise est à je. (au lieu de : Cette valise est à moi.)
related_grammar_rules: Expressing possession with être à + disjunctive pronoun/noun
Possessive pronouns replace noun + possessive adjective

sources.source_text: Remember that the most common way of expressing possession is by using être à + the disjunctive pronoun. When one wants to stress the ownership or identify different items of a similar nature, the possessive pronoun is used.

sources.source_text: Vous voulûtes lui faire un compliment.

unresolved_items.reason_uncertain: Appears inside exercise 16·1; possibly a collocation but not explicitly taught.

sources.source_text: Il y a cinquante kilomètres d'ici à Paris. It's fifty kilometers from here to Paris.
